translations.tangshi-300-1: A lone wild swan comes in from the sea; it does not deign to look at the palace moat. Sideways it spies a pair of kingfishers, nesting in the Triple-Pearl Tree. Perched high on that precious bough, do they never fear the golden pellets of the hunt? Fine robes invite people's fingers; soaring too high, one provokes even the envy of the gods. Now I roam the boundless dark on high—what is there for the archer to covet?
translations.tangshi-300-2: Orchid leaves flourish in spring; osmanthus blossoms gleam white in autumn. Each thrives in its own season, making the season itself a festival. Who would have thought the recluse of the woods would love them at a mere breath of their scent? Plants and trees keep to their own true nature—they never ask to be plucked by a fair hand.
translations.tangshi-300-3: The recluse returns to sleep alone; lingering cares wash away into a solitary clarity. I hold this poem up to the high-flying bird, asking it to carry my feelings far away. All day I cherish an empty longing—who can be moved by such perfect sincerity? The flying and the sunken are parted by nature's law; what can comfort my earnest heart?
translations.tangshi-300-4: South of the river grow red oranges, still green in their groves through the winter. Surely it is not merely the warmth of the soil—they keep a heart that endures the cold. They are fit to be offered to honored guests, yet deep barriers keep them from reaching the court. Fate is only what one encounters; its cycles cannot be traced. People speak only of planting peach and plum—but does this tree give no shade?
translations.tangshi-300-5: At dusk I come down from the blue-green mountain, the mountain moon following me home. I look back at the path I came by, veiled in dusk-blue haze. Together we reach a farmstead, where a child opens the wicker gate. Green bamboo leads into a hidden path; blue vines brush my traveler's robes. Joyfully we find our rest, and for a while we pass the wine cup. We sing long to the wind in the pines until the song ends and the river stars grow thin. I am drunk and you are merry—blissfully, together we forget all worldly schemes.
translations.tangshi-300-6: A pot of wine among the flowers; I drink alone with no companion. I raise my cup to invite the bright moon—and with my shadow we become three. The moon does not understand drinking; my shadow only trails my body. For now they keep me company, moon and shadow, for pleasure must be seized while spring lasts. I sing and the moon sways; I dance and my shadow scatters. Awake we share our joy; drunk, each goes his own way. Let us pledge an eternal friendship without feeling, to meet again far beyond the Milky Way.
translations.tangshi-300-7: The Yan grass is like green silk; the Qin mulberry bends low with its green branches. The day you long for home is the day my heart breaks. Spring wind, we were never acquainted—why do you slip into my silk curtains?
translations.tangshi-300-8: O Great Peak, what can I say? Its green stretches endless across Qi and Lu. Nature has gathered all wonders here; its light and shade split dawn from dusk. Risen clouds swell within my breast; I strain my eyes to watch the birds fly home. The day will come when I climb to its very summit and see all mountains small below.
translations.tangshi-300-9: In life we seldom meet—our comings and goings like Shen and Shang, stars that never share the sky. What evening is this evening, that we share this lamplight? Our vigorous years lasted so briefly; our temples have gone grey. Of the friends I ask after, half are ghosts, and the cry of it burns my heart. Who would have thought that after twenty years I would again climb your hall? When we parted you were unmarried; now sons and daughters stand in a row. Smiling, they honor their father's old friend and ask where I have come from. Before the questions and answers are done, you send the children to lay out wine and millet. In the night rain we cut fresh chives; the new-cooked rice is mixed with yellow grain. You say how rare such meetings are and drain ten cups in one go. Ten cups and still not drunk—for I feel deeply the kindness of an old friend. Tomorrow the mountains will stand between us; the affairs of the world, both yours and mine, vast and uncertain.
translations.tangshi-300-10: In all the age there was a beauty of matchless grace, dwelling in solitude in an empty valley. She says she was born to a good family, now fallen to live among the weeds and trees. In those years when Guanzhong fell into rebellion, her brothers were all slaughtered. What good were their high offices? They could not even gather in her kin. The world despises families in decline; all affairs turn as swiftly as a candle in the wind. Her husband was a fickle man, his new bride fair as jade. Even the acacia knows the hour to close its leaves; mandarin ducks never sleep alone. He sees only the new bride's laughter—how could he hear the old wife weep? The spring water is clear in the hills, once it leaves the hills it turns muddy. Her maid returns from selling her pearls; together they pull vines to patch the thatched roof. She picks flowers but does not put them in her hair; she gathers cypress leaves by the double handful. In the cold the green of her sleeves is thin; at sunset she leans against the tall bamboo.
translations.tangshi-300-11: Parted by death, we swallow our sobs at once; parted in life, the ache is endless. The land south of the river is a miasmic place; of the exile there comes no word. That you entered my dream shows how constantly I think of you. But you are caught in the net of the law—how could you have wings? I fear it is not the soul of your living self; the road is too far to be measured. Your spirit comes where the maple woods are green; it returns through the darkness of the mountain passes. The sinking moon floods the roof beams; I still half-believe it lights your face. The waters are deep, the waves wide—do not let the dragons catch you.
translations.tangshi-300-12: Floating clouds drift all day long; the wanderer, long absent, never comes. Three nights running I have dreamed of you—the closeness of it shows the depth of your care. In the dreams you always leave too soon, in distress, saying the journey was hard. The rivers and lakes are full of storms; your boat, you fear, may capsize. As you went out the gate you scratched your white head, as though bearing a lifetime's unfulfilled ambitions. Officials' caps and canopies crowd the capital, yet this man alone is worn and wasted. Who says the net of heaven is wide? Growing old, his own body is caught in it. A fame lasting a thousand autumns—that is a lonely affair after one's death.
translations.tangshi-300-13: I dismount and offer you wine, asking where you are bound. You say life has not gone your way, and you will go home to rest at the edge of South Mountain. Only go—and ask no more. The white clouds are endless there.
translations.tangshi-300-14: In this enlightened age none stay in hiding; men of talent all come to serve. So even a recluse of East Mountain could not keep gathering ferns. Having reached the capital, the Golden Gate stands far—yet who says my way was wrong? You crossed the Huai and the Yangtze in the Cold-Food season, stitching spring clothes in Luoyang. Wine is set along the Chang'an road, but our kindred hearts must part. Soon you will row your cassia-wood boat, and before long brush the wicker door of home. Distant trees will escort the departing traveler; the lone city stands against the setting sun. My counsel was simply not accepted—do not say that true friends are few.
translations.tangshi-300-15: They say when you enter Yellow Flower Vale you always follow the Green Creek along. It winds with the mountains in a myriad turns, yet the whole journey is less than a hundred li. Its voice clamors among the scattered rocks; its colors rest still in the deep pines. It ripples past water chestnut and waterweed, clear and calm, mirroring the reeds. My heart has always been at ease, quiet as this clear stream. Let me stay here on the great flat rock, and end my days fishing.
translations.tangshi-300-16: Slanting sunlight falls on the village lanes; in the humble alleys cattle and sheep come home. An old man, thinking of his herd boy, leans on his staff by the wicker gate. Pheasants call as the wheat comes into ear; the silkworms sleep as the mulberry leaves grow thin. Farmers shoulder their hoes, pausing to greet each other with lingering talk. Before this scene I envy their leisure and ease, and sadly I chant the old song, 'Oh, to go home, to go home.'
translations.tangshi-300-17: The world prizes beauty—how long could Xishi stay obscure? In the morning a girl washing silk by the Yue stream, by evening a consort in the Wu palace. In her lowly days was she any different from the crowd? Only when she grew noble did all see how rare she was. Court favor deepened her loveliness; the lord's love settled all rights and wrongs. The silk-washing companions of those days could not ride home in her carriage. Let me tell the neighbor's daughter: how can you hope to win favor by knitting your brows in imitation?
translations.tangshi-300-18: In the white clouds of North Mountain, the recluse delights in his own contentment. Gazing toward each other, I climb the hill for the first time, my heart following the wild geese until they vanish. Melancholy rises with the thin dusk; the mood comes from the clear autumn air. From time to time I see villagers returning, walking the sands, resting at the ferry. Trees at the sky's edge look like shepherd's purse; the isle by the river is like a moon. When will you come with wine, to get drunk with me at the Double-Ninth?
translations.tangshi-300-19: The mountain light suddenly sets in the west; the pond moon rises slowly in the east. Loosening my hair, I take the night's coolness, lying at ease by the open window. The lotus wind brings its fragrance; bamboo dew drips with clear, faint sounds. I would take up my singing lute to play—how I regret there is no kindred soul to hear it. Moved by this, I think of my old friend, whom I long for in dreams till midnight.
translations.tangshi-300-20: The setting sun crosses the western ridge; the valley ravines are suddenly dark. The moon rises through the pines, bringing the night's cool; the wind in the springs fills the air with clear sound. The woodcutters have all gone home; the misty birds settle to roost. My friend had promised to spend the night here—I wait with my lone lute along the vine-covered path.
translations.tangshi-300-21: Reclining in the southern studio, I draw the curtain—the moon has just emerged. Its clear light washes the waters and trees, rippling and spreading across the window. Slowly it waxes and wanes; clear and calm, it outlasts all ages. My fair friend stands by the river's bank; on this night he must be chanting in bitter homesickness. A thousand miles lie between us—what can be done?—but the breeze carries the scent of orchids and pollia to him.
translations.tangshi-300-22: A single thatched hut on the summit, a climb of thirty li straight up. I knock—no servant answers; peering in I see only a desk and bench. If he has not gone out driving his covered cart, he must be fishing by the autumn river. Missing each other, we never meet; to my effort all I have is vain admiration. The grass is fresh in the recent rain; the sound of pines comes through the evening window. In this moment, attuned to such secluded stillness, my heart and ears are fully cleansed. Though we never shared the host's courtesy of meeting, I have grasped the truth of pure quietude. My zest spent, I start down the mountain—why must I wait for that man?
translations.tangshi-300-23: My quiet intent never breaks off; from here I drift wherever I chance to go. The evening wind blows my boat along a flowery path into the stream's mouth. With nightfall it turns into the western ravine; beyond the mountains I watch the Southern Dipper. Mist over the pool billows and drifts; the forest moon sinks low behind me. Let the affairs of life spread vast and vague—I wish only to be an old man with a fishing pole.
translations.tangshi-300-24: The clear creek runs deep beyond measure; over his hidden dwelling floats a single cloud. Through the pines a thin moon shows; its clear light, it seems, shines still for you. In the thatched pavilion, flower shadows sleep; in the herb garden, moss patterns spread. I too would bid the world farewell and join the phoenixes and cranes of West Mountain.
translations.tangshi-300-25: The pagoda rises as if surging forth, soaring alone as high as the palaces of heaven. Climbing it, I seem to leave the world below; the stairway coils through empty air. Towering, it presses down on the divine land; its majesty seems the work of spirits. Its four corners block the white sun; its seven storeys touch the blue sky. Looking down I point to the high-flying birds; stooping, I hear the wind's alarm. The linked mountains roll like waves, rushing eastward as if at court. Green locusts line the imperial road; how delicate the palace halls! Autumn comes sweeping from the west, bleak across all the land. Over the northern heights of the Five Tombs, for ten thousand ages the green haze lies. The pure truth is plain to be grasped; the supreme cause has long been my faith. I swear I will hang up my official's cap and leave, for the Way offers boundless sustenance.
translations.tangshi-300-26: [Preface:] In the guimao year, bandits from the Western Plains entered Daozhou, burning, killing and looting, and left only when nearly everything was gone. The next year the bandits attacked Yongzhou and took Shao, but they withdrew without touching the borders of this prefecture—was that because we had the strength to resist them? Rather, they pitied us, wounded as we were. Yet what makes the officials so relentless in their exactions? I therefore write this poem to show the magistrates. In years of peace I dwelt in mountain forests for twenty years, springs at my doorstep and ravines before my gate. The land tax came at a fixed season, and I slept till the sun was high. Then suddenly the times turned; for several years I served with the army myself. Now I govern this prefecture, and the mountain tribes riot again. The city is small, so the bandits did not massacre it; the people are poor, and they pitied them as pitiful. That is why the neighboring lands fell, while this prefecture alone survived whole. The envoy carries the king's command—yet is he not worse than the bandits? Those who exact the levies press the people like fire upon a fry. Who can cut short people's lives to make himself a worthy official of the age? I would lay down my credentials, take up a pole and punt my own boat, move my family where fish and barley grow, and grow old by the rivers and lakes.
translations.tangshi-300-27: Armed guards stand rank on rank with painted halberds; in the quiet chamber incense smoke hangs still. A sea storm arrives; coolness spreads through the pavilions by the pond. My oppressive illness nearly dissolves, and honored guests again fill the hall. I am ashamed of my lofty dwelling, for I have not seen my people live in ease. Once the mind grasps a truth, right and wrong disperse; nature at peace, all formalities are forgotten. Rich fare is forbidden in this season—fortunate we may taste the vegetables and fruit. Bending, I drink a cup of wine; lifting my head, I listen to verses of gold and jade. The spirit rejoices, the body grows light; my intent seems to ride the wind aloft. In Wu the arts and letters flourish; assembled talents abound like waters today. Then I know what a great prefecture is—not merely strength in wealth and tribute.
translations.tangshi-300-28: Mournfully I leave those I love dearly; drifting, I enter the mist and smoke. The returning boat is bound for Luoyang; over the Guangling trees, a temple bell fades. This morning we part here—where shall we meet again? Human affairs are a boat upon the waves; how can it hold its course against the swirling current?
translations.tangshi-300-29: This morning the prefecture studio is cold, and I suddenly think of the guest in the mountains. He gathers brushwood at the stream bottom and returns to cook his plain white stones. I would take a gourd of wine to comfort him on this stormy evening, but fallen leaves blanket the empty hills—where would I find his tracks?
translations.tangshi-300-30: A traveler came from the east, his clothes carrying the rain of Baleng. I asked what brought him here: he has gone to the hills to buy an axe. In the dim light the flowers are just opening; the swallows, flying high, have newly hatched their young. When we parted yesterday, it was still last year—now spring is here, and a few more threads of white mark my temples.
translations.tangshi-300-31: Furled sails linger at the Huai town; the moored boat draws near a lonely post station. Vast winds rise, rippling the waves; in the dim gloom the sun sinks at dusk. People go home as the mountain town darkens; geese descend onto the white reed-isles. Alone at night I remember the Qin passes, a traveler who hears the bell and cannot sleep.
translations.tangshi-300-32: Hemmed in all year within the official quarters, I go out to the suburbs into the open clarity of dawn. The willows scatter in the mild wind; the green hills ease my troubled thoughts. Nestled among the shrubs I rest as I please; along the stream I wander back and forth. In the light rain the fragrant fields are misted; where is the spring dove calling? My heart delights in this seclusion, yet time and again my duties hold me back; bound to my work, my steps stay hurried. In the end I will leave this and build my hut here—for then, I hope, I may truly follow Tao Yuanming.
translations.tangshi-300-33: All day long my heart is heavy, and the journey stretches on and on. Today my daughter departs, going up the great river in a light boat. Since your childhood, bereft of your mother, my care for you has grown all the more tender. Your younger sister was raised by her elder; now, parting, the two of you weep without end. Facing this, my own heart knots in sorrow, but duty calls you on—I cannot keep you. Brought up without a mother's teaching within, you go to serve a mother-in-law—that is my worry. Fortunately you are entrusted to a good family, where kindness and care should leave you blameless. Frugality is truly to be honored; why must a dowry be complete? In filial reverence keep the wife's way; in bearing and bearing-with, follow your lord's ways. We part this very morning—when again shall I see you? In idle hours I first sought to console myself; faced with the feeling, suddenly I cannot hold it in. Coming home I look at your little sister, and tears stream down along my cap-strings.
translations.tangshi-300-34: I draw water from the well to rinse my teeth in the cold, and clear my mind, brushing the dust from my robe. At leisure I take up the palm-leaf scripture and step out of the eastern studio to read. The world chases after traces and never grasps the true source. I hope to reach the words the ancients left behind in dark meditation, but how can my cultivated nature ever ripen? The monk's courtyard is still; moss colors merge into the deep bamboo. The sun rises over remnants of mist and dew; the green pines look freshly bathed. Serene, beyond all speech, the joy of awakening fills the heart—self-sufficient and complete.
translations.tangshi-300-35: Long burdened by the trappings of office, I am fortunate in this exile to the southern tribes. At ease I keep company with farming neighbors; by chance I seem a wanderer of woods and hills. At dawn I plow, turning dewy grass; at night my boat bumps along the stream over stones. Coming and going I meet no one, singing long under the boundless blue of Chu sky.
translations.tangshi-300-36: Cicadas sing in the empty mulberry woods along the Xiaoguan road in the eighth month. Out beyond the frontier and back in again, everywhere yellow reed-grass. The men of You and Bing have always grown old on the battlefields. Do not imitate the wandering knights who only boast of their fine purple horses.
translations.tangshi-300-37: Watering the horses as we cross the autumn stream, the water is cold, the wind cuts like a knife. On the level sands, the sun not yet set, dimly we see Lintao. In the battles at the Long Wall of old, all said their ardor ran high. Yellow dust covers ancient and modern alike; white bones lie scattered among the wormwood.
translations.tangshi-300-38: The bright moon rises over the Tianshan, between the vastness of cloud and sea. The long wind, ten thousand leagues, blows past the Jade Gate Pass. The Han army marched down the Baideng road; the Hu watch the shore of Qinghai Bay. These lands have been battlegrounds since time began—no one who went there ever returned. The garrison soldiers gaze at the frontier's hues, their faces bitter with longing for home. Tonight, in some high tower, a woman sighs without cease.
translations.tangshi-300-39: A girl of Qin, like pretty Luo Fu, picks mulberry leaves by the green water. Her white hands work the green twigs; in red dress she glows bright in the daylight. 'My silkworms hunger—this one must leave; let not your five-horse carriage delay her.'
translations.tangshi-300-40: Mirror Lake stretches three hundred li, its lotus blossoms bursting into bloom. In the fifth month Xishi comes to gather them, crowds pack the banks of Ruoye. Her boat turns back without waiting for the moon—for she is bound for the king of Yue's palace.
translations.tangshi-300-41: One sheet of moonlight over Chang'an, the sound of pounding clothes from ten thousand households. The autumn wind cannot blow it away—always it is longing for the Jade Gate Pass. When will the Hu invaders be pacified, and the good men come home from their distant campaigns?
translations.tangshi-300-42: At dawn the courier departs from the post station; all night she wadded the lining of his campaign robe. Her white hands drew the needle, cold; how could she bear to hold the scissors? The garment is cut and sewn and sent to the far road—how many days before it reaches Lintao?
translations.tangshi-300-43: When my hair first covered my forehead, I played before the gate, breaking flower branches. You rode a bamboo horse, coming round the bench, tossing green plums. We lived together on Changgan Lane, two children with never a suspicion between us. At fourteen I became your wife; my bashful face never once opened. I lowered my head toward the dark wall; a thousand calls, and not once did I turn. At fifteen I finally relaxed my brow, wishing to be dust and ash with you forever. I always kept the faith of the pillar-holding lover—why would I ever climb the Husband-Watching Terrace? At sixteen you went on a far journey, past the Yanyu Rock of Qutang. In the fifth month no one may pass there; the monkeys cry in the sky, mournfully. The footprints by the gate where you lingered—one by one they sprout green moss. The moss grows too deep to sweep away; fallen leaves come early in the autumn wind. In the eighth month butterflies arrive, flying in pairs over the western garden's grass. Seeing this wounds my heart; sitting in sorrow I watch my rosy face age. Whenever you come down from the Three Ba, send word home ahead. I will go to meet you, however far the road—I'll go all the way to Changfengsha.
translations.tangshi-300-44: The wutong tree waits to grow old with its mate; mandarin ducks die paired together. A chaste wife prizes dying with her husband; giving up her life, she is just so. Though waves may surge, she swears they will never rise again—her heart is the water in the well.
translations.tangshi-300-45: From the threads in a loving mother's hand comes the coat on the wanderer's back. Before his departure she sews stitch upon stitch, fearing his long-delayed return. Who says the heart of an inch of grass can ever repay the light of three spring suns?
translations.tangshi-300-46: Before me I see no ancients; behind me, no one yet to come. Thinking of the vastness of heaven and earth, alone I shed tears of sorrow.
translations.tangshi-300-47: This man went soldiering on the long frontier, a lad of You and Yan from his youth. Betting his life beneath the horse's hooves, he has always held his seven-foot frame cheap. Men dare not step before his blade; his whiskers bristle like a hedgehog's spines. Yellow clouds at the foot of Long Mountain, white snow flying—until he repays his lord's favor he cannot go home. The young wife of Liaodong, fifteen years old, plays the pipa with practiced grace. Now she sounds the frontier tune on the Qiang flute, and the tears of all three armies fall like rain.
translations.tangshi-300-48: In the fourth month the south wind blows, the barley yellow; the jujube flowers have not fallen, the paulownia leaves long. We parted by the green hills at dawn and see them again at dusk; the neighing horse at your gate makes me think of home. O Marquis Chen, how open and upright you stand, with curling beard, tiger brows, and broad forehead. Your belly stores ten thousand scrolls of books; you would not bow your head to rot among the weeds. At East Gate we buy wine and drink with our company; your heart makes light of the world's ten thousand affairs as goose down. Drunk you lie, not knowing the white sun has set; sometimes idly you gaze at the lone cloud, high. Great waves on the long river join the darkening sky; the boat halts at the ford and cannot cross. The wanderer of Zheng has not reached home; the traveler of Luoyang sighs in vain. I hear your old woods have many who know you—you left office just yesterday; how are they treating you now?
translations.tangshi-300-49: The host has wine; let us rejoice tonight. He asks the guest of Guangling to play the singing lute. Moonlight shines on the city walls, crows half in flight; frost chills the myriad trees and the wind cuts through clothes. A bronze brazier, bright candles—candles adding brilliance. First he plays 'Lushui,' then 'The Consort of Chu.' One note sounded and every creature falls still; the whole company silent, the stars grown few. On the clear Huai I serve as envoy over a thousand li—dare I say that from this night the cloud-and-mountain life begins for me?
translations.tangshi-300-50: The daughter of Cai long ago made the sounds of the Hu reed-pipe—one strum, eighteen stanzas. The Hu people shed tears that wet the frontier grass; the Han envoy, heartbroken, faced the returning exile. Old fortresses grey in the cold of beacon fires; the great wilderness sunken deep, flying snow white. First he brushes the shang strings, then the jue and yu—autumn leaves in the four suburbs rustle in alarm. Master Dong, you commune with the spirits; even goblins steal into the deep hills to listen. Slow or fast, every touch answers your hand; as the music turns and returns, it seems to feel. A hundred birds scatter and regather in the empty hills; a thousand miles of floating clouds darken, then clear. The cry of a fledgling wild goose, lost from its flock at night; the grief of a Hu child cut off from his mother's voice. The river stills its waves; the birds cease their singing. In the Wusun tribe the homeland lies far away; at Lhasa, in the dust of the sands, sorrow is born. Then the quiet tone changes and suddenly floats free—the long wind sweeps the forest, rain pounds the tiles. Leaping springs rush splashing off the treetops; wild deer trot past the hall, lowing. In Chang'an the city walls join the eastern palace precinct; the Phoenix Pool faces the green-chain gate. Great talent, careless of fame and gain—morning and evening I hope to see you arrive, lute in arms.
translations.tangshi-300-51: Cut bamboo on South Mountain to make the bili-pipe—this instrument first came from Kucha. Passing into Han lands, its tunes grow ever stranger; a Hu man of Liangzhou plays it for me. Neighbors who hear it sigh in sympathy; far travelers, homesick, all shed tears. The world knows how to listen but not how to appreciate; the pipe sings freely amid the whirlwind. It is withered mulberry and old cypress in whistling cold; the nine fledgling phoenixes chirping in confusion. Dragon's moan and tiger's roar burst forth at once; all sounds, a hundred springs, join in the autumn. Then suddenly it turns into the Yuyang beat—yellow clouds bleak, the white sun dimmed. A variation makes it seem one hears the willows of spring; blossoms of Shanglin dazzle like new. On New Year's night in the high hall, bright candles lined in rows—one cup of wine, one tune at a time.
translations.tangshi-300-52: The mountain temple bell rings; day has darkened. At the ferry of Yuliang, crowds jostle for the crossing. People follow the sandy path toward the riverside village; I too take my boat home to Lumen. The Lumen moon lights the mist-parted trees—suddenly I arrive at the hermitage where Pang Degong once dwelt. The stone gate, the pine path—forever lonely and still; only the recluse comes and goes.
translations.tangshi-300-53: I am by nature the madman of Chu, who sang the phoenix song mocking Confucius. Green jade staff in hand, at dawn I leave Yellow Crane Tower. I seek the immortals among the Five Peaks and do not shun the distance; all my life I have loved to roam famous mountains. Mount Lu flowers beside the Southern Dipper, its nine-fold screen unrolling like brocaded clouds. Its shadow falls on Mirror Lake with an indigo sheen; before the golden palace two long peaks part. The Silver River hangs upside down over the Three Stone Bridges; the Incense Burner waterfall gazes back from afar. Winding cliffs and piled crags soar into the pale blue. Green reflections and red mists shine upon the morning sun; no bird flies so far as the long sky of Wu. Climbing high, the spectacle between heaven and earth; the great river runs boundless eastward in yellow. Yellow clouds ten thousand li shift in the wind's mood; nine streams of white water flow like snow mountains. Happily I make this song of Mount Lu, for the mood rises from Mount Lu itself. Idly I gaze into the Stone Mirror, which clears my heart; where Lord Xie once walked, green moss is buried. If early I take the elixir of return and shed worldly feeling, the threefold lute-heart of the Way is newly formed. Far off I see, in the colored clouds, immortals with lotus in hand, coursing toward the jade capital. I have made a rendezvous above with the boundless at the ninth heaven's height—would that I might take Lu Ao with me to roam the Great Purity.
translations.tangshi-300-54: The seafarer speaks of Yingzhou, lost in misty waves, truly hard to find. The people of Yue speak of Tianmu, which one may glimpse through the clouds' brightening and darkening. Tianmu joins the sky, towering, its power outstripping the Five Peaks and veiling Red Wall. Mount Tiantai, forty-eight thousand feet, stoops toward it as if to fall, tilted southeast. I would follow it in dream to Wu and Yue, flying past Mirror Lake in a single night, its moon upon me. The lake moon shines on my shadow and sees me to Shan Creek, where Lord Xie's lodging still remains; the clear water ripples and gibbons cry faintly. I put on the wooden clogs of Lord Xie and climb the ladder into the blue clouds. Halfway up the cliff I see the sea-sun; in the air I hear the Cock of Heaven. A thousand crags, ten thousand ravines—the path uncertain; spellbound by flowers, leaning on rocks, I find dusk suddenly come. Bears roar and dragons howl, thundering through the rock-pools; the deep woods tremble, the layered peaks shudder. The clouds darken as if about to rain; the waters ripple, rising mist. With a crack of thunder, lightning splits; hills collapse and crumble. The stone gate of the hidden heaven thunders open—a boundless blue, bottomless, where sun and moon shine on a terrace of gold and silver. Rainbows for robes, wind for steeds; the lords of the clouds come thronging down. Tigers pluck the se-strings, phoenixes whirl the chariots; immortals stand in ranks like hemp. Suddenly my soul starts, my spirit stirs; I wake with a gasp and a long sigh—only my pillow and mat of the waking hour remain; the mists and glow of the dream are gone. The pleasures of the world are likewise; all things ancient and modern flow east like water. When I leave you, my friend, when shall I return? For now I leave the white deer by the green cliff, to ride to famous mountains whenever I must go. How could I bow and scrape to serve the mighty, so that I cannot show a happy face?
translations.tangshi-300-55: The wind blows willow blossoms till the whole tavern is fragrant; the Wu girl presses the wine and calls the guests to taste it. The young men of Jinling come to see me off; those leaving, those staying, all drain their cups. I ask you: try asking the east-flowing stream—which is longer, its water or the feeling of this parting?
translations.tangshi-300-56: What abandoned me—the days of yesterday—cannot be held back. What troubles my heart—the days of today—bring endless fret. The long wind, ten thousand li, escorts the autumn geese; facing this, one may drink deep in the high tower. Your writing has the substance of Penglai and the sinews of the Jian'an era; among them Xie Tiao of old stands fresh and clear. Both of us cherish soaring fancy, our bold thoughts winging toward the sky, wishing to climb the blue heaven and embrace the bright moon. Draw a sword to cut the water—the water flows on; raise the cup to drown sorrow—sorrow grows heavier. Human life, when it does not go as wished—tomorrow morning I will loose my hair and toy with a little boat.
translations.tangshi-300-57: Do you not see, along the Zouma River by the Snow Sea's edge, level sands stretching vast and yellow into the sky? In the ninth month at Luntai the wind howls at night; stones big as bushel-measures litter the riverbed and roll everywhere with the wind. The Hu horses grow fat on the yellowing grass. West of Gold Mountain the beacon smoke flies; the great general of the Han marches his army west. The general's golden armor stays unremoved at night; marching at midnight, spear-tips knock against each other. The wind's edge cuts like a knife across the face; the horses' hair is flecked with snow, sweat steaming. The five-flower and linked-coin horses sweat turns to ice in an instant; in the tent, as he drafts the proclamation, the ink in his inkstone freezes. The Hu horsemen hearing of it must tremble in their guts—surely they know better than to meet him blade to blade. We await you at the west gate of Cheshi to present the victory!
translations.tangshi-300-58: At night the horns blow on the walls of Luntai; over Luntai's north wall the war-star sets. Feathered dispatches last night passed Quli; the chanyu is already west of Gold Mountain. From the garrison towers the west looks black with beacon smoke; the Han troops mass north of Luntai. The commander, bearing his yak-tail standard, marches west on campaign; at dawn the flutes sound and the great army moves. War-drums thunder on all four sides till the snow-seas surge; the three armies shout till the Yin Mountains shake. In the barbarian forts, soldier-spirit massed to the clouds; on the battlefield, white bones tangled in grass roots. In Sword River the wind is fierce, snowflakes broad; at Sand Mouth the stones freeze and horses' hooves slip off. The vice-chancellor toils loyally through hardship and pain, vowing to repay his lord and quiet the border dust. Who throughout history has not read the records of fame?—today his merit outshines the ancients.
translations.tangshi-300-59: The north wind rolls along the ground, snapping the white grass; in the Hu sky, snow flies already in the eighth month. Suddenly it seems a night of spring wind has come; on a thousand trees, ten thousand trees, pear blossoms open. They drift through the pearl blinds, wetting the silk curtains; the fox-fur coat is no warmth, the brocade quilt too thin. The general's horn bow cannot be drawn; the commandant's iron armor stays cold on his body. Across the vast sea, a hundred fathoms of ice in every crevasse; gloom-grey clouds congeal for ten thousand miles. In the middle army wine is set out for the departing guest—Hu lute, pipa and Qiang flute. Evening snow falls thick before the camp gate; the wind tugs the red flag, frozen, it cannot flutter. I see you off at Luntai's east gate; when you leave, snow fills the mountain road. The mountains turn, the road bends—no more sight of you; in the snow remain only the marks where your horse passed.
translations.tangshi-300-60: Since the founding of the dynasty, for paintings of saddle-horses, divine skill was counted unique in the Prince of Jiangdu. For thirty years the General has borne his fame; in the human world one again sees the true Chenghuang. He once portrayed the late Emperor's Zhaoyebai; ten days of thunderous splendor flew by Dragon Pool. From the imperial treasury, the deep-red agate plate; the jieyu carried the edict, the cairen came to claim it. The plate bestowed, the General bowed and danced home; fine silks and gauzes chased one another to his door. When nobles and powerful houses obtained his brushwork, their screens suddenly glowed with radiance. Of old, Emperor Taizong's curly-maned bay; of late, the Guo family's Lion-Bloom. In the General's new painting there are two horses—again he makes connoisseurs sigh long. Both are war-mounts worth a myriad foes; in plain silk, vast and dim, they open the sand-wind. The other seven are also matchless, far apart like a cold sky mixed with mist and snow. Frost hooves trample in the long catalpa lanes; grooms and stableboys stand in solemn ranks. How lovable, the nine horses contending in spirit; proud glances, clear and high, their air deep and steady. Tell me, who loved them with such devoted heart? Behind, Wei Feng; before him, Zhi Dun. I remember when the Emperor toured to Xinfeng Palace, kingfisher banners brushing the sky as he came eastward. Thirty thousand steeds bounding and bold—all with sinew and bone the same as in this painting. Since the treasure-offering to the River Lord and the end of imperial tours, no more shooting crocodiles in the river's waters. Do you not see—before the pines and cypresses at the Golden-Millet Mound, the dragon-steeds are all gone; only birds call in the wind.
translations.tangshi-300-61: The General is a descendant of Emperor Wu of Wei; today of common station, a man of the Blue Gate. Heroic partition of the land has long passed, yet the grace of his culture and spirit lives on. Learning calligraphy he first studied under Lady Wei, only regretting he never surpassed Wang Xizhi. He knew not that old age would come upon him; rank and riches to him were floating clouds. In the Kaiyuan era he was often summoned to court; favored, he repeatedly mounted the Nanxun Hall. The portraits of the Lingyan meritorious officials had faded; the General's brush opened them fresh faces. On the good ministers' heads the hats of the worthy; at the fierce generals' waists the great-feathered arrows. The Duke of Bao and the Duke of E, their hair stirring, stood in gallant spirit as if still fighting drunk. The late Emperor's heavenly steed, the Jade-Flower Roan—mountain-like painters tried their portraits, none alike. That day it was led beneath the red steps, standing apart at the Changhe Gate, a rising wind about it. The edict bade the General spread the plain silk; in brooding concentration his design took shape. In an instant, from the ninefold palace a true dragon emerged, washing ten thousand ages of common horses empty away. The Jade Flower now hung upon the imperial couch; the couch and the courtyard stood facing, statue to statue. The Son of Heaven smiled and urged the grant of gold; the grooms and the Grand Stableman stood dumbfounded. His disciple Han Gan had early entered the inner chamber, able too to paint horses in every distinctive form. Han Gan paints only the flesh, not the bones—how it dulls the very spirit of the Hanluo steeds. The General's painting is good because it holds the divine; meeting fine gentlemen now and then, he also paints their true likeness. Now, adrift amid war and weapons, he time and again portrays ordinary passers-by. At the end of his road he meets the scorn of vulgar eyes; in all the world none is poor as he. Only see: under great fame since ancient days, frustration clings to a man all his days.
translations.tangshi-300-62: Now I am joyless and long for Yueyang; my body would soar but illness pins it to the bed. The fair one, lovely, is parted from me by the autumn waters; she bathes her feet in Lake Dongting, gazing to the eight farthest corners. The great swan flies off into the darkening where sun and moon turn white; green maple leaves redden, the sky rains frost. In the Jade Capital the host of gods gather at the Northern Dipper; some ride qilin, some ride phoenixes. Lotus-petal banners fall through mist and smoke; their shadows stir inverted images, rocking the Xiao and Xiang. The lords of the starry palace drunk on jasper wine; the feathered immortals are few, none at their side. I seem to hear that of late, like Red Pine Master, he must be Han Zhangliang of the Han. He once followed the Liu house to settle Chang'an; the strategy tent unchanged, his spirit grieves. How dare I speak of the state's success or failure?—his face refuses the stench of rank, he dines on sweetgum incense. His long sojourn in the south is what antiquity pitied; the Old Man of the South Pole should grant him long life. Why does the fair one stand parted by autumn waters? How can we bring him into the Hall of Jade to present to the throne?
translations.tangshi-300-63: Before the temple of Kongming stands an old cypress; its boughs are like bronze, its roots like stone. Its double trunk, rain-polished, forty arm-spans around; its ink-blue foliage climbs two thousand feet into the sky. Lord and minister met in their time of destiny, and even the trees are cherished still by men. When clouds come, its breath joins the long reach of Wu Gorge; when the moon emerges, its cold reaches the snow-white mountains. I remember the road once winding east of Brocade Pavilion Pavilion, where the temples of lord and liegeman shared one walled grove. Lofty were the branches, ancient in the open plain; deep and still the painted colors in the empty windows. Rooted in fine ground, yet spreading all alone, high and solitary in the dark, it meets fierce winds. Its upholding must be the work of divine power; its uprightness comes from nature's own craft. Should the great mansion totter, it would need beams and pillars—ten thousand oxen would turn their heads at the weight of that mountain. Without displaying patterns the world already marvels; though it never refuses the axe, who would convey it hence? Its bitter heart cannot escape boring ants; yet its fragrant leaves forever shelter the phoenix. Men of purpose, recluses—grieve not; great timber has been hard to use since ancient times.
translations.tangshi-300-64: [Preface:] There was once a fair woman, Lady Gongsun, whose dance of the sword swept all four quarters. The watchers, hill-like, turned pale with dismay; heaven and earth themselves rose and sank for a long while. Flashes like Yi shooting down the nine suns; soaring like hosts of gods driving dragons in flight. Arriving like thunder restraining its gathered rage; ceasing like rivers and seas holding frozen light. Red lips, pearl sleeves—both have fallen silent; only late in her life has a disciple inherited the fragrance. The fair dancer of Linying, here in White Emperor City, dances this very piece, her spirit radiant. She and I talked long; moved by the times, I stroked past events, and grief deepened. Of old the late Emperor's eight thousand palace ladies, in the sword dance Gongsun stood first. Fifty years have passed like a turn of the hand; the world convulsed with dust and darkness dimmed the royal house. The disciples of the Pear Garden scattered like smoke; the lingering grace of the woman musician faces the cold sun. Before the Golden-Millet Mound the trees are already arm-girt; at Stone City on the Qutang the grass soughs bleak. The tortoiseshell feast, urgent strings—the song ends once more; joy at its height brings sorrow, and the moon rises east. This old man knows not where he is going, his feet callused, in desolate hills, his sorrow mounting as he hurries on.
translations.tangshi-300-65: [Preface:] Old Man the Wanderer brews wine from the public fields' rice; on his rest days he carries wine to the lake and takes a drunk. Merrily drunk, he leans on the lake shore, reaches his arm to the stone fish to draw wine, has the boat carry it round, and gives all seated a drink. In his fancy he leans on Mount Ba, pouring at Mount Junshan, his companions sitting ring-wise around Lake Dongting, the wine-boat drifting, brushing the waves as it comes and goes—so he makes a song to draw it out. Stonefish Lake is like Dongting; in summer the water rises to fill it, and Mount Junshan greens. The hills for a wine-jar, the waters for a goblet; the drinkers sit plain to see on the isles and sandbanks. Day after day the long wind raises great waves, yet it cannot stop the people ferrying the wine-boat. I hold a long gourd and sit on Mount Ba, pouring wine for the whole company to scatter their cares.
translations.tangshi-300-66: Mountain rocks jagged, the path narrow; at dusk I reach the temple, bats flying. I enter the hall and sit on the steps—new rain has fallen full; plantain leaves spread broad, gardenias grow fat. The monk speaks of fine Buddha-paintings on the old walls; by torchlight I look, but little is seen. They spread the bedding, dust the mat and set out soup and rice; coarse fare, yet enough to fill my hunger. Deep in the night I lie still—all insects' sounds cease. The clear moon emerges from the ridge, its light entering the doorway. At dawn I go alone, where there is no road, going in and out, high and low, through all the mist. Mountain-red, ravine-green, riotously bright; now and then pines and chestnuts, all ten arm-spans around. Standing in the current, barefoot, treading the stream stones; the water-sound tinkles, the wind blows my clothes. Such is life, joyous in itself—why must one be hobbled and haltered for others? Alas, my friends, the few of my party—how can we grow old and never return?
translations.tangshi-300-67: Thin clouds roll away on all four sides, the river of heaven gone; the clear wind sweeps the sky, the moon spreads its waves. Sands level, waters stilled, sounds and shadows gone—one cup for you, friend; it is time you sang. Your song's voice is sour, the words so bitter I cannot hear it to the end, tears raining down. Lake Dongting joins the sky, the Jiuyi peaks high; dragons and serpents appear and vanish, apes and flying-squirrels howl. Nine deaths in ten we reached our posts; we dwell in silence like fugitives in hiding. Rising from bed we fear snakes; eating, we fear poison; the sea-air, damp and swarming, reeks of fish and blood. Yesterday before the prefecture they beat the great drum—the new emperor succeeding the sage, ascending like Kui and Gao. The amnesty traveled ten thousand li in a day; even death-row crimes were all remitted. The exiled were recalled, the banished returned; stains washed away, the court ranks purified. The prefecture submitted my name; the governor's office suppressed it—balked and thwarted, I could only be shifted to Jingman. The post of adjutant, a petty office not worth speaking of—I might well be flogged in the dust. My peers of the same year mostly set off on the high road; the way of heaven is dark and steep, hard to climb after. Enough of your song—now hear mine; my song is of another kind tonight. Once a year the bright moon is fullest tonight; life follows fate, not any other. With wine at hand and not to drink—what would become of tomorrow's brightness!
translations.tangshi-300-68: In sacrifice rank the Five Peaks are treated as three dukes; ringed and guarding on four sides, the sacred mountain stands in the center. The land of fire lies wild, rife with goblins; Heaven lends the gods' power to make it sole sovereign. It spews clouds, vents mist, hiding half its flanks—though it has a summit, who could ever reach it? I come just in the season of autumn rains; the yin-air is dim and dark, no clear wind blows. With concentrated heart I pray in silence—and there is a response; can it be that uprightness moves things so? In a moment the stillness sweeps clean and the host of peaks emerge; looking up I see them jutting, propping the blue void. Purple Canopy stretches on to join Pillar of Heaven; Stone Granary tumbles and heaps toward Zhurong. Awed, my very soul stirs; I dismount and bow, then follow a single pine-shaded path to the sacred palace. Scattered murals on the walls, red pillars aglow with color; paintings of demons fill in the blue and red. Mounting the steps, stooped, I offer dried meat and wine, wishing with these poor gifts to make plain my heart. The old temple-keeper knows the god's intent; watchful, sidelong, he can read the omens. Cup and blocks in hand he guides my throw: he says this cast is the luckiest, none can match it. Banished to these savage wastes, lucky not to have died, with food and clothing barely enough I am content to end my days. Hopes of marquis, king, general, chancellor I long since cut off—even if the god wished to bless me, how could he work it? At night I lodge in the Buddhist temple, climbing the high gallery; stars and moon half-hidden, the clouds grow pale. Gibbons cry, the temple bell sounds, I know not the dawn is near; the cold sun rises glaring in the east.
translations.tangshi-300-69: Scholar Zhang holds the Stone-Drum script in hand and urges me to write a Stone-Drum song. With Du Fu gone and the banished immortal dead, my meager talent—what can it do with the stone drums? The rule of Zhou declined, the four seas seethed; King Xuan rose in wrath and wielded his heavenly lance. He threw wide the Bright Hall to receive the court's homage, the lords' swords and pendants chiming one against another. He hunted at Qiyang to display his prowess; beasts from ten thousand li were all netted in. To carve his merit and proclaim it to ten thousand generations he cut drums from the rock, felling the towering cliff. Among his attendant ministers, talents and arts all first-rate, the chosen ones composed and engraved, leaving them by the hills. Rain-lashed, sun-scorched, wildfire-burned, goblin-guarded, fretted and exhorted—Sir, where did you get this paper copy? Every hair and whisker preserved without error. The words stern, the sense dense, hard to read; the letter-forms neither like clerical nor tadpole script. Deep in years, how avoid missing strokes, as if a sharp sword had chopped through live horned-dragons. Phoenixes soar and wheel, hosts of immortals descending; coral trees and jasper branches intertwined. Gold cords and iron chains clink with sturdy clasps; ancient tripods leaping from the water, dragons darting shuttles. The pedant scholars compiling the Odes did not include them—the two 'Ya' sections being cramped, without range. Confucius journeyed west but never reached Qin; picking the stars, he left out the sun and moon. Alas—I love antiquity but was born too late; facing this, my tears pour down in twin streams. I remember when I first received the summons of the Doctorate—this was the year just renamed Yuanhe. An old friend then serving in the western canton measured the site for me to dig the hollow. Washing my cap, bathing, I reported to the libationer: such a supreme treasure as this—how many can survive? Wrapped in felt, packed in matting, they could be brought at once; ten drums need only a few camels to carry. Present them at the Grand Ancestral Temple to rank with the Gao tripod—its luster and worth would surpass a hundredfold. Should the sage grace permit them kept at the Imperial Academy, the students could study and debate them. When the classics were viewed at Hongdu, still the crowds jammed and choked—sit and watch the whole nation come running in a bustle. Scrape away moss, pick out lichen, reveal the joints and angles; set them firm and level, safe and steady. A great hall with deep eaves to shelter and cover them, so they endure long ages, safe from harm. The high officials of the court, old hands at worldly affairs—would they ever be moved to act? Only fawning and hesitating. Herdboys strike flints on them, cattle whet their horns on them—who again will lay a hand to stroke and caress them? Daily wearing, monthly melting, they sink toward oblivion; six years I look west, all my chanting vain. Wang Xizhi's vulgar script pandered to charm; a few pages of it could still trade for white geese. Eight dynasties after Zhou have fought their wars to an end; no one gathers them up—what can be done about it? Now in this age of peace, its days without trouble, authority rests on the Ru learning, honoring Confucius and Mencius. How could I present this for deliberation above? Would I could borrow a mouth like a hanging river. The song of the stone drums ends here—ah, my intent, I fear, will come to nothing.
translations.tangshi-300-70: The old fisherman moors at night by the western cliff; at dawn he draws the clear Xiang and burns his Chu torch. Mist dissolves, the sun comes out, no person in sight—a single sound of the oar-pole, and the mountains and waters turn green. Looking back toward the sky's edge, he drifts down midstream; on the cliff, unwitting clouds chase one another.
translations.tangshi-300-71: The Han emperor prized beauty and longed for a face that could topple a kingdom; ruling the realm for many years, he sought such a one in vain. A daughter of the Yang house came of age, raised deep in the inner chambers, unknown to the world. Born lovely, hard for such gifts to hide, one morning she was chosen to stand beside the throne. One turning glance, one smile, and a hundred graces were born; the powdered ladies of the six palaces paled to nothing. In the chill of spring she was granted a bath at Huaqing Pool; the hot spring's water, smooth, washed her whitening skin. Attendants raised her up, delicate and strengthless—just then newly receiving the imperial favor. Cloud-coiffure, flower-face, gold step-tremblers; warm the lotus-canopied tent through the spring night. Spring nights felt bitterly short, the sun rose high, and from then on the lord no longer held dawn court. Sharing joy, attending feasts, no idle moment; spring excursions, spring outings, night after night hers alone. Three thousand beauties of the rear palace—three thousand favors fixed on one body. Gold-household adornment ready, she serves the night in sweet delicacy; from jade-pavilion banquets she returns drunk with spring. Sisters and brothers all received fiefs—splendor shed on her whole household. Thus it made the hearts of parents under heaven turn: rather than sons, they wished for daughters. The Li Palace, high above, pierces the blue clouds; immortal music drifts on the wind, heard everywhere. Slow songs and languid dances, strings and pipes congealing—the lord watched all day and never had enough. Then the Yuyang war-drums beat from the earth, startling apart the 'Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Dress' tune. Dust and smoke rose from the ninefold palace walls; a thousand chariots and ten thousand riders fled southwest. The kingfisher banners swayed, going, stopping; a hundred and more li out the capital's gate. The six armies would not march—nothing could be done; the moth-brows writhed and died before the horses. Flower hairpins fell to the ground, none to gather them; kingfisher tail-feathers, gold birds, jade hair-pins. The lord covered his face, unable to save her; looking back, blood and tears flowed mingled together. Yellow dust spread drearily, the wind bleak; up the winding cloud-post road they climbed to Sword Gallery. Below Emei Mountain few travelers passed; banners colorless, the daylight thin. The Shu river green, the Shu mountains blue; the sacred lord's longing morning and night. In the temporary palace the sight of the moon was a heart-breaking hue; in night rain the sound of the bell tore the entrails. Heaven turned, earth spun, the dragon coach returned; coming here he lingered, unable to leave. In the earth below Mawei Slope—no more jade-like face, only the place where she died to no purpose. Lord and ministers looked at each other, all their robes wet; east they gazed toward the capital gate and let the horses take them home. Back home, the pools and gardens all as before; Taiye's lotus, Weiyang's willows. Lotus like her face, willow like her brows—how facing these could tears not fall? On spring-wind, peach-and-plum blossom days; on autumn-rain, wutong leaf-fall times. The western palace and southern inner courts were thick with autumn grass; fallen leaves covered the steps, the red dust unswept. The Pear Garden disciples' hair had newly whitened; the pepper-chamber matrons and the green-browed maids grown old. In the evening palace fireflies flew, thoughts stirless; the lone lamp's wick burnt out, still no sleep. The slow drums of the long night's first watch; the bright starry river edging toward dawn. The mandarin-drake tiles cold, heavy with frost-flowers; who shares the chill of the kingfisher quilt? Life and death parted, a whole year gone by; her soul has never once come into his dreams. A Daoist of Linqiong, a guest of Hongdu, could summon spirits with his utmost sincerity. Moved by the lord's tossing, turning thoughts, he had the adept seek her eagerly. Parting the air, riding the breath, swift as lightning; ascending the sky, entering the earth, he searched her everywhere. Up to the ends of the blue, down to the yellow springs—in both places vast and dim, nowhere found. Suddenly word of a fairy mountain on the sea; the mountain hangs in nothingness, faint and dim. Pavilions and terraces, delicate, rise in five-colored clouds; within, graceful, many fairy maidens. One among them bears the name Zhenzhen—snowy skin, flower looks, much like her. At the west wing of the golden palace they knock on the jade door; the word passes through Xiaoyu to report to Shuangcheng. Hearing that a messenger of the Han-house Son of Heaven had come, in the nine-flowered canopy her dream-startled soul. She takes her robe, pushes the pillow, rises and wanders; pearl blinds and silver screens unrolling one after another. Cloud-tresses half awry from her new sleep, flower-crown unadjusted, she comes down the hall. The wind lifts her immortal sleeves, fluttering up—they still seem the dance of the 'Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Dress.' Jade face, lonely, tears trailing—a spray of pear blossoms in spring rain. In feeling she gazes at the lord and thanks him; since their parting, voice and face both far and dim. In the Zhaoyang Palace the love was ended; in Penglai Palace the days and months are long. Turning her head to look down upon the mortal realm—no Chang'an to be seen, only mist and dust. Only with old tokens would she show her deep feeling; the gilded box and gold hairpin she sends. One prong of the pin kept, one leaf of the box—the pin split, the gold divided, the box broken apart. If only their hearts would be firm as that gold and box—on earth or in heaven, they would meet again. At parting, earnestly she sent word again; within the words was a vow only the two hearts know. On the seventh day of the seventh month, in the Long-Life Hall, at midnight when no one was near, the whispered time: In heaven we wish to be paired birds; on earth we wish to be joined branches. The sky and earth may someday end; this regret goes on and on, never ceasing.
translations.tangshi-300-72: [Preface:] In the tenth year of Yuanhe I was demoted to Adjutant of Jiujiang. The next autumn, seeing a guest off at Penpu, I heard someone playing the pipa in a boat at night; listening to its tones, they rang with the music of the capital. Asking who it was, she proved a former singing-girl of Chang'an who had studied the pipa under two masters, Mu and Cao. Her years had advanced, her beauty had faded, and she had given herself as wife to a merchant. I had wine brought and had her play several tunes to her heart's content; when the music ended she was desolate. She told of her happy days as a girl, and of her present drifting, worn and haggard, turning from river to lake. I had been two years out of office, content and at ease, but moved by her words, that night I first felt the sting of exile, and so composed this long song to give her, six hundred and sixteen words in all, named 'Song of the Pipa.' At night by the Xunyang river-head I saw a guest off; maple leaves and reed-blossoms rustled in the autumn wind. The host dismounted, the guest stayed in the boat; raising wine to drink, there was no music of strings. Drunk, without joy, gloomily we parted; parting, the river stretched boundless, soaking the moon. Suddenly I heard pipa sounds on the water; the host forgot to go home, the guest would not set off. Following the sound I quietly asked who was playing; the pipa stopped, and she hesitated to speak. I moved my boat near, inviting her to meet; more wine added, the lamp relit, the feast reopened. After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons she came out at last, still hugging the pipa, half-hiding her face. She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few notes—before a melody formed, feeling was already there. String by string, stifled, note by note, longing—like telling a life's frustrated ambitions. Head lowered, fingers moving on, she played on and on, pouring out the boundless matters of her heart. Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, stroking and picking again—first 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Six-Slip.' The thick strings clamored like pelting rain; the thin strings whispered like private speech. Clamoring and whispering interwove—great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate. Like orioles' warble gliding beneath the flowers; like a choked spring weeping down the shoals. The spring-water cold and harsh, the strings congealing to silence—a stifled pause when silence out-sounds sound. Then a silver bottle suddenly burst, the water spurting forth; iron riders sprang out, blades and lances ringing. At the tune's end she drew the plectrum across the strings' heart—four strings, one sound, like tearing silk. East boat and west boat, wordlessly still; only the white autumn moon in the river's heart seen. She mused, set the plectrum back among the strings, straightened her gown, and rose with composed face. She said: 'I was once a girl of the capital, my home below Hama Hill. At thirteen I finished learning the pipa; my name stood in the first division of the music bureau. When a tune ended, even masters praised me; made up, each time I was envied by the Qiuniang. Young lords of the Five Tombs vied to give me silks; one song won crimson gauze beyond counting. Inlaid combs of silver snapped on the beat; my blood-red skirt was stained and overturned with wine. Laughing and merry this year and the next; autumn moons and spring winds idled away. My brother joined the army, my aunt died; day in, day out, my looks faded. At the gate, horses and carriages grew few; grown old, I married a merchant. The merchant prizes profit and holds parting cheap; last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. Coming and going I keep the empty boat at the river-mouth; around the boat the moon is bright, the river water cold. Deep at night I suddenly dream of my girlhood things; waking from the dream I weep, my rouged tears running.' I had sighed already at the pipa; hearing these words, I sighed again. We are both fallen souls at the world's far end—what need that we knew each other before? I left the imperial capital last year; demoted, sick, I lie in Xunyang town. Xunyang is remote, without music; all year I hear no string or pipe. I live near the Pen River, the land low and damp; yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house. What is heard there morning and evening? Cuckoos weeping blood, gibbons wailing. On spring-river blossom mornings and autumn-moon nights I often take wine and drink alone. How could there be no mountain songs and village pipes?—they rasp and squawk, hard on the ear. Tonight, hearing your pipa's speech, it is like hearing immortal music, my ears momentarily bright. Do not refuse—sit again and play one more tune; for you I write this 'Song of the Pipa.' Moved by my words she stood silent long, then sat back down, tightening the strings—their pitch turned quicker. Mournful, not like her earlier sound; the whole company hearing it again all hid their weeping. Who wept most among the seats? The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked.
translations.tangshi-300-73: The Yuanhe Son of Heaven had a martial bearing—what men were those, Xuanyuan and Fuxi. He swore to wash away the accumulated shame of the former sages, sitting in the Dharma Palace holding court over the four barbarians. In Huaixi a rebel band held out for fifty years—wolf breeds leopard, leopard breeds bear. They held no mountains or rivers but held the level plain; long spears and sharp lances could be wielded at the sun. The emperor gained a sage minister, the minister named Du—the rebels hacked him, yet he did not die, the spirits sustaining him. Girded with the seal of state he served as commander-in-chief; gloomy winds blew chill around the imperial standard. Su, Wu, Gu and Tong served as claws and teeth; the protocol officers, the outer secretaries, carrying their brushes followed. The campaign adjutant, wise and brave, a hundred and forty thousand strong as tigers and leopards. They entered Cai, bound the rebel, offered him at the Grand Temple—a feat none could rival, favor beyond measure. The emperor said: 'You, Du, merit first; your staff officer Han Yu should make the inscription.' Han bowed his head, dancing with joy: 'Inscribing in metal and stone, this servant can do. In ancient times what the world calls a great brush—this task belongs not to office.' Of old, those who met their duty never yielded; his words done, the emperor nodded his chin again and again. He withdrew, fasted, sat in a small pavilion; soaking his great brush, how freely it flowed! He altered words of the 'Yao Dian' and 'Shun Dian,' revised lines of the 'Qing Miao' and 'Sheng Min.' The text complete, in cursive-breaking style written on paper, at dawn he bowed twice and spread it on the red steps. The memorial said: 'Your servant Han Yu, risking death, presents this: singing the sacred merit, I write it upon the stele.' The stele stood three zhang high, characters like bushel-measures; borne on a sacred tortoise, coiled with hornless dragons. Lines wondrous, words weighty—few understood them; slanderers told the Son of Heaven he had favored his own. A hundred-foot long rope hauled the stele down; coarse sand and great stones ground it smooth. But this writing of the duke is like primal breath—it had already entered people's livers and spleens. The Tang basin, the Confucian tripod had their inscriptions; today the vessels are gone, the words remain. Alas—the sage emperor and the sage minister, both radiant and resplendent, shedding pure light. If this writing of the duke is not shown to posterity, how may we match the Three and Five? Would I might write ten thousand copies and recite them ten thousand times, spittle flying from my lips, callus on my right hand. Hand it down through seventy-two generations as the foundation of the feng-shan's jade tally and Bright Hall.
translations.tangshi-300-74: [Preface:] In the twenty-sixth year of Kaiyuan, a traveler who had followed the Censor-in-chief Lord Zhang beyond the frontier returned and made a 'Yan Song' to show Gao Shi; moved by the garrison affairs, I matched it. Han-house smoke and dust rose in the northeast; Han generals left home to crush the remnant rebels. Men by nature prize sweeping valor; the Son of Heaven gave extraordinary favor. Banging gongs, beating drums, they came down past Yuguan; banners streaming along between Jieshi. The commandant's feathered dispatches flew across the desert; the chanyu's hunting fires lit Wolf Mountain. Mountains and streams desolate to the edge of the borderland; Hu riders pressed on, mixed with wind and rain. At the front the soldiers were half alive, half dead; beneath the tents the beauties still sang and danced. Late autumn in the great desert, the frontier grass withered; a lone city in the setting sun, men in arms few. Bodies bearing the lord's favor, ever underrating the foe; strength spent at the mountain passes, the siege unrelieved. The iron-clad guards long on distant duty, toiling long after parting; the jade-white chopsticks must have wept. South of the city the young wives near heartbreak; north of Ji the soldiers look back in vain. The swaying borderland—how could it be crossed? The uttermost wilds, vast and dim—what more is there? Killing-air rose three watches as battle-clouds; cold sounds all night passed the warning-clapper. White blades gleaming, blood flying thick—dying for honor, who ever cared for reward? Do you not see how bitter the battlefield's wars—today we still remember General Li!
translations.tangshi-300-75: By day we climb the mountains to watch the beacon fires; at dusk we water the horses beside the Jiao River. Travelers in the sand-blurred dark hear the clapper's sound; the princess's pipa fills the air with hidden grief. Wild clouds for ten thousand li, no walls or towns; rain and snow falling thick join the great desert. Hu geese cry mournfully, flying night after night; Hu children, tears falling in pairs. Word comes the Jade Gate is still barred—we must give our lives to chase the light chariots. Year after year war-bones are buried beyond the wastes; all for nought we see the grapes enter the Han house.
translations.tangshi-300-76: A daughter of Luoyang lives opposite my door—her talent and looks just past fifteen. Her lord rides a white-maned horse with jade-studded bridle; her maid brings a golden platter of carp sashimi. Painted pavilions and vermilion towers face each other in rows; red peaches and green willows hang toward the eaves. Gauze curtains deliver her onto the seven-scented carriage; jeweled fans welcome her home to the nine-flowered canopy. Her madcap lord's wealth came in his youth; his spirit and pride more extravagant than Jilun's. He dotes on his jasper girl, teaching her the dance himself; coral trees he gives away without a care. In the spring window at dawn the Ninefold flame dies—Ninefold petals fluttering, sparks fly in patterns. After the games she never has a moment to practice music; made up, she only sits fumigating incense. Her city acquaintances are all the splendid sort; day and night they call at the houses of Zhao and Li. Who pities the Yue girl, face like jade, washing silk by the river, poor and lowly?
translations.tangshi-300-77: In his years of fifteen and twenty, on foot he wrested a Hu horse and rode.
translations.tangshi-300-78: A fisherman's boat follows the stream, loving the spring hills; peach blossoms line both banks of the ancient ford. Sitting I watch the red trees, not knowing how far I've come; the green creek runs out and still no person appears. Then a hidden path winds from the mountain's mouth—the mountain opens into a broad vista, suddenly level land. From afar I see one place where cloud-trees cluster; nearing it, a thousand homes scattered among flowers and bamboo. A woodcutter first speaks the names of Han; the dwellers still wear the clothes of Qin. The people dwell together at the source of Wuling, raising fields and gardens beyond the world of things. Moonlit, beneath the pines, the houses are still; at sunrise, above the clouds, chickens and dogs make clamor. Startled, the country folk hurry to gather, vying to lead the stranger home, asking after the capital. At dawn the lanes are swept open among falling blossoms; at dusk the fishermen and woodcutters come in by the water. At first they fled the troubled world; having become immortals, they never returned. Who within the gorges knew the affairs of men? From the world beyond, one gazes in vain at clouds and mountains. Not doubting that spirit-realms are hard to reach, yet my worldly heart not stilled, I long for my home county. Out of the cave, no matter what hills and waters lay between, I resolved to wander forever away from home. I thought I knew the way by heart and would not lose it—how could I know the peaks and ravines had changed since then? Then I only remembered going deep into the mountains—how many bends of green creek to the cloud-forest. When spring comes the whole stream is peach-blossom water; I cannot tell where to seek the immortal source again.
translations.tangshi-300-79: Ah—how high, how steep! The road to Shu is harder than climbing the blue sky! Cancong and Yufu, founders of old—how dim and far their age! Since then, forty-eight thousand years, no traffic with the land of Qin. Westward, facing Taibai, only birds have their path, a track that could cross to Emei's crest. Only when the earth split, mountains fell, and strong men died did the sky-ladders and stone bridges link up. Above, a peak where the six dragons of the sun turn back; below, a river whose rushing waves fold back on themselves. Even the yellow crane cannot fly over; gibbons that would cross grieve, finding no handholds. How coiling is Green-Mud Ridge—a hundred paces, nine windings, winding round the rock crags! Touching the stars, passing the lodges, I look up breathless, hand on my heart, sitting down with a long sigh. I ask you, traveler west—when will you come back? The fearful road, the sheer cliffs cannot be climbed! Only mourning birds cry in the ancient trees; male flying, female following, they wheel through the woods. Then the cuckoo's cry—in the moonlit night, grieved, in the empty mountains. The road to Shu is harder than climbing the blue sky—hearing this, one's rosy cheeks wither! Linked peaks not a foot from the sky; withered pines hang upside down against the sheer cliffs. Flying torrents and plunging falls contend in roaring; the cliff-waters hurl boulders, thundering through ten thousand ravines. Such is its peril! Alas, you traveler from afar—why have you come? Sword Gallery stands sheer and towering: one man guards the pass, ten thousand cannot open it. If the guardian proves no loyal kin, he turns into wolves and jackals. Morning you shun fierce tigers; evening you shun long snakes—they grind their fangs and suck blood, killing like hemp. Though Brocade City is called a happy place, better to go home early. The road to Shu is harder than climbing the blue sky! Turning sideways to look west, I sigh without end!
translations.tangshi-300-80: Long longing—here in Chang'an. The cricket cries in autumn by the golden well-railing; thin frost is chill, the matting cold. The lone lamp burns dim; longing nears its breaking; I roll up the curtain to gaze at the moon and sigh in vain. The fair one, flower-like, stands beyond the clouds. Above, the long sky of deepest blue; below, the rippled waves of the clear stream. Heaven long, road far, the soul's flying is bitter; the dream-spirit cannot reach the mountain passes' hardship. Long longing—it wracks the heart and liver!
translations.tangshi-300-81: The daylight gone, the flowers hold the mist; the moon turns whitely, the sleepless one grieved. The Zhao zither has just fallen silent on its phoenix pillars; the Shu lute is about to sound its paired-mandarin strings. This melody holds a feeling no one can convey—I wish to send it with the spring wind to Yanran. I remember you, far, far away, parted by the blue sky. Those once rippling eyes have now become a springing fountain of tears. If you do not believe my heart is broken—come home and look in the bright mirror before me.
translations.tangshi-300-82: Pure wine in the golden goblet, ten thousand coins the measure; dainties on the jade plate, worth ten thousand cash. I set down the cup, fling away the chopsticks—I cannot eat; I draw the sword and look about, my heart at a loss. I would cross the Yellow River, but ice seals the stream; I would climb Mount Taihang, but snow fills the mountain. Idly I fish by the blue creek; then again I dream of boating past the sun's shore. Hard, hard the going! So many forked roads—which is the way? The day will come when I ride the long wind and break the waves, my cloud-white sail hoisted straight across the blue sea.
translations.tangshi-300-83: The great road is broad as the blue sky—yet I alone cannot get out. I am ashamed to chase the lads of Chang'an's altar-clubs, betting chestnuts on red cocks and white dogs. I would rap the sword and sing my bitter song, trailing my gown in a lord's gate—no, that does not suit my heart. In Huaiyin the market crowd laughed at Han Xin; in the Han court the nobles envied Jia Yi. Do you not see—in olden days the Yan house honored Guo Wei, sweeping the path and bowing low, without suspicion? Ju Xin and Yue Yi, grateful for the favor, gave their livers and laid bare their hearts to repay a lord of worth. King Zhao's white bones now twine with creeping grass—who again would sweep the Golden Terrace? Hard the going—home I go!
translations.tangshi-300-84: Have ears—rinse them not in the Yingchuan waters; have mouths—eat not the ferns of Shouyang. Holding one's light, blending with the world, one prizes being nameless; what need to match one's lone loftiness against clouds and moon? I see that the worthy and successful of old who did not withdraw in time all destroyed themselves. Wu Zixu was cast away upon the Wu River; Qu Yuan in the end drowned by the Xiang's banks. Could Lu Ji's heroic talent save himself? Li Si halted his carriage—how bitter that he did so too late! The crane's cry of Huating—how could one ever hear it again? The grey hounds of Shangcai—scarcely worth mentioning! Do you not see Zhang Han of Wu, called the man who understood life—suddenly, in the autumn wind, he remembered his journey east to Jiangdong? Enjoy for now one cup of wine in life—why must one chase a thousand-year name beyond the grave?
translations.tangshi-300-85: Do you not see—the Yellow River's waters come from the sky, rushing to the sea, never to return? Do you not see—before the bright mirror in the high hall, one grieves at white hair: morning it was black silk, by evening turned to snow. In life, when the mood is high, one must drink deep—do not let the golden goblet stand empty against the moon! Heaven made my talent for some use; a thousand gold spent will come back again. Boil the sheep, butcher the ox, and make merry—for once, we must drain three hundred cups! Master Cen, Master Danqiu—bring in the wine, do not stop! I sing you a song; bend your ears and listen! Bells and drums, jade-fare—such riches are not worth prizing; I only wish to stay drunk forever and never wake! Since olden days the sages and worthies have all been lonely—only the drinkers leave their names behind! The Prince of Chen once feasted at Pingle Lodge, wine ten thousand coins the measure, indulging in wild merriment. Why should the host say his money is short?—go straight and buy more wine to set before you. My five-flower horse, my thousand-gold fur coat—call the boy, take them out to trade for fine wine, and together with you melt away the sorrows of ten thousand ages!
