translations.tangshi-300-86: Carts rumble, horses neigh; the marchers, bows and arrows each at the waist. Fathers, mothers, wives, children run to see them off; the dust rises so thick Xianyang Bridge cannot be seen. They clutch at clothes, stamp their feet, bar the road weeping; the sound of the weeping rises straight up to the clouds. A passerby by the roadside asks a marcher; the marcher only says the call-ups come too often. Some went north to guard the river at fifteen, and at forty were sent west to garrison the fields. When they left, the village headman bound their heads with cloth; they came back white-haired, only to be stationed at the border again! At the frontier posts blood flows like sea-water—and the Martial Emperor's appetite for expanding the borders is not yet sated. Have you not heard—in the Han house's two hundred provinces east of the mountains, a thousand villages, ten thousand hamlets overgrown with thorns and wormwood? Even with strong women wielding hoe and plow, the grain grows wild in the fields with no rows. And worse, the Qin soldiers endure hard fighting—driven like dogs and chickens. Though the elder has questions to ask, how dare a laborer pour out his grievances? Take this very winter, for example: the troops west of the passes have not been stood down. The county officials urgently demand the taxes—but from what will the taxes come? Truly we learn that bearing sons is bad; instead, bearing daughters is good. Daughters may still be married to the neighbor; sons are buried, gone among the hundred grasses! Have you not seen—at the shore of Qinghai, since ancient times no one has gathered the white bones? The new ghosts complain in vain, the old ghosts weep; in the drizzling rain, damp and dark, their voices whimper.
translations.tangshi-300-87: On the third day of the third month the air is fresh; by the waters of Chang'an there are many lovely ladies. Their grace full, their bearing distant, gentle and true; skin fine and smooth, flesh and bone evenly turned. Embroidered gauze robes gleam in the late spring—gold-woven peacocks, silver unicorns. What is on their heads?—kingfisher leaf-combs drooping at the lips of their temples. What is seen behind?—pearl-studded waists, settling snug on the figure. Among them are the kin of the pepper-chamber, beneath cloud-canopies—granted the titles of the great states, Guo and Qin. Purple-hump camel meat steams in the emerald cauldron; crystal platters circulate the white-scaled fish. Rhinoceros chopsticks, sated and weary, long unmoved; the phoenix knife minces finely, all to no purpose. The yellow-gates' whips fly without stirring the dust, as the imperial kitchens in endless succession deliver the eight delicacies. Pipes and drums wail in strains that move ghosts and gods; guests and attendants swarm, packing the key thoroughfares. Then whose saddle-horse comes pacing last?—dismounting by the balustrade onto the brocade carpet. Willow catkins like snow fall over the white duckweed; the blue bird flies off bearing a red kerchief. His hands could scorch—power beyond compare; do not, take care, step forward—the chancellor will glare!
translations.tangshi-300-88: The old man of Shaoling swallows his sobs; on a spring day he steals his way along the winding Qutang shore. At the river's head the palace gates are locked, a thousand doors—for whom do the slim willows and new rushes turn green? I remember when the rainbow banners came down to the southern park, and all the sights of the park took on fresh color. The foremost lady of Zhaoyang Palace rode in the same carriage, attending the lord at his side. Before the carriage the palace girls bore bows and arrows; their white horses champed on golden bits. One turned and shot upward into the sky—one arrow brought down the paired wings of flying birds. Where now are those bright eyes, those white teeth?—a blood-stained wandering soul cannot come home! The clear Wei flows east; Sword Gallery lies deep; those who went and those who stayed have no news of each other. Human life has feeling; tears wet my breast—do the river's waters and flowers ever know an end? At dusk the Hu horsemen fill the city with dust; I would go south of the city but find myself gazing north.
translations.tangshi-300-89: On the walls of Chang'an, white-headed crows at night fly and cry at Yanqiu Gate; then they peck at the great houses of other families—within the houses the grandees flee the Hu. Golden whips snapped, nine horses dead; kin could not wait for one another in the gallop. A precious jade ring at the waist, of blue coral—the poor princeling weeps by the roadside! I ask him; he will not tell his name, only says in misery he begs to be a slave. A hundred days he has crawled through thorn-brakes; no part of his skin is whole. The descendants of High Emperor all have the imperial nose; the dragon seed is by nature different from common men. Wolves and jackals hold the city; the dragon is in the wilds—princeling, take good care of your thousand-gold body! I dare not speak long at the crossing; let me stand with you for a moment only. Last night the east wind blew the stench of blood; from the east came camels filling the old capital. The stalwarts of Shuofang have such fine martial skill—why were they once so valiant and now so foolish! In secret I hear the Son of Heaven has already yielded the throne; his sage virtue brought the southern chanyu to submit north of the desert. The Huemao warriors, gashing their faces, beg to wash away the shame—do not breathe a word of this; others may be lying in wait! Grieve, princeling, take good care—do not be careless; the auspicious aura of the Five Tombs never fails.
translations.tangshi-300-90: What did the Master do, darting and busy all his age? The land is still the town of the Zou clan; the house is itself the palace of the King of Lu. He sighed over the phoenix, lamenting his own ill fortune; he grieved for the unicorn, mourning that his Way had run out. Now I see the offering set between the two pillars—the very same as in his dream of old.
translations.tangshi-300-91: Over the sea the bright moon is born; at the ends of the earth we share this moment. The beloved grieve at the long night; all night long longing rises. I snuff the candle, loving the brimming light; I throw on my coat, feeling the dew thicken. I cannot bear to give it cupped full in my hands—I go back to bed, to dream of the tryst.
translations.tangshi-300-92: The capital walls buttress the triple Qin; through wind and mist I gaze toward the five fords. The feeling of this parting, yours and mine—both of us are wanderers in officialdom. If within the four seas there is a knowing heart, the ends of the earth are like next door. Do nothing at the forked road like children, wetting your kerchiefs together.
translations.tangshi-300-93: [Preface:] To the west of the walls of my place of confinement stands the court hall, with several ancient locusts. Though their life-force can be known—like the ancient tree of Yin Zhongwen—here cases are heard, like the sweet pear beneath which the Earl of Zhou and Shao gave audience. Whenever the evening sunlight sank in the shade and the autumn cicadas cried sparsely, their voice, mournful and subdued, cut more keenly than I had ever heard. Can a man's heart differ from former times, or does the insect's sound grow sadder to an ear grown sad? Alas!—sound moves the feelings; virtue mirrors the worthy... (the cicada) keeps its purity, inheriting the high conduct of gentleman and sage; casts off its skin, possessing the spirit-poise of the immortal's feathered ascent... I have lost my way in hardship; my emotion rises in response to things—I pity the drifting of its weak wings, and mourn the loneliness of its lingering cry. Not that I claim any literary merit—only to voice my hidden sorrow.] The cicada sings on the western road; the prisoner-guest's longing invades. How can I bear its black-templed shadow coming to face my white-headed chant? Dew heavy, it can hardly fly on; wind strong, its voice easily sinks. No one believes its pure height—who will declare my heart?
translations.tangshi-300-94: Alone among official travelers, I am startled most by the freshness of the season's signs. Cloud-rose sunlight emerges from the sea; plum and willow carry spring across the river. The warm air hastens the yellow birds; the clear light turns the green duckweed. Suddenly I hear you singing an old-style air; my homeward thoughts nearly wet my kerchief.
translations.tangshi-300-95: I hear that at the Huanglong garrison the troops have not stood down for years. Pitiable—the moon of the women's chambers, forever shining over the Han army's camp. The young wife's spring feelings tonight; the good man's feelings last night. Who could take up banners and drums, and win back Longcheng in one campaign?
translations.tangshi-300-96: In the sun-month the geese fly south—by repute they turn back here. My own journey is far from over; when shall I ever return? The river still, the tide newly fallen; the woods dim in unmelted miasma. Tomorrow at the place where I gaze toward home—I should see the plum on the ridge.
translations.tangshi-300-97: The traveler's road beyond the green hills; my boat on the green water before. The tide levels, both banks wide; the wind true, one sail hangs. The sea-sun rises from the waning night; river spring enters the lingering year. Where will my letter home reach?—to the returning geese, by Luoyang's side.
translations.tangshi-300-98: Early morning I enter the ancient temple; the first sun shines on the tall groves. The winding path leads to a hidden place; the chan-cells deep in flowers and trees. The mountain light gladdens the birds' nature; the pool's reflection empties the human heart. Here all ten thousand sounds fall still—only the bell and chime remain.
translations.tangshi-300-99: Stride by stride we hurry to the cinnabar steps; divided into bureaus, parted by the Purple Tenuity. At dawn we follow the imperial standards in; at dusk we come home trailing court incense. White-haired, I grieve that flowers fall; the blue clouds—I envy the birds that fly. In this sage reign there is no flaw in affairs—of itself my memorials grow few.
translations.tangshi-300-100: I love Master Meng, whose grace and spirit are famed under heaven. In rosy youth he cast off cap and carriage; white-headed, he lies among pines and clouds. Drunk beneath the moon, he often reached the Sage; lost among flowers, he would not serve his lord. A high mountain—how could one look up to its top?—I only bow and sip of his clear fragrance.
translations.tangshi-300-101: Crossing far beyond Jingmen, I come to roam in the land of Chu. The mountains end with the level plains; the river flows into the great waste. Beneath the moon, a sky-mirror flying down; from the clouds, a sea-tower formed. Still I love the water of home, escorting my boat ten thousand li.
translations.tangshi-300-102: Green hills lie athwart the northern wall; white water winds round the eastern city. Here, once we part, a lone tumbleweed goes on a journey of ten thousand miles. A floating cloud—a wanderer's mind; the setting sun—an old friend's feeling. Waving hands, from here we go; the horses neigh, xiao-xiao, parting.
translations.tangshi-300-103: The Shu monk, cradling the green-silk lute, comes down from the west, from Emei's peak. He sweeps the strings once for me—I seem to hear pines in a thousand ravines. The traveler's heart is washed by the flowing water; the lingering tones merge with the frosty bell. Before I know it, the green hills are in dusk; autumn clouds have darkened, layer upon layer.
translations.tangshi-300-104: At night on the western river at Niuzhu, the blue sky without a single cloud. Boarding the boat I gaze at the autumn moon, vainly remembering General Xie. I too can chant the lofty verse—only that man can no longer hear it. Tomorrow morning I will hoist the sail; the maple leaves fall thick and fast.
translations.tangshi-300-105: Tonight the moon over Fuzhou—in her chamber she watches alone. From afar I pity the little children, who do not yet understand longing for Chang'an. Incense-mist dampens her cloud-coiffure; the clear light chills her jade arms. When shall we lean on the empty curtain together, both lit by the moon, our tear-tracks dried?
translations.tangshi-300-106: The state is broken; mountains and rivers remain. Spring in the city; grass and trees grow deep. Moved by the times, flowers splash tears; hating parting, birds startle the heart. Beacon fires have run through three months; a letter from home is worth ten thousand gold. My white head, scratched ever shorter, scarcely holds a hairpin anymore.
translations.tangshi-300-107: Flowers fade in the dusk behind the palace walls; twittering, the roosting birds pass by. Stars hang low, stirring ten thousand households; the moon, near the ninefold heaven, grows brighter. Sleepless, I listen for the golden keys; on the wind I fancy the jade pendants. Tomorrow morning there are sealed memorials—time and again I ask how the night goes.
translations.tangshi-300-108: On this road of old I came over in allegiance, when Hu hordes swarmed in the western suburbs. To this day my shattered gall trembles; surely some souls were never summoned home. Lately I was allowed back to the capital—was my transfer the Supreme One's will? Without talent, daily aging, I rein in my horse and gaze at the thousand gates.
translations.tangshi-300-109: The garrison drums cut off men's passage; on the autumn frontier, one goose cries. The dew turns white from this night; the moon is brighter in my homeland. Brothers all scattered, scattered—no home to ask after life or death. Letters sent, long failing to arrive—how much more, with the war not yet stilled.
translations.tangshi-300-110: The cool wind rises at the sky's edge—how fares the gentleman? When will the wild swan arrive?—autumn waters are many on the rivers and lakes. Literary work begrudges a fate fulfilled; mountain goblins rejoice when men err. You must be speaking with the wronged soul there—casting your poems as offerings to the Miluo.
translations.tangshi-300-111: Seeing you off this far, here we part; the green hills, in vain, hold their feeling. When shall we grasp cups again? Last night the moon traveled with us. The assembled prefectures sang your praises with regret; through three reigns you went in and out in honor. Now you return alone to your village place—in solitude to nurse your remaining years.
translations.tangshi-300-112: In another land, on duty again, I rein in my horse to part from the lone grave. Near tears, no dry earth below; low in the sky, broken clouds. Playing chess we kept company, host and guest—like the Duke of Xie; sword in hand I seek the lord of Xu, like Jizi. Only forest flowers are seen falling; an oriole sings, heard by the departing guest.
translations.tangshi-300-113: Fine grass on the bank in the thin wind; a lone night-boat with its towering mast. Stars bend low over the level wilds' expanse; the moon surges with the great river's flow. How could fame rest on writing?—office should end with age and illness. Drifting, drifting—what is it like? A single sand-gull between heaven and earth.
translations.tangshi-300-114: Of old I heard of the waters of Dongting; today I climb the tower of Yueyang. Wu and Chu split to southeast and east; heaven and earth float day and night. From kin and friends not a single word; old and sick, only a lone boat. War-horses north of the mountain passes—leaning on the railing, tears and snivel stream.
translations.tangshi-300-115: The cold hills turn ever more azure; the autumn waters babble all day. Leaning on my staff outside the wicker gate, facing the wind I listen to the evening cicadas. At the ford the setting sun lingers; from the village a single smoke-column rises. Then I meet Jieyu, drunk again, singing wildly before the Five Willows.
translations.tangshi-300-116: Empty mountains after the new rain; the air turns to evening autumn. Bright moon shines between the pines; clear spring flows over the stones. Bamboo rustle—the washerwomen return; lotus stirs—the fishing boat comes down. Let the spring fragrance fade as it will—the wanderer may well stay on.
translations.tangshi-300-117: The clear stream girdles the long thickets; carriage and horses go on, leisurely. The flowing water, as if with intent; the evening birds return together with me. A desolate city fronts the ancient ford; the setting sun fills the autumn hills. Far, far beneath Mount Song's heights, I come home and close my gate for good.
translations.tangshi-300-118: Taiyi nears the heavenly capital; its linked ranges reach to the sea's corner. The white clouds, looking back, close in; the blue mist, entering, is seen no more. The fields' divisions change at the middle peak; sun and shade differ in every ravine. I would seek some household to lodge in—across the water I ask a woodcutter.
translations.tangshi-300-119: In my later years I love only quiet; the ten thousand affairs no longer concern me. Looking to myself, no long-range plans—vainly I know to return to the old woods. The pine-wind loosens my girdle; the mountain moon shines on my lute-playing. You ask the principle of failure and success—a fisherman's song sinks deep into the shore.
translations.tangshi-300-120: I did not know the Temple of Accumulated Fragrance—several li into the cloud-peak. Ancient trees, a path where no one goes; deep in the mountains, from where does the bell ring? Spring-sound chokes on the steep rocks; the sun's color chills the green pines. At dusk, by the empty pool's bend, in calm meditation I subdue the poisonous dragon.
translations.tangshi-300-121: Ten thousand ravines' trees pierce the sky; a thousand hills echo with cuckoos. One night's rain in the mountains; a hundred-fold springs from the treetops. Shu girls tribute pongee cloth; Ba people litigate over taro fields. Wen Weng turned to teaching—do not rest only on the worthies of old.
translations.tangshi-300-122: The Chu frontier meets the three Xiang; Jingmen links the nine streams. The river flows beyond heaven and earth; mountain hues are there, and not there. Towns float on the foreshore; waves stir the far sky. Fine are Xiangyang's wind and sun—I leave my drunkenness to the Mountain Sire.
translations.tangshi-300-123: In middle years I greatly loved the Way; late in life I settled by South Mountain's edge. When the mood comes, I gladly go alone; the fine moments are known to no one. Walking to where the water ends, I sit and watch the clouds rise. By chance I meet an old man of the woods; talking, laughing, with no time to go home.
translations.tangshi-300-124: In the eighth month the lake's waters level, holding the void, merging with the sky. Vapor steams over Cloud-Dream marsh; waves shake the city of Yueyang. I would cross but have no boat or oars; idly to sit shames this enlightened reign. Watching the anglers at ease—vainly I hold the feeling of envying the fish.
translations.tangshi-300-125: Human affairs have their succession of change; coming and going makes ancient and present. The rivers and hills keep their famed sites; our generation climbs and looks again. Waters fallen, the fish-weir shoals; the sky cold, Dream Marsh deep. The words on Duke Yang's stele stand still—reading them done, tears wet my lapels.
translations.tangshi-300-126: Lying in the woods I grieved that spring would end; opening the casement I surveyed the splendor of things. Suddenly I met the Blue Bird's messenger, inviting me into Red Pine's house. The cinnabar stove first lit its fire; the immortal peaches were just bursting into bloom. If a childlike face could be kept—why regret getting drunk on the rosy clouds!
translations.tangshi-300-127: No more memorials to the northern palace—I return to my shabby hut at South Mountain. Without talent, abandoned by an enlightened lord; much ailing, grown distant from old friends. White hair hurries old age on; the green sun presses the year's end near. Ever cherishing sorrow, unable to sleep—pine-moon night at my window, all in ruins.
translations.tangshi-300-128: My old friend has chicken and millet ready and invites me to his farm. Green trees close ranks by the village; blue hills slant beyond the wall. Opening the windows we face the threshing-yard and garden; raising the wine we talk of mulberry and hemp. When the Double-Ninth comes, I will come again for the chrysanthemums.
translations.tangshi-300-129: I have long wished to lie on a single hill; the three paths I sorely lack the means to keep. This northern land is not my wish; East Grove—I remember my master. Gold spent, the fuel of cassia burnt out; high ambitions wither year by year. Evening after evening the cool wind comes; hearing the cicadas only adds sorrow.
translations.tangshi-300-130: The mountains darken; I listen to the gibbons' grieving; the grey river rushes through the night. Wind sounds in the leaves of both banks; the moon shines on a single lone boat. Jiande is not my homeland; Weiyang—my thoughts turn to my old companions. I will take my two tracks of tears and send them far off to the west of the sea.
translations.tangshi-300-131: Silent, silent—to what end? Morning after morning I come home in vain. I would seek the fragrant grasses and go—yet I regret parting from my old friend. Who among those in power lends support? A true friend is rarely found in the world. I can only keep to my solitude—and close again the gate of my old garden.
translations.tangshi-300-132: The trees shed their leaves; the geese go south; the north wind brings cold upon the river. My home lies by the bend of the Xiang—far away beyond the Chu's cloud-edge. Homeward tears, all spent in travel; the lone sail, watched to the sky's end. Losing my way, I would ask the way—level sea at dusk, stretching on and on.
translations.tangshi-300-133: The ancient terrace after its leaves have fallen; on an autumn day, the heart that gazes toward home. In the wild temple few visitors come; cloud-peaks, the waters divide them deep. The setting sun rests on the old ramparts; cold chimes fill the empty woods. Saddened by the affairs of the Southern Dynasties—the long river alone flows till now.
translations.tangshi-300-134: A fallen general of the southern campaign, who once drove a hundred thousand troops. Dismissed, he returns with no ancestral estate; grown old, he clings to this enlightened age. Alone he stood, and the three frontiers were still; his sword alone knows how he scorned his life. Vast, the Han River and Jiang—at sunset, where does he go now?
translations.tangshi-300-135: I gaze after you into the breadth of misty waters; waving my hand, tears wet the kerchief. The flying bird vanishes—where? The green hills stand empty, facing me. One sail on the long river grows far; spring at the five lakes, the setting sun. Who sees, on that sandbar isle, the white duckweed of longing's grief?
translations.tangshi-300-136: Along the whole path I have come, moss shows traces of sandals. White clouds lean on the quiet sandbar; spring grass closes the idle gate. Past the rain I gaze at the pines' color; following the mountains I reach the water's source. The stream-flowers and the chan-mind—facing each other, words are forgotten too.
translations.tangshi-300-137: Homeward heart, sharpest in the new year; alone at the sky's edge, I weep. Age has come to live beneath others; spring returns before the traveler. Ridge gibbons share my dawn and dusk; river willows share wind and mist with me. Already like the exile of Changsha—from now, how many more years?
translations.tangshi-300-138: In the superior kingdom you dwelt as fate allowed; the road you came was like a journey in a dream. Floating sky-deep, the grey sea far; leaving the world, the dharma-boat light. Water-moon joins with chan-stillness; fish and dragons listen to the Sanskrit sound. Only I love that single lamp's shadow—ten thousand li of brightness within the eyes.
translations.tangshi-300-139: Springs and ravines girdle the thatch; cloud-rose rises from the ivy screens. I love the bamboo in the fresh rain; I love the hills in the sunset hour. Idle egrets roost always early; autumn flowers fall, ever later. The houseboy sweeps the vine-path—yesterday I had an appointment with an old friend.
translations.tangshi-300-140: Once we were guests together on the Jiang and Han; meeting, each time we came home drunk. Since we parted like floating clouds, ten years have flowed by like running water. Laughter and joy—the feeling as of old; thin and sparse, our temples streaked. Why do I not go back north?—facing the autumn hills here on the Huai.
translations.tangshi-300-141: In the Chu river's light rain, at the hour of Jianye's evening bell. Dim and vast, the sails come in heavy; dark and deep, the birds depart slow. The sea-gate deep, out of sight; shore trees far off, holding their wet. The feeling of seeing you off is boundless; my soaked lapels rival the scattered threads.
translations.tangshi-300-142: The long mat meets the wind early; the empty city dulls the moonlight. The starry river, one autumn goose; pounding-blocks, a thousand households in the night. The season, I see, is surely late; the hoped-for heart, though lying abed, lingers long. All along chanting your fine lines—before I know it, the crows are already calling.
translations.tangshi-300-143: The road ends where the white clouds end; spring runs as long as the green creek. From time to time falling blossoms arrive, far along the flowing water, fragrant. The idle gate faces the mountain road; deep in willows, the study hall. Secluded light, every bright day; clear radiance shines upon my clothes.
translations.tangshi-300-144: The autumn moon is full again; the city walls, a thousandfold in the night. Once more we meet as in Jiangnan—I turn and doubt we met in a dream. Wind stirs the branches, startling the dark magpies; dewy grass covers the cold insects. Long a traveler, always fit to get drunk; holding each other back, we dread the dawn bell.
translations.tangshi-300-145: Old frontier-pass, withered grass everywhere; parting—just now—is truly sad! The road goes out beyond the cold clouds; the man returns in the time of evening snow. Orphaned young, he wandered early; in many hardships I knew you late. Hiding tears, vainly facing each other—in wind and dust, when shall we meet?
translations.tangshi-300-146: After ten years of war and chaos, grown up, we meet at last. I start at a stranger's surname at first sight; naming you, I remember your childhood face. All the sea-changed affairs since we parted, told till the evening bell of the darkening sky. Tomorrow, on the road to Baling—how many more ranges of autumn hills?
translations.tangshi-300-147: We parted by the rivers and seas of old; several times since, mountains have stood between. Meeting suddenly, I turn and doubt it a dream; grieving together, each asks the other's years. A lone lamp, cold, shines on the rain; deep in bamboo, darkness, floating smoke. Then tomorrow's parting-grief still to come—with the farewell cup we linger, passing it between us.
translations.tangshi-300-148: A still night, neighbors on no side; a poor, run-down dwelling, the old estate gone to seed. In the rain, yellow-leaved trees; by the lamp, a white-headed man. For my long sinking alone I feel ashamed that you visit so often. All our lives we were destined to be close—and besides, we are kin of the Cai house!
translations.tangshi-300-149: In the world's turmoil we fled south together; now times are calm, and you alone go back north. In a foreign land white hair grew on us; in the old country you will see the green hills as they were. The morning moon passes ruined ramparts; the thronged stars lodge at the old pass. Cold birds and withered grass—everywhere accompanying your grieving face.
translations.tangshi-300-150: The air of a hero between heaven and earth—for a thousand autumns, still awesome. Power split into the three-legged tripod; the enterprise restored the five-zhu coin. Gaining a chancellor who could found a state; bearing a son who took no pattern from the worthy. Desolate—the former dancers of Shu, come to dance before the palace of Wei.
translations.tangshi-300-151: The year before last we campaigned against the Yuezhi; below the city the whole army was lost. Between Hu and Han all news was cut off; in life and death, the longest parting of all. No one gathers the abandoned tents; the returning horses know the tattered flags. I would make offerings—yet doubt you still live; at the ends of the earth I weep at this hour.
translations.tangshi-300-152: Thick, thick the grasses on the plain—withering and flourishing once a year. Wildfire cannot burn them out; the spring wind blows them back to life. Their far fragrance invades the ancient road; their clear green joins the ruined walls. Again I see off the noble traveler; lush, lush, they brim with parting's feeling.
translations.tangshi-300-153: In the inn no good companion; my gathered feelings turn all silent. The cold lamp, remembering old matters; a stray goose's cry startling my sad sleep. Far dreams of home return near dawn; letters from home arrive a year late. Fair are the mist and moon on the grey river—and a fishing boat tied at the gate.
translations.tangshi-300-154: Red leaves rustle in the evening; at the long pavilion, one gourd of wine. Remaining clouds return to Taihua; scattered rains pass over Zhongtiao. Tree-hues recede with the mountains; the river's sound fades toward the sea. Tomorrow we reach the imperial land—and still I dream of fishers and woodcutters.
translations.tangshi-300-155: Through the long night the clear zither sounds; the west wind rises in the green vines. Dying fireflies perch on the jade dew; early geese brush the Silver River. Tall trees, dense still at dawn; far mountains, ever more in the clear light. One leaf falls in Huainan—I feel of a sudden old amid mist and waves.
translations.tangshi-300-156: High perching by nature—hard to be filled; its futile laments waste its voice. At the fifth watch, sparse, about to break off; a whole tree of green, without pity. In petty office, the branch still drifts; the old garden's weeds already grown level. I trouble you most for your warning—I too keep my whole household pure.
translations.tangshi-300-157: Desolate—the 'Precious Sword' song; drifting and mooring, the year nearly spent. Yellow leaves still in wind and rain; from the blue towers, pipes and strings for themselves. New friends meet the scorn of a shallow age; old good friends parted by a broken bond. Heart-broken at Xinfeng wine—to drown sorrow, how many thousand coins the measure?
translations.tangshi-300-158: The guests have all gone from the high pavilion; in the small garden, flowers fly wildly. Irregularly they link along the winding lanes; far and long they escort the slanting rays. Heart-broken, I cannot yet bear to sweep; eyes worn through, still I would have them return. The flower-heart turns with spring's end; what it gains is wetting the clothes.
translations.tangshi-300-159: The guest gone, the waves calm at the railing; the cicadas hushed, dew fills the branches. Forever longing at this season; leaning, standing, time moves on of itself. The Northern Dipper and spring, both far away; the envoy from Nanling, delayed. At the world's end, counting dreams by divination—I doubt, mistaken, that you have found a new friend.
translations.tangshi-300-160: The sinking sun enters the western range; to a thatched hut I visit the lone monk. Fallen leaves—where is the man? Cold clouds—how many layers of road? Alone he strikes the evening's first chime; idly he leans on a single staff. The world, within a grain of dust—for it would I hold to love and hate?
translations.tangshi-300-161: A deserted garrison, yellow leaves falling—he leaves the old pass in high resolve. The high wind at Hanyang's ford; the first sun over Yingmen's hills. On the river, how many of our company remain? From the sky's edge a lone oar returns. When shall we meet again?—with wine in the cup to soothe the parting face.
translations.tangshi-300-162: On the Ba plain the wind and rain have settled; at evening I see the geese's ranks pass often. Fallen leaves—trees of a foreign land; a cold lamp—a lone man in the night. In the empty garden white dew drips; against the lone wall, a wilderness monk for neighbor. Long have I lodged by this suburban gate—in what year shall I offer up this body?
translations.tangshi-300-163: The dew's vapor gathers in cold light; the faint sun sinks over the Chu hill. Gibbons cry in the trees of Dongting; the man rides in a magnolia boat. From the broad marsh the bright moon rises; grey mountains flank the tumbling streams. The lord among the clouds I do not see—all night long I grieve alone at autumn.
translations.tangshi-300-164: A frontier horn sounds through the clear autumn; the garrison man leans on the watchtower. Spring wind faces the Green Mound; the white sun sets over Liangzhou. No troops bar the great desert; travelers roam the farthest borders. The Hu feeling is like these waters—forever wishing to flow south.
translations.tangshi-300-165: Far, far the road through the Three Ba; a sojourner's body in danger, ten thousand li from home. In jumbled hills, on a night of lingering snow, alone I greet the spring of a foreign land. Gradually I grow distant from flesh and blood; I grow close instead to my boy servant. How can I bear it—just now drifting, and tomorrow a new year begins?
translations.tangshi-300-166: The homing ranks to the frontier are all gone—a single shadow, where does it go alone? In evening rain it calls and loses its companions; over the cold pond it hesitates, slow to alight. Cloud-bar mist low, it crosses in the dark; the pass-moon, cold, keeps it company. Not that it is sure to meet the fowler's bolt—yet flying alone, of itself, invites suspicion.
translations.tangshi-300-167: Too early my beauty brought me ruin; I would make up, but laze before the mirror. Favor is not bestowed for looks—then how am I to paint my face? The wind warm, the birds' cries turn faint; the sun high, the flower-shadows layer deep. Year after year the girls by the Yue stream remember each other, gathering lotus blooms.
translations.tangshi-300-168: The clear zither grieves through the long night; round its strings, wind and rain mourn. A lone lamp; I hear the Chu horn; the sinking moon sets over Zhang Terrace. The fragrant grass is already late in the day; my old friend has not come at all. No letter home can be sent—the autumn geese turn south again.
translations.tangshi-300-169: He moved his house to the city's edge, yet the wild path runs in through mulberry and hemp. Lately he planted chrysanthemums by his fence—not yet blooming, though autumn has come. I knock at the gate; no dog barks. About to leave, I ask the western neighbor: the word comes back—he has gone into the mountains, and returns each day only at sunset.
translations.tangshi-300-170: The man of old has ridden the yellow crane away; here nothing remains but Yellow Crane Tower. The yellow crane, once gone, never returns; for a thousand years the white clouds drift on, on. In the clear daylight, Hanyang's trees, distinct row on row; lush, lush, the fragrant grass of Parrot Isle. At dusk, where lies my homeland?—the misty waves on the river set one grieving.
translations.tangshi-300-171: Towering Taihua looks down on Xianyang; the three peaks beyond the sky were not carved by any blade. Before Emperor Wu's shrine the clouds are about to disperse; over the Cactus Palm the rain has just cleared. Rivers and mountains pillow north on the Qin passes' peril; post-house trees stretch west, level toward the Han altars. Let me ask the fame-and-profit travelers by the road: none of them is like studying long life here.
translations.tangshi-300-172: One climb to the Yan Terrace and the traveler's heart startles—pipes and drums blare in the Han generals' camp. Ten thousand li of cold light rise from the heaped snow; dawn-color stirs the perilous banners on the three frontiers. Beacon fires on the battleground press upon the Hu moon; by the sea, cloud-mountains embrace the walls of Ji. In youth I was no clerk who cast down his brush—but for merit I would still beg to take the long tether.
translations.tangshi-300-173: This morning I hear the wanderer singing the parting song; last night thin frost first crossed the river. The wild swan is hard to bear within sorrow; how much more the cloud-mountains one passes as a traveler! The gate-towers' tree-hues hurry the chill nearer; toward evening the pounding-stones of the imperial gardens grow many. Do not look on Chang'an as a place of pleasure—it idles the years away in vain.
translations.tangshi-300-174: Emperor Wen of Han had his high terrace; climbing it this day, the dawn light opens. The cloud-mountains of the three Jin all face north; the wind and rain of the two mausoleums come from the east. The gate-commandant as warden—who could know him now? The river-side old immortal went and never returned. I would seek straightaway the magistrate of Pengze—to share drunk and happy the chrysanthemum-cup.
translations.tangshi-300-176: Alas—for this parting of yours, how does it find you? I rein in my horse, cup in mouth, asking after your exile. At Wu Gorge the gibbons' wailing brings rows of tears; to Hengyang the returning geese carry how many letters? Far on autumn sails at Qingfeng River; sparse old trees by White Emperor's wall. In this enlightened age, favor falls like rain and dew—this parting is only for a while; do not linger in doubt.
translations.tangshi-300-177: Cock-crow on the purple lanes, the dawn light chill; orioles warble as spring colors fade in the imperial city. The golden palace's morning bell opens ten thousand gates; on the jade steps the immortal guard throngs a thousand officials. Flowers greet the sword-pendants, the stars just setting; willows brush the banners, the dew not yet dry. Alone, the guest of Phoenix Pool—a song of Yangchun, hard for all to match.
translations.tangshi-300-178: The red-turbaned timekeeper delivers the dawn tally; the wardrobe ministers just present the kingfisher-cloud robe. The ninefold heaven's Changhe gates open wide on palace halls; the lords of ten thousand lands bow to the imperial crown. The sun's rays just touch the immortal palms and they stir; incense smoke floats close beside the embroidered dragon. Court done, they must draft the five-colored edicts; pendant-sounds return toward the head of Phoenix Pool.
translations.tangshi-300-179: The Wei winds on, bending round the Qin barriers; Yellow Mountain of old slants round the Han palace. The imperial coach goes far out beyond the willows of a thousand gates; from the gallery-way I look back on the Upper Garden's flowers. Twin phoenix watch-towers in the clouds—the imperial city; spring trees in the rain, ten thousand homes. Riding the yang-breath to keep the season's charge—it is not the Sovereign's playful tour of fine sights.
translations.tangshi-300-180: Long rains in the empty woods, the cooking-smoke late; they steam the pigweed, cook the millet, to feed the eastern fields. Vast and dim, the water-fields where egrets fly; dark and dense, the summer woods where orioles sing. In the hills I train stillness, watching the morning hibiscus; beneath the pines, pure fast, I pick the dewy mallow. The old man of the wilds is done vying for seats with others—why should the sea-gulls still doubt him?
translations.tangshi-300-181: Cave-gates and high towers veiled in lingering light; peach and plum in dense shade, willow-catkins flying. Within the palace precincts the sparse bell, the offices late; in the ministries the birds cry, the clerks are few. At dawn I sway my jade pendants hurrying to the golden hall; at evening I present the imperial writs, bowing at the chain-gate. I would force myself to follow you, but age forbids—soon, pleading illness, I will lay aside my court robe.
translations.tangshi-300-182: Where shall I seek the Chancellor's shrine?—outside Brocade-Official City, cypresses thick and dark. Green grass on the steps mirrors its own spring hue; an oriole behind the leaves—its fine song in vain. Thrice he visited, brooding over the plans for the whole realm; two reigns he served, opening and sustaining—the old minister's heart. He marched out, the victory not won, his body first to die—forever making heroes wet their lapels with tears!
translations.tangshi-300-183: North and south of my cottage, all spring water; only the flocks of gulls come day after day. My flowery path has never been swept for a guest; my wicker gate today first opens for you. Far from market, the platter's meal has no double flavors; poor at home, the wine-jar holds only the old brew. Will you drink with the old neighbor across the fence?—I'll call him over to finish the remaining cups!
translations.tangshi-300-184: On West Mountain, white snow, the three garrisons; at the southern shore, the clear river, the Ten Thousand Li Bridge. Within the four seas, wind and dust keep my brothers apart; at the sky's edge, tears—a lone body, far away. Only this late age, given to much sickness; not a drop or mote in answer to the sage reign. Riding out beyond the suburbs, I strain my eyes—I cannot bear how daily the world's affairs run thin.
translations.tangshi-300-185: Beyond Sword Pass, sudden word that Jibei is retaken; at first hearing, tears and snivel soak my clothes. I look back at my wife and children—where is their sorrow?—carelessly I roll up my poems and books, wild with joy. In broad daylight I must sing aloud and drink deep; with spring's green for company, let us go home! Straight through from Ba Gorge, piercing Wu Gorge, then down to Xiangyang, heading for Luoyang!
translations.tangshi-300-186: The wind keen, the sky high, gibbons wailing sad; the islet clear, the sands white, birds wheeling home. Boundless, the falling leaves rustle down; endless, the long river rolls on. A thousand li from home, grieving at autumn, always the traveler; a hundred years of sickness, alone I climb the height. Hardship and bitter regret thicken my frosted temples; poor and adrift, I have newly stopped even the cup of thick wine.
translations.tangshi-300-187: Flowers near the high tower wound the traveler's heart—ten thousand regions in trouble, here I climb. The brocade river's spring color comes from heaven and earth; the floating clouds of Jade-Beacon Fortress change ancient and present. The Pole Star's court above never alters—O western mountain brigands, do not press your incursions! Pitiable—the Last Lord still has his temple; at dusk I chant for a while the 'Liangfu Song.'
translations.tangshi-300-188: Clear autumn in the headquarters, the well-side wutong chill; alone I lodge in the river city, the candle-stand burnt down. All night the horn sounds, mournful, talking to itself; the mid-sky moonlight is fine—but who is there to see it? Wind and dust creep on; letters are cut off; the passes are bleak, the road hard to travel. I have endured ten years of loneliness and drift—forcing myself to roost, for now, on a single branch.
translations.tangshi-300-189: The year's end; yin and yang hurry the short days; at the sky's edge frost and snow clear into a cold sky. At the fifth watch the drums and horns sound, mournful and grand; over the Three Gorges the starry river's shadows tremble. Wild weeping from a thousand houses—news of war; at several spots the barbarian songs rise from the fishermen and woodcutters. The sleeping dragon, the leaping horse—all end as yellow earth; affairs and letters drift on in idle silence.
translations.tangshi-300-190: Scattered and torn in the northeast's wind and dust, I drifted and wandered between heaven and earth in the southwest. Three Gorges towers and terraces held me, sun and moon on end; the five streams' dressed tribes shared their clouds and hills with me. The Jie-barbarian served his lord to the end, faithless; a wandering poet grieving at the times, and not yet home. Yu Xin's whole life was desolation itself—in his last years his verses stirred the river passes.
translations.tangshi-300-191: In the falling leaves I deeply know Song Yu's grief—graceful, learned, he too is my master. Gazing into a thousand autumns, I shed tears in vain; desolate, a different age, not his time. His old homestead by rivers and hills keeps nothing but literary ornament; the cloud-and-rain terrace in ruins—was it ever a dreamer's thought? Most of all the Chu palace is wholly vanished; boatmen point at where it might have been, doubting to this day.
translations.tangshi-300-192: Ten thousand hills and a thousand ravines hurry toward Jingmen; the village where Bright Consort grew up still stands. Once gone from the Purple Terrace into the northern desert, she left only the green mound facing the dusk. From her painted portrait, who ever knew her spring-wind face?—her girdle-gems returned in vain, the moonlit soul. A thousand years the pipa has spoken in Hu speech; clearly in its tunes her grief and grievance are told.
translations.tangshi-300-193: The lord of Shu campaigned against Wu and halted in the Three Gorges; the year he died was also at Yong'an Palace. The kingfisher banners are only imagined in the empty hills; the jade halls stand void in a wilderness temple. In the old shrine the fir and pine nest the water-cranes; at the seasonal rites the village elders come and go. The shrine of the Martial Marquis stands always nearby—one body, lord and minister, share their sacrifices.
translations.tangshi-300-194: Zhuge Liang's great name hangs through the universe; a founding minister's remaining image, solemn, high, and pure. The tripartite division—he turned it with his stratagems; through ten thousand ages in the cloud-sky, a single feather. Between Bo and Zhong, we see Yi Yin and Lü Shang; his command settled as if certain put Xiao and Cao to shame. Fate moved, the Han's mandate could not return in the end—his will resolved, his body spent in the toil of the army.
translations.tangshi-300-195: How could my life's course foresee receiving so kind an edict? Of worldly affairs I knew only how to learn the drunkard's song. Over the river the moon is bright; Hu geese pass; in Huainan the trees fall; Chu hills abound. For my lodging I am glad, for now, to be near the grey-sea shores; I face my shadow—what can be done about my white hair? Today we are all grown old and tottering—I am ashamed you still urge me to beware the winds and waves.
translations.tangshi-300-196: Three years an exiled official, here he tarried; for ten thousand ages remains the exile of Chu's grief. Through autumn grass I seek alone the traces of the man gone; in the cold woods, in vain I see the hour of the slanting sun. Though Wen of Han was enlightened, his grace ran thin; the Xiang waters, heartless, how could they know my mourning? Silent, silent, the rivers and hills where leaves fall—pity him: for what affair was he driven to the sky's edge!
translations.tangshi-300-197: The sandbars are waveless, smokeless again; the Chu traveler's longing grows ever fainter-far. At Hankou the sunset slants on the crossing birds; the autumn waters of Dongting stretch far to meet the sky. The lone city, hills at its back, sounds its cold horn; the lone garrison by the river moors its boat at night. Jia Yi presented memorials, anxious for the Han house—driven to exile in Changsha, pitied by ancient and present alike.
translations.tangshi-300-198: In the second month the orioles fly over the Upper Forest; the spring city, the Forbidden Purple, darkens at dawn. The Eternal Joy bell fades beyond the flowers; Dragon Pool's willow-hues deepen in the rain. The yang-warmth never melts the hatred of a dead-end road; toward the cloud-sky I long keep the heart that holds the sun. Ten years I have presented my fu and not yet met favor—I blush to show my white hair to those with flowered hairpins.
translations.tangshi-300-199: Among the blossoms last year I parted from you; today the blossoms open—another year gone. The world's affairs, vast and dim, none can foresee; spring's gloom, dark and deep, I sleep alone through it. My body full of sickness—I long for my fields; in my district, fugitives from famine—I blush at my salary. I hear you wish to come and ask after me—the west tower's moon has waxed and waned how many times?
translations.tangshi-300-200: First I saw the Five-Storeyed towers on the immortal terrace; the scene, chill and clear, after the night's rain has cleared. The mountain hues join far off with the Qin trees' dusk; the pounding-stones nearby announce the Han palace's autumn. Sparse pines, their shadows falling—the empty altar still; fine grasses, their scent idle—the little grotto secluded. What need to seek some realm beyond the world?—in the human world there is, after all, a Cinnabar Hill of its own.
translations.tangshi-300-201: Orioles warble and swallows chatter, announcing the new year; the road to Mayi and Longdui stretches several thousand li. My home by the layered walls neighbors the Han park; my heart follows the bright moon to the Hu sky. From her loom the brocade-letters tell a lifelong regret; the flowering branch by the tower laughs at her sleeping alone. I ask the Rong-campaigning Chariot-General—when will you turn your banners and carve your merit on Yanran?
translations.tangshi-300-202: Clouds part; far off I see the city of Hanyang—still a lone sail's day-journey away. The merchant sleeps by day, knowing the waves are calm; the boatmen talk at night, feeling the tide arise. Through the Three Xiang, my sorrowing temples meet the autumn hues; a heart for home ten thousand li faces the bright moon. The old estate is all gone with the wars—how much more can I bear the drums of war along the river?
translations.tangshi-300-203: The high tower on the city walls meets the great wilderness; the sea-sky sorrow spreads, boundless and dim. Startling winds buffet the lotus waters; dense rains slant against the vines on the wall. Range upon range of ridge-trees block the thousand-li gaze; the river's turns are like nine coiled entrails. Together we came to the tattooed lands of the Hundred Yue—still, letters and word from one another stall in a single region.
translations.tangshi-300-204: Wang Jun's tower-ships came down from Yizhou; the royal aura of Jinling dimmed and folded. A thousand-fathom chain of iron sank to the river's bottom; a single banner of surrender emerged from Stone City. How many times has the human world grieved over past affairs? The mountain's shape, as of old, pillows on the cold current. From now on, with all four seas as one home—yet at the old ramparts, bleakly, reeds and rushes in autumn.
translations.tangshi-300-205: The youngest girl, whom Lord Xie doted on most, married me, a Qianlou, and every turn of life went wrong. Seeing I had no clothes she searched the straw hamper; humoring me for wine she plucked off her gold hairpin. Wild greens for meals, content with long bean-leaves; fallen leaves for fuel, gazing up at the old locust. Today my salary passes a hundred thousand—for you I hold the sacrifice and keep the fast.
translations.tangshi-300-206: What we once said in jest about after death—today it all stands before my eyes. Your clothes I have given away, nearly all; your needlework remains—I cannot bear to open it. I still think of our old love and pity the maids; in dreams I have also sent you money. Truly I know this grief is every person's—yet a poor couple's every affair is grief.
translations.tangshi-300-207: Sitting idle I grieve for you, and for myself—of a hundred years, how much is there? Deng You had no son—I will seek to know my fate; Pan Yue's laments for the dead still wasted his words. The same grave, dark and dim—what is there to hope for? Meetings in other lives are harder still to expect. I can only keep my eyes open all the long night—to repay a lifetime of brows that never unfurrowed.
translations.tangshi-300-208: Times hard, the year lean, the ancestral estate emptied; brothers sojourning, each to west and east. Fields and gardens desolate after shield and spear; flesh and blood scattered along the roads. Mourning my shadow, parted like geese a thousand li; torn from our roots, scattered like tumbleweed in the ninth-month wind. Gazing at the same bright moon, we must all be weeping—one night, the homeward heart, the same in five places.
translations.tangshi-300-209: The brocade lute, for no reason, fifty strings; one string, one bridge, recalling the flowering years. Zhuangzi's dawn dream, a butterfly, lost; the departed emperor's spring heart, entrusted to the cuckoo. In the blue sea, under the moon, pearls shed tears; in the warm sun of Blue Fields, jade breathes mist. This feeling—could it have waited to become a memory? Even then, at the very moment, it was already lost.
translations.tangshi-300-210: Last night's stars, last night's wind, west of the painted tower, east of the cassia hall. Our bodies have no wings of rainbow phoenixes to fly paired; our hearts have the single point of the magic rhinoceros-horn, through which all passes. Across the seats, the hook-passing game, the spring wine warm; divided into teams, the riddle-shooting, the wax-lamp red. Alas—I heard the drum and must answer to my office, galloping my horse to the Orchid Terrace, like a whirling tumbleweed.
translations.tangshi-300-211: The palaces of Purple Spring locked in mist and rosy clouds—he would take Ruined City for his imperial home. Had the jade seal not passed to the sun-browed one, the brocade sails would have reached the ends of the earth. By now no fireflies from the rotting grass; for all ages, crows at dusk in the drooping willows. If, underground, you meet the Last Lord of Chen—would it be right to ask him again for the 'Courtyard Flowers'?
translations.tangshi-300-212: Coming was empty words; gone—no trace at all; the moon slants on the tower, the fifth-watch bell. In dreams, crying at the far parting, hard to call back; the letter, hurriedly finished, the ink not yet thick. Candlelight half-hoods the golden kingfisher; musk-scent faintly passes the embroidered lotus. Liu Lang already grieved that Penglai Mountain was far—now it lies ten thousand ranges beyond Penglai.
translations.tangshi-300-213: The east wind soughs; fine rain comes; beyond the lotus pond, a faint roll of thunder. The gold toad-guard nibbles the lock—incense-smoke enters; the jade tiger draws the rope—the well-bucket returns. Jia's daughter peeped through the curtain at the young officer Han; Consort Fu left her pillow for the Prince of Wei's talent. Let not the spring heart vie to bloom with the flowers—an inch of longing, an inch of ash.
translations.tangshi-300-214: Gibbons and birds still seem to dread the tally-bearing dispatches; wind and clouds always come to guard the piled brushwood. In vain he made his commander-in-chief wield the divine brush; in the end we saw the surrendering king ride the relay-cart. With the talents of Guan Zhong and Yue Yi, he was not unworthy—but Guan and Zhang, their lives cut short, what could he do? In other years, passing the shrine at Brocade Lane, his 'Liangfu Song' finished, regret remains.
translations.tangshi-300-215: Meeting is hard; parting is hard, too; the east wind powerless, the hundred flowers ruined. The spring silkworm spins till death before its silk is done; the candle's tears run dry only when it burns to ash. At dawn's mirror, I grieve only that my cloud-coiffure changes; chanting at night, you must feel the moonlight cold. Penglai lies not far from here—O blue bird, diligent, go and look for me.
translations.tangshi-300-216: Mournfully I lie in the new spring, in my white lined gown; White Gate stands desolate, the heart at odds with all it wished. The red tower, parted by the rain, gazed at in cold; pearl blinds adrift with lamplight—I return alone. Far roads—you must grieve at spring's lateness; the night's last watch—still I keep my dim dream. The jade ear-plugs, the sealed letter—by what road could they reach you? Ten thousand li of cloud-gauze, a single wild goose flying.
translations.tangshi-300-217: Phoenix-tail fragrant gauze, thin, in how many folds; the round green-patterned canopy, sewn deep in the night. A fan shaped from the moon's soul—my shyness, hard to hide; the carriage went with thunder's rumble—no words passed between us. Once was the lonely dark, the gold cinders waning; since then no word at all, though the pomegranates redden. My dappled colt is tied only by the bank of drooping willows—where, to the southwest, does a good wind blow?
translations.tangshi-300-218: Heavy curtains hang low in the Hall of No-Sorrow; lying down, the clear night stretches fine and long. The goddess's life was ever a dream; the little maiden's dwelling never had a groom. The storm-waves never believed the water-chestnut bough too weak; the moon-dew—who taught the laurel leaves their fragrance? I know full well that longing serves no use—yet let it not hinder me that a pure madness is sadness.
translations.tangshi-300-219: The calm, empty waters face the slanting sunbeams; the winding isle, dim and boundless, joins the green-blue. Waveside, horses neigh—I watch the boat leave; by the willows people rest, awaiting the ferry home. Several clumps of sand-grass—flocks of gulls scatter; ten thousand acres of river-fields, one egret flies. Who understands taking a boat to seek Fan Li—among the misty waters of the five lakes, alone forgetting all schemes?
translations.tangshi-300-220: Su Wu's soul dissolved before the Han envoy; the ancient shrine, the tall trees—both lost in mist. At the cloud's edge, wild-geese broken off from the Hu sky's moon; on the ridge, sheep return through the frontier grass's smoke. The day he came back, the towers were no more the tent of old; the day he went, his cap and sword—he was in his prime. At Maoling he never saw the marquisate's seal bestowed; in vain he weeps over the autumn waves at the river of time.
translations.tangshi-300-221: In the twelve-storied towers all finish their dawn makeup; from the Immortal-Gazing Tower they gaze for the lord. The lock holds the golden beast-rings, cold in a chain; the water-clock's copper dragon drips—the day is long. Cloud-coiffure done, she faces the mirror again; about to change her gauze robe, she adds more incense. Peeking afar where the main hall's curtain parts—a palace girl in tunic and trousers sweeps the imperial bed.
translations.tangshi-300-222: Behind the wicker gate I never knew brocade's fragrance; wanting to entrust a good matchmaker only wounds me more. Who loves a lofty grace and style out of fashion? All admire the thrifty dressing of the day. I dare boast my ten fingers' needlework clever; I do not make my painted brows compete for length. My bitter regret: year after year I stitch gold thread—making bridal gowns for other women.
translations.tangshi-300-223: The young wife of the Lu house, amid tulip incense; a pair of swallows roost on the tortoiseshell beams. In the ninth month the cold pounding-stones hurry the leaves; ten years of frontier duty—she remembers Liaoyang. North of the White Wolf River, letters have ceased; south of the city, by Vermilion Phoenix Gate, the autumn nights are long. For whom does she hold her sorrow, unseen, alone?—and worse, the bright moon shines upon her flowery gown.
translations.tangshi-300-224: Empty mountains—I see no one; only the sound of voices is heard. The returning light enters the deep wood, and shines again upon the green moss.
translations.tangshi-300-225: Sitting alone in the secluded bamboo grove, I play the lute and give a long whistle. Deep in the woods no one knows—the bright moon comes to shine on me.
translations.tangshi-300-226: In the hills I have finished seeing you off; at dusk I close the wicker gate. The spring grass will green again next year—but will the noble traveler return?
translations.tangshi-300-227: The red beans grow in the southern lands; when spring comes, how many sprays will bloom? Gather them, I pray, more and more—for nothing loves longing like this.
translations.tangshi-300-228: You have come from my homeland—you must know the things of home. The day you left, by the carved window—had the winter plum blossomed yet?
translations.tangshi-300-229: Into the mountains you go, deep or shallow—you must enjoy their every beauty to the full. Do not imitate the man of Wuling who roamed the Peach Blossom Spring only for a while.
translations.tangshi-300-230: Fair are the southern ridges of Zhongnan; their piled snow floats above the clouds. The forest's edge shows the clearing sky's hue; in the city, evening's cold grows.
translations.tangshi-300-231: I move my boat to moor by the misty isle; at dusk the traveler's sorrow renews. The wilds so wide, the sky hangs lower than the trees; the river so clear, the moon comes near to men.
translations.tangshi-300-232: Spring sleep, not waking at dawn; everywhere I hear singing birds. The night's wind and rain sounds—how many blossoms have fallen, who knows?
translations.tangshi-300-233: Before the bed, bright moonlight—I wonder if it is frost upon the ground. I lift my head to gaze at the bright moon; I lower my head and think of home.
translations.tangshi-300-234: The beauty rolls up the pearl curtain, sits deep within, her moth-brows knit. I see only the wet track of tears—I know not whom her heart resents.
translations.tangshi-300-235: His merit capped the tripartite realm; his fame set in the Eight-Array plan. The river flows; the stones do not turn—his lasting regret: the lost chance to swallow Wu.
translations.tangshi-300-236: The white sun leans on the hills to sink; the Yellow River flows into the sea. To see a thousand miles farther, climb one storey higher.
translations.tangshi-300-237: Grey-grey the Bamboo-Grove Temple; faint, faint, the bell's evening sound. Hat on back, carrying the slanting sun, into the green hills he goes home, alone, far.
translations.tangshi-300-238: Cold-clear on the seven strings; listening still, the wind in the pines. The old melodies—I have always loved them; but people today play them no more.
translations.tangshi-300-239: A lone cloud, a wild crane—how could such dwell in the world of men? Do not buy Mount Wozhou—the men of the day already know that place.
translations.tangshi-300-240: Thinking of you on this autumn night; strolling, I chant into the cool sky. In the empty mountains pine-cones fall—the recluse, surely, is not yet asleep.
translations.tangshi-300-241: The singing zither with its golden-millet bridges; her white hands before the jade house. To win a glance from the young lord of Zhou—time and again she plucks the wrong string.
translations.tangshi-300-242: On the third day she goes down to the kitchen, washes her hands, and makes the broth. Not yet knowing her mother-in-law's taste, she first sends it to her sister-in-law to taste.
translations.tangshi-300-243: Last night my skirt-band loosened; this morning the money-spiders fly. My rouge and powder I must not lay aside—could it be my husband is coming home?
translations.tangshi-300-244: From a thousand mountains the birds' flight is gone; on ten thousand paths human traces are wiped out. A lone boat, an old man in rain-cape and hat, fishes alone in the cold river snow.
translations.tangshi-300-245: A sparse and desolate ancient traveling palace; the palace flowers bloom red in loneliness. A white-headed palace woman remains, sitting idle, speaking of Xuanzong.
translations.tangshi-300-246: New-brewed wine with its green foam, a little red-clay stove. Evening comes; the sky threatens snow—could you stay for one cup?
translations.tangshi-300-247: Three thousand li from my homeland; twenty years deep within the palace. One song of 'Hemanzi'—and both tears fall before my lord.
translations.tangshi-300-248: Toward evening my heart grew ill at ease; I drove the carriage up the ancient plain. The setting sun is boundless in its beauty—only, it is near the dusk.
translations.tangshi-300-249: Beneath the pine I ask the boy; he says the master's gone to gather herbs. 'He's only somewhere in this mountain—deep in the clouds, I know not where.'
translations.tangshi-300-250: Beyond the ranges, letters have ceased; through winter, and again spring has come. Nearing home, my heart grows only more fearful—I dare not ask the traveler coming toward me.
translations.tangshi-300-251: I beat away the yellow orioles, bid them not sing on the branches. Their singing startles my dream—where I would reach Liaoxi.
translations.tangshi-300-252: High hangs the Big Dipper's seven stars; at night Geshu carries his blade. Even now the watching nomads dare not cross Lintao to pasture their horses.
translations.tangshi-300-253: Where does your family live?—my own home is at Hengtang. I moor my boat a moment to ask: perhaps we are from the same home country.
translations.tangshi-300-254: My home faces the waters of the Nine Rivers; coming and going, I keep to the Nine Rivers' side. We are both of Changgan—yet never knew each other, born and raised.
translations.tangshi-300-255: On the jade steps white dew rises; the long night soaks my silken socks. She draws back the crystal curtain and gazes, bright and clear, at the autumn moon.
translations.tangshi-300-256: Vulture-feather arrows, gold Pugu bows; swallow-tail streamers, embroidered Maowhu banners. Alone he stands, proclaiming the new command—ten thousand camps shout as one.
translations.tangshi-300-257: The woods darken, the grass starts in the wind; at night the general draws his bow. At dawn they search for the white-feathered arrow—embedded deep in the stone's edge.
translations.tangshi-300-258: The moonless dark, wild geese flying high; at night the chanyu steals away in flight. We would chase him with our light cavalry—heavy snow covers bows and blades.
translations.tangshi-300-259: Wild camp-tents screen the jasper feast; the Qiang and Rong come to hail the returning troops. Drunk, in their golden armor they dance; thunder-drums shake the mountains and streams.
translations.tangshi-300-260: I married a merchant of Qutang—morning after morning he fails the tryst he promised. Had I known the tide keeps its time, I would have married the tide-play boy.
translations.tangshi-300-261: I left home a youth and come back an old man; my accent unchanged, my temple hairs thinned. The children see me, a stranger, and smiling ask: 'Guest, where have you come from?'
translations.tangshi-300-262: Dimly a flying bridge parts the wild mist; west of the rocky point I ask the fisherman's boat. The peach blossoms all day drift with the current—the grotto, by which bend of the clear stream?
translations.tangshi-300-263: Alone in a foreign land, a stranger among strangers; every festive day I miss my kin twice over. Far away I know my brothers, at the climbing place, wear dogwood sprigs—all but one man short.
translations.tangshi-300-264: Cold rain joins the river; at night I enter Wu. At dawn I see the guest off—the Chu hills stand lonely. If my kin and friends in Luoyang ask after me: a heart of ice within a jade flask.
translations.tangshi-300-265: The young wife in her chamber never knew sorrow; on a spring day, made up, she mounts the green tower. Suddenly she sees the willow's green by the road—she regrets she sent her husband off to seek a noble title.
translations.tangshi-300-266: Last night the wind opened the dew-well peaches; over Weiyang's front hall the moon-wheel hung high. The dancers of Pingyang newly received favor—beyond the curtain, the spring chill brings her a brocade robe.
translations.tangshi-300-267: Grape wine in a night-glowing cup; about to drink, the pipa hurries us on horseback. Do not laugh if we lie drunk on the battlefield—since olden days, how many warriors ever returned?
translations.tangshi-300-268: My old friend takes leave west of Yellow Crane Tower, amid misty blossoms in the third month, bound for Yangzhou. The lone sail's distant shadow vanishes into the blue sky's end—only the Long River seen, flowing to the sky's edge.
translations.tangshi-300-269: At dawn I leave White Emperor City, high in the colored clouds; a thousand li to Jiangling, returned in a single day. The gibbons on both banks cry without ceasing—the light boat has already passed ten thousand-fold mountains.
translations.tangshi-300-270: East I look toward home—the road stretches on and on; both sleeves are sodden, the tears will not dry. Meeting on horseback, no paper or brush—will you carry word for me: all is well?
translations.tangshi-300-271: Often seen in the Prince of Qi's mansion; heard now and then before Cui Jiu's hall. Now, just when Jiangnan's scenery is at its best, in the season of falling blossoms I meet you again.
translations.tangshi-300-272: Alone I love the secluded grasses growing by the ravine; above them, orioles sing deep in the trees. The spring tide brings rain, urgent in its evening coming; at the wild ferry no one—an empty boat drifts athwart.
translations.tangshi-300-273: The moon sets, crows cry, the frost fills the sky; riverside maples, fishing lamps, I face them in sad sleep. Beyond Gusu's walls, Cold Mountain Temple—at midnight the bell sounds, reaching the traveler's boat.
translations.tangshi-300-274: Nowhere in the spring city do flying flowers not swirl; in the Cold-Food east wind the imperial willows slant. At dusk in the Han palace the candles are passed out; thin smoke drifts into the houses of the five lords.
translations.tangshi-300-275: Deep in the night, moonlight fills half the houses; the Northern Dipper droops, the Southern Dipper slants. Tonight I first feel the spring air's warmth—the insects' sounds newly pierce the green window-screen.
translations.tangshi-300-276: The sun sets beyond the gauze window, dusk gathering; in the golden house, unseen, the tear-tracks. The lonely empty court, spring nearly late; pear blossoms cover the ground—the gate stays shut.
translations.tangshi-300-277: Year after year, Golden River and Jade Pass again; morning after morning, whip and blade-ring. Three springs' white snow returns to the Green Mound; ten thousand li of Yellow River winds round Black Mountain.
translations.tangshi-300-278: From the sky's halfway point of the Jade Tower rise pipes and song; the wind carries the palace maidens' laughing voices in harmony. The moon-palace's shadows part; the night water-clock is heard; the crystal curtain rolled up, near the River of Autumn in the sky.
translations.tangshi-300-279: Before Huile Peak the sand is like snow; outside the Surrender-Receiving City the moon is like frost. I know not where the reed-pipe sounds—one night, every man on campaign gazes toward home.
translations.tangshi-300-280: By Zhuque Bridge wild grasses bloom; at Wuyi Lane's mouth the slanting evening sun. The swallows that of old before the halls of Wang and Xie—now fly into the houses of ordinary folk.
translations.tangshi-300-281: New makeup suits her face as she comes down the vermilion tower; spring light locked deep, the whole courtyard grieves. Walking to the central court she counts the blossoms—an alights upon her jade hairpin.
translations.tangshi-300-282: Tears soaked the silk kerchief, no dream would come; deep in the night, from the front hall, the sound of singing to accompaniment. Her rosy face not yet old, the favor already cut off—leaning on the incense-warmer she sits until dawn.
translations.tangshi-300-283: Moon-traces pass the palace gates and trees; her charming eyes watch only the egrets' roost by night. Slantwise she plucks her jade hairpin by the lamp's edge—to pry open the red flame and save the flying moth.
translations.tangshi-300-284: The slanting sun shines on the Spirit-Gathering Terrace; red trees bloom to greet the dawn dew. Last night the retired emperor newly bestowed the tally—Taizhen enters the curtain with a smile.
translations.tangshi-300-285: The Lady of Guo bears the lord's favor; at dawn she rides her horse through the palace gates. She disdains that rouge would stain her complexion—lightly sweeping her moth-brows, she makes her morning court.
translations.tangshi-300-286: At Jinling's ferry, a little hill-top lodge; one night's lodging, and the traveler's sorrows come of themselves. The tide falls in the night river beneath the slanting moon; two or three sparks of fire—that is Guazhou.
translations.tangshi-300-287: Silent, silent, in flower season, the courtyard gate shut; the beauties stand paired by the jasper rails. Holding a feeling, about to speak of palace matters—before the parrot, they dare not speak.
translations.tangshi-300-288: In the bridal chamber last night the red candles burned; waiting for dawn, before the hall, to bow to her new parents. Makeup done, she asks her husband in a low voice: 'Is the depth of my painted brows in fashion?'
translations.tangshi-300-289: In clear times, having taste is called incompetence; in leisure I love the lone cloud, in stillness the monk. About to take a single banner and go off to rivers and seas, from Leyou Plain I gaze toward Zhaoling.
translations.tangshi-300-290: A broken halberd sunk in the sand, the iron not yet rusted; I brought it up myself, washed and ground it, and recognized the former dynasty. Had the east wind not given young Zhou his chance—spring deep in the Bronze Sparrow Terrace would have locked the two Qiao sisters.
translations.tangshi-300-291: Mist veils the cold water, moonlight veils the sand; at night I moor by the Qinhuai, near a wine-house. The singing girls know not the grief of a fallen kingdom—across the river they still sing 'Courtyard Flowers.'
translations.tangshi-300-292: Green hills faint and far, the waters stretch long; autumn is spent, yet Jiangnan's grasses are not withered. On a moonlit night by the Twenty-Four Bridges—where is the fair one now, teaching the playing of pipes?
translations.tangshi-300-293: Down and out, drifting the rivers and lakes with a boat of wine; waists slender as Chu's, girls light as held in the palm. Ten years, one waking, a Yangzhou dream—won only the name of a fickle lover of the green houses.
translations.tangshi-300-294: Silver candles, autumn light chill on the painted screen; with a little gauze fan she swats at the drifting fireflies. The palace steps' night air is cold as water—sitting, she gazes at the Herd-Boy and Weaver Girl stars.
translations.tangshi-300-295: Graceful and slender, thirteen just past, like a cardamom bud at the tip of its branch in early second month. Along ten miles of Yangzhou road in the spring wind—every beaded curtain rolled up is not her equal.
translations.tangshi-300-296: Full of feeling, yet it seems always without feeling; even before the wine-cup, no smile can form. The candle has a heart, and grieves at parting too—shedding tears for others until dawn.
translations.tangshi-300-297: The splendid affair scattered, chased off by fragrant dust; the heartless water flows on, the grass springs on its own. At dusk in the east wind the birds' complaining cries—the falling blossoms still resemble the woman who leapt from the tower.
translations.tangshi-300-298: You ask when I will return—no return date yet; the night rain on Mount Ba swells the autumn pool. When shall we trim the candle together by the west window, speaking of this time of night rain on Mount Ba?
translations.tangshi-300-299: Song's clouds, Qin's trees—long parted in our dwellings; the twin carp, far, far, a single sheet. Ask no more after the old guest of the Liang garden—the sick Xiangru of Maoling, in autumn rain.
translations.tangshi-300-300: Because of the cloud-screened room, boundlessly sweet; spring nights in Phoenix City, the chill done, come dreaded. For no reason she married a lord with a golden turtle badge—betraying the fragrant quilt for morning court.
translations.tangshi-300-301: On a whim he toured south, no curfew declared—who in the ninefold palace ever heeded the censor's sealed memorials? The spring wind had the whole nation cut palace brocade—half for saddle-cloths, half for sails.
translations.tangshi-300-302: The Queen Mother of the West opens her carved window at Jasper Pool; the Song of Yellow Bamboo rises, moving the earth with grief. The eight steeds ran thirty thousand li a day—why did King Mu never come again?
translations.tangshi-300-303: The mica screen deepens the candle's shadow; the long river sinks, the morning stars go down. Chang'e must regret stealing the elixir—night after night, a heart against the blue sea and sky.
translations.tangshi-300-304: In the Xuan Chamber he sought the worthy and questioned the exiled minister; Jia Yi's talent and style were beyond all peer. Pitiable—the midnight's empty courtesy at the mat's edge: he asked not of the people's lot, but of ghosts and gods!
translations.tangshi-300-305: On the icy mat and silver bed no dream would form; the blue sky like water, the night clouds light. The geese's cries pass far beyond Xiao-Xiang—within the twelve-storied tower the moon shines on, alone.
translations.tangshi-300-306: Xuanzong turned his horse back as Consort Yang died; the cloud-and-rain love hard to forget, sun and moon made new. In the end it was the deed of a sage and enlightened Son of Heaven—compared to whom, at the well of Jingyang Palace?
translations.tangshi-300-307: Beyond the azure railings the embroidered curtain hangs low; the scarlet screen painted with broken-branch sprays. On the eight-foot dragon-mustard, square brocade bedding—the weather already cool, the cold not yet come.
translations.tangshi-300-308: River rain drizzles, the river grass grows even; the six dynasties like a dream, the birds cry in vain. Most heartless of all are Tower City's willows—still veiling the ten-mile dike with their mist.
translations.tangshi-300-309: Swearing to sweep the Huns away, never sparing themselves—five thousand in sable-and-brocade fell among the Hu dust. Pitiable: the bones by the banks of the Wuding River—still the men in the deep chambers' dreams.
translations.tangshi-300-310: My parting dream lingers long to the Xie house; the little cloisters wind round, the curved rails slant. Full of feeling, only the moon in the spring courtyard—still shining for the parted one on the fallen blossoms.
translations.tangshi-300-311: The whole Cold-Food season's rain, the grass lush and green; the wind over the wheat sprouts, willows mirrored on the dike. We all alike have homes we cannot return to—O cuckoo, do not sing beside my ear.
translations.tangshi-300-312: The morning rain of Weicheng dampens the light dust; the guest-house green, the willow color fresh. I urge you: finish one more cup of wine—west of Yangguan Pass there are no old friends.
translations.tangshi-300-313: The laurel soul newly risen, the autumn dew faint; the thin gauze already too light, she has not yet changed her gown. Deep in the night she long plucks the silver zither with care—her heart dreads the empty room, she cannot bear to return.
translations.tangshi-300-314: At dawn, broom in hand, the golden hall opens; for a while she wanders with her round fan. Her jade face is not equal to the cold crow's color—it still carries the sunlight's shadow from Zhaoyang Palace.
translations.tangshi-300-315: The moon of Qin times, the passes of Han times; the long-marching men of ten thousand li have not returned. If only the Flying General of Dragon City were here—the Hu horses would never be let cross the Yin Mountains!
