translations.tangshi-300-316: The Yellow River rises far up among the white clouds; a lone walled city amid mountains ten thousand ren high. Why should the Qiang flute grieve at the willow song?—the spring wind never crosses the Jade Gate Pass.
translations.tangshi-300-317: Clouds recall her robes, flowers recall her face; the spring wind brushes the balustrade, dew-rich splendor. If not seen upon the Mountain of Gathered Jade, then met by moonlight at the Jasper Terrace.
translations.tangshi-300-318: One spray of crimson, dew-gathered fragrance; the cloud-and-rain of Mount Wu were heartbreak in vain. Tell me: in the Han palace who was her like?—lovable Zhao Feiyan, leaning on her fresh-made-up self.
translations.tangshi-300-319: Famed flower and kingdom-toppling beauty, both charmed, each other delighting; always winning the lord's smiling gaze. Leaning on the rail at the Aloes Pavilion's north—the spring wind dissolves boundless regret.
translations.tangshi-300-320: I urge you: do not cherish the golden-threaded gown; I urge you: cherish the hours of your youth. When the blossoms open and may be plucked, pluck them straightway—do not wait till blossomless, vainly breaking the bough!
translations.songci-300-1: Near the time of Pure Brightness. The green birds on the branch are heartsore. A pity—that one stretch of clear song is all given over to the dusk. I would pour it out low to the willow-flowers, but fear the willow-flowers are too fickle to understand grieving at spring. Thinking of my lodgings in the land of Chu, the tender feelings of parting—who is there to keep me warm? The empty cup weeps by night; the green mountains do not speak; the waning moon stands at the door. Before the emerald-jade tower there is only a single wave of Xiang waters, rocking the Xiang clouds. Heaven long, dreams short—I ask when I shall see Taogen again. In this plight, surely in all the human world there is no paired blade that can cut away the sorrow-scars on the heart.
translations.songci-300-2: Wet clouds cling to the wild geese's shadows. Gazing down the road of travel, sorrowing and lost, the threads of parting hard to put in order. A thousand gold buys the light of time—but only the sparse bell hastens the dawn, and jumbled crows cry the dark home. The flowers, dimmed, know better. So much feeling—we met in dreams. Even the floating clouds, never coming back at all, should still send word of themselves. Solitary, far. The heart that vowed with the phoenix, the journey that would ride the crane—later meetings have no certainty. The silk of feeling waits to be cut, and only stirs up the old-time grievance. I fear Heaven may let those paired swallows, somewhere, be stained again with leftover rouge and powder. Facing the mirror-flower, I would tell my longing—and see who has grown thinner.
translations.songci-300-3: Blushing red and lightly knit with regret, fallen by the evening wind, one shred of embroidery spotting the doubled matting. On the old dike the swallow-tails part; cassia-poled boats, light gulls, the treasure-harness leaning on the last clouds. A thousand strands of green lament; gradually the road enters the immortal cove, the ford gone lost. The entrails wind in vain; through the flowers, from time to time, I see the turned-away waist of Chu. Hesitant, lingering. Writing at the gate in despondence, the fallen shoe tugging at my thoughts—those trysts in the shadows, hard to fix. Then I first realize: the lingering feeling is owed to the eyes; the loosened girdle comes from spring. Tomorrow's affairs will chill with the lone smoke, making the whole lake wind and rain, grieving the man. The mountain brows darken; dusty waves pale-green, without a trace.
translations.songci-300-4: Breaking smoke, parting thoughts. The things that concern me—the setting sun reddens and hides in the frosted trees. Half a pot of autumn water offers to the yellow flowers, their fragrance scattering west in wind and rain. Even with the jade harness, the light flight of swift wings—who mourns, desolate, at the ancient terrace in ruins? I remember drunkenly treading the Southern Screen; the painted fan choked, the cold cicada tired of dreaming, not knowing Man or Su. For a while I face the old festival, passing the cup; dust on the paper, moth in the brush—the broken stanza, a whole year too lazy to compose. The small moon's slanting shadow turns past the eastern hedge; the night is cold, the last crickets talk. White hair comes early from a myriad strands of sorrow. The sudden gale, let it whirl away the black gauze cap. Carelessly I take up the dogwood to look—only making the appointment for next year, at the green-blue heights.
translations.songci-300-5: Sunlit threads tug my thoughts awry. Facing the grey river, the slanting sun, the flowers fly, the man far away. The drooping willows darken the Wu gardens. Just when the tavern flags grow cold in mist, the river bridge warm in wind. The orchid feeling, the sweet-iris gaze—stirring longing, spring-rooted by the wine's edge. How could they know the chanting frame, wound and worn, gradually making the old gown re-cut. Broken-hearted. Drifting red, a thousand waves; the waning moon, the lone tower—never can keep the swallows. Song-dust congeals on the fan. I would trust a message, resolved to break the clasp—then try, lamp raised, to write, and still lean, unable to bear it, the letter's page secretly rolled away with tears. Sent to the leftover clouds and remnant rains of Penglai—she too should dream of me.
translations.songci-300-6: Embroidered canopy, mandarin-duck pillars. Red feeling dense; heavy cloud of hair low-guarding the Qin tree. Fragrant roots leaning together, calyxes joined with jeweled clasps, the brocade-screened woman envies. The east wind sleeps its fill on the crossed branches, just dreaming flowers, the jade hairpin's swallow prongs. Screened by the brimming candle, fully lighting the joyous clusters; the widowed moon, neglected, passes in shame. In the human world ten thousand feelings go lonely; accustomed to the Huaqing baths, the spring brims with wind and dew. Linked chignons warmed together, knotted hearts in one knot, toward the place of received favor. Who would sing the Song of Everlasting Regret for them? The dark hall locked, autumn-lamp night-whispers. Telling the old tryst—unfailing the spring vow, dawn-crimson and dusk-jade.
translations.songci-300-7: Mist-veiled waters, the Xiling road of peach-leaf ferry—ten years of heartbroken soul at the tide's tail. The old willow climbed again; the light gulls gather where we parted; the ruined pavilion I lean on alone. A cool gust rises sudden; dim over misty shallows sails fly; evening mountains lie blue-green. Only there are river flowers, with me facing the autumn mirror, shining on haggardness. In the splendid hall the candles dim as the guest is seen off; where the eye-waves turn back, fragrant grace flowed like water. Ice-gathered bones, snow-dipped soft scallions—I still remember the deep meaning of sharing the melon. The clear cup unwashed; dreams never wet the wandering clouds, vainly staining the remnant tears. A pity, the autumn night—in jumbled crickets and scattered rain.
translations.songci-300-8: Listening to wind, listening to rain, I pass the Pure Brightness. Grieving, I draft the burial-flower inscription. Before the tower the green darkens on the road where we parted—one thread of willow, one inch of tender feeling. In the biting chill of spring I grow drunk with wine; in the tangled dawn-dreams orioles cry. Day after day I sweep the grove-pavilion of the West Garden; still I enjoy the clearing sky. Yellow wasps again and again dart at the swing-ropes—there, of old, her slender hand's scent clings. Grieved that the paired mandarin-ducks never come—on the secluded steps, in one night, moss grows.
translations.songci-300-9: The last cold is just bullying my wine-sick state; I close the aloes-wood embroidered door. The swallows come late, flying into the western city, as if to say the spring business is ending. Painted boats carry the Pure Brightness past; in clear mist slowly rising over the trees of the Wu palace. Thinking of my wandering feeling adrift, turned with the wind into light floss. Ten years by West Lake: hitching the horse by the willows, chasing the tender dust and soft mist. Upstream against the red, gradually drawn into the immortal stream; Jin'er secretly sent my hidden heart. Leaning on the silver screen—spring wide, dreams narrow; torn red wets the song-fan, gold-threaded gown. The dusk causeway empty, lightly I give the slanting sun wholly back to the gulls and egrets. The secluded orchids soon age, the pollia grows again; in the watery country I still lodge a journey. After parting I sought the Six Bridges—no word; affairs past, the blossoms fallen, jade buried and fragrance interred, several times over in wind and rain. Long waves envied her glance; distant mountains blushed at her brows; fishing lamps divided their shadows where we lodged on the spring river—I remember that time, the short oar at Taogen Ferry. The green house faintly as of old; at parting, on the ruined wall, I wrote a poem, tear-ink dim and pale with dust. From the perilous pavilion I gaze to the limit; grass colors to the sky's end, the wind blowing my temples till they chill through the ramie. Secretly I check: the traces of parting, the happy spittle—still staining the mermaid-silk; the phoenix lost its homing, the broken luan idles from its dance. Earnestly I would write the long regret within a letter—the blue cloud-ranges, the grey sea, the sunken wild-geese; vainly my longing strums into the mournful zheng's bridges. Heartbroken, the thousand-li Jiangnan; the grieving tune summons once more—but is the broken soul still there?
translations.songci-300-10: Seeing a guest off on the Wu riverbank. Just in the trial-frost night chill, maples fall on the long bridge. Gazing, the sky unending; behind the city, fading far; the parting pavilion dim, the grieving water stretching long. The kingfisher fragrance scattered, the red-clad lotus aged; evening sorrow locks the remnant willow's brow. Thinking of the slender waist—in olden days Lord Shen once moored his orchid boat there. The immortal's phoenix gulps its jasper flute; sorrowing, the broken soul sees the far one off—hard to summon back even with the Nine Disputations. The drunken chignon keeps its gaze; by the small window we trim the candle; the song-borne regret rides up into the silver sky. White autumn will not follow the boat away; fallen red rides a single leaf in the cold wave. I dream of kingfisher-tail hairpins; the grieving swan must be passing now beyond the southern watchtower.
translations.songci-300-11: The countryside has just had its rain. I see the ruined leaves scattered, still dancing though the wind has stilled. The slanting sun hangs in the deep trees, mirroring heavy sorrow and light frown—the far mountain's brows, charming. The old road by which we came: the cliff-flowers, honey-yellow, half in bloom. Till now, only the waters by the stream see a person and know him, as of old. Wordless. The post-house deep and still; I dismount and search again the place I once inscribed. Bored and weary in travel—parting's grief is the bitterest. Even if I keep her sachet and hide her mirror, when some year I come again—will the peach-blossom face still be there? Thinking of that dim little chamber, its secluded window—sometimes I go to it in dreams.
translations.songci-300-12: Rain came in the night. Thanks to the east wind's being begged to hold it back—the crabapple is just at its most bewitching; let it stay a while. Quiet the courtyard and house. I try to listen closely: orioles warble, swallows chatter—clearly they share a person's sorrow, fearing spring's going. Fine trees: the green shade first turns at noon. The doubled curtains not yet rolled up, just risen from sleep, I watch in loneliness the wind-blown floss. Secretly I flick clear tears, sending them to the misty waves—to tell the old friend at the river's head that I am worn to this. Colored paper in numberless sheets; set aside the greetings—and when they arrive, there is never any certainty at all. Heartbroken, the setting sun, a thousand mountains at dusk.
translations.songci-300-13: Weak willow-silk, a thousand strands. Tender yellow spread evenly where the crows cry. The chill enters the gauze gown; spring is still shallow—one round of wind and rain has passed. I ask the swallows when they came: by the green-water bridge-side road, at the painted tower—did they see that certain person? I imagine her quietly closing her cloud-window, dust filling the silent strings and high bridges. Yu Xin's sorrow was like this—for whom do all the gathered brow-wrinkles come? Standing alone in the east wind, I flick tear-wet eyes and send them off with the misty waves east-flowing. Thinking of the long spring days idle, how a person, weary, will pass them; idling by the pillow, the orioles' hundred turns of song. They wake me to listlessness; the slanting sun still lights the flowery knoll.
translations.songci-300-14: Outside the relay-station, beside the broken bridge, blooming in loneliness with no master. Already at dusk, grieving alone—and then further beset by wind and rain. No wish to struggle bitterly for first place in spring; let the whole flock of fragrant ones be jealous. Fallen, crushed into mud and ground into dust—only the fragrance remains as of old.
translations.songci-300-15: Locked is the grief of parting, stretching on without end—it first scented the road when you came. The embroidered-curtain person longs for the far one; secretly let fall her pearl tears, weeping to see off the traveler's wheel. The long pavilion stays before the eyes, and layer upon layer, the distant waters, the lone cloud. Only gazing to the tower's height, all day long my eyes break trying to see the noble one home. Heartbreak. After parting by the pond, the places I once walked—the green once envied her light skirt. In that season, holding her white hand, amid the flying flowers and drifting floss, we walked slowly through the fragrance. Her rosy face has changed in vain, while year after year the fragrant intent stays ever new. All over the green fields—wander, play, drink and sleep; do not fail your youth.
translations.songci-300-16: Climbing high to gaze far. Just then: the old capital in late autumn, the air first turning crisp. For a thousand li the clear river like white silk, the green peaks clustered like arrows. Sails returning, boats departing in the last of the sun; against the west wind, wine-flags slant upright. Painted boats in the pale clouds; the starry river white with rising egrets—a scene no painting could match. I think of olden days: splendor vied in chase; I sigh at the gate, the tower-top—grief and ruin followed one another. For a thousand years, from these heights, facing this, one sighs idly at glory and shame. The six dynasties' old affairs flow off with the waters; only the cold mist and fragrant grass congeal green. Even now the singing girls from time to time still sing the leftover tune of 'Courtyard Flowers.'
translations.songci-300-17: Spring cannot be kept. The orioles spend all their song. The ground full of ruined red, palace brocade soiled—last night the wind and rain in the southern garden. Xiao Lian first takes up the pipa. At dawn my longing circles the world's ends. She will not enter the painted hall's vermilion doors—the spring wind is at ease among the willow-catkins.
translations.songci-300-18: Cold pounding-blocks at the guest lodge; a painted horn in the lone city. One stretch of autumn sound enters the vastness. The east-returning swallows go off over the sea; the south-coming geese alight on the sandbars. The Chu terrace's wind, the Yu tower's moon—as if it were yesterday. Helplessly bound by that fame and gain; helplessly delayed by those loves and longings. A pity—the free and gallant spirit is always left idle. Carelessly of old I left the words upon the huabiao pillar; today it has spoiled my tryst at the Qin tower. When the dream ends, when the wine wakes—I turn it over in my mind.
translations.songci-300-19: Spring cannot be kept. The orioles spend all their song. The ground full of ruined red, palace brocade soiled—last night the wind and rain in the southern garden. Xiao Lian first takes up the pipa. At dawn my longing circles the world's ends. She will not enter the painted hall's vermilion doors—the spring wind is at ease among the pear blossoms.
translations.songci-300-20: After the dream, the tower chambers locked high; sobered from wine, the curtains hang low. Last year's spring regret comes back again. Falling blossoms, the man standing alone; in fine rain, swallows flying paired. I remember first meeting Xiaoping—the double heart-pattern on her gauze gown. On the pipa's strings she told her longing. That same bright moon is here still—it once shone on the colored clouds going home.
translations.songci-300-21: The wind at the floss-fluttering head of spring nearly spends its cold. Fallen powder, drifting red—day after day the fragrance forms ranks. New wine adds to old wine's drowsiness. This spring's regret is no less than last spring's. Butterflies gone, orioles flown—no place to ask. Across the water, the high tower; I have gazed to the breaking of the twin-fish letters. Vexed and stirred, the layered ripples cross an inch of heart. The slanting sun only draws nearer to the dusk.
translations.songci-300-22: Drunk, we parted at the west tower; awake, I cannot recall it. Spring dreams, autumn clouds—gathering and scattering, truly easy. The slanting moon at the half-window; still I sleep little. The painted screen idly spreads the green of Wu's mountains. Wine-traces on the clothes, the poem's characters—dot by dot, line by line, all the feeling of desolation. The red candle pities itself, having no good plan—in the night's cold it sheds tears in vain for a person.
translations.songci-300-23: In dream I enter Jiangnan's misty water-roads. Walking through all of Jiangnan, I never meet the one I parted from. In sleep my heart melts—no place to tell it. Waking, I grieve that the melting was in vain. I would pour out this feeling into a letter on white silk. Floating geese, sinking fish—in the end there is no proof. So I lean on the slow strings and sing the threads of parting—heartbroken, shifting to break the Qin zheng's bridges.
translations.songci-300-24: With colored sleeves she earnestly offered the jade cup; in those years I gave myself over till my drunk face reddened. We danced till the willow-moon at the tower's heart sank low; we sang till the peach-blossom fan-shadow wind was spent. Since parting, remembering our meetings—how many times in dream and soul was I with you! Tonight at last I hold the silver lamp up to look—still fearing this meeting is in a dream.
translations.songci-300-25: The spirit's dreams at the mountain passes stretch long; from the fish and geese, word and dust are few. My two pitiable temples, still green—grow old only for longing. In the dream of home by the green gauze window, I will say to her, tell everyone: truly parting is hard—not like meeting, which is good.
translations.songci-300-26: I could not keep her. Drunk, she loosed the orchid boat and went. One oar through green waves on the spring-water road, past every place where dawn orioles cry. At the ferry the willows, green-green; branch by branch, leaf by leaf, the feeling of parting. From this day on, send no more brocade letters—the painted tower's cloud-and-rain has no surety.
translations.songci-300-27: The swing's courtyard in the doubled curtains' dusk. At leisure with my colored brush I inscribe the embroidered door. Over the wall, the red apricot's after-rain blossoms; beyond the gate, the green willow's after-wind floss. Zhaoyun's letters have ceased—who knows where she is? She must have gone with the King of Xiang's spring dream. The purple steed knows the old wandering tracks—neighing past the painted bridge, the eastern stretch of road.
translations.songci-300-28: The mournful zither sounds once its Xiang River tune; note by note it writes out the green of Xiang's waves. Slender fingers on thirteen strings—finely conveying the hidden grief. Before the feast her autumn-water eyes move slowly; the jade bridges of the pegs slant like flying geese. When she plays to the point of breaking the heart—the spring-mountain brows and dark lashes droop low.
translations.songci-300-29: The east wind again plays its heartless trick—the gorgeous powder and tender red blown all over the ground. The blue tower's curtain-shadows do not screen out sorrow; it is like the heart of this day last year. Who would have thought I meddled wrongly in spring's ruinous affairs—everywhere climbing and gazing, I once wasted my tears. Now the gold cup should be drained deep—how many more times can I watch the fallen blossoms through drunkenness?
translations.songci-300-30: The old scent, the remnant powder—as at first. Human hearts, worse than I could wish. One spring still brought a few lines of writing; since autumn the letters grow ever fewer. The phoenix quilt cold, the mandarin-duck pillow lone. The grieving bowels wait on wine to relax. Even if the dream-soul had one, it would come to naught—how much more, when there is not even a dream.
translations.songci-300-31: At the sky's edge, on the bronze immortal's palm, dew turns to frost; the clouds trail the geese's script, long. Green cup and red sleeves suit the Double Ninth well—human feelings like those of home. Orchid pendants of purple, chrysanthemum pins of yellow—earnestly I marshal my old wildness. I would trade deep drunkenness for desolate sorrow; only do not let the clear song break the heart.
translations.songci-300-32: Green shade—spring at its end; flying floss circles the incense pavilion. At evening, her kingfisher brows in palace style, deftly copying the distant mountains. The inch of wild heart, unsaid, is already known to the sidelong waves. The painted curtain screens it round. The newly taught tune is wondrous—secretly she lets idle people steal and hum it. Last time your letter was full of hidden words—the meaning shallow, the sorrow hard to answer. Last night your poem had the returning pattern—the rhyme perilous, and I am too languid to match it. Wait until the pipes and songs are done; remember to stay a moment longer. No need for red candles. After the idle clouds go home, the moon at the old corner of the courtyard rail.
translations.songci-300-33: South of the street green trees, spring abounding in floss—snow filling the road of spring excursions. The trees' heads, flower-brilliance mixed with tender clouds; beneath the trees, people's houses with vermilion doors. Idly I mount the north tower, the sparse curtains rolled high—seeing straight through to the trees south of the street. Leaning on the railing till it's done, still too listless to go—several times in the dusk rain. Late spring, horse pacing on the green moss, once lingering long beside the deep shade. Fallen blossoms still there, the fragrant screen shut empty—her face, who knows where now.
translations.songci-300-34: Beyond the winding railings the sky is like water; only last night I leaned on it still. At first I matched the bright moon to the tryst—always at the moon's full-time gazing for the man's return. The gauze gown worn through, its former scent remains; the old feeling—who would have it changed? One spring of parting grief, too listless to tune the strings—still two idle rows of tears before the treasure zheng.
translations.songci-300-35: The painted screen at the sky's edge; the dream returns, dim and clear, to the cloud-waters of the ten isles. Hand plucking red paper, I write the letter to send—writing out the boundless affairs of wounding at spring. By the parting shore, the high tower once I idly leaned on, facing the thousand li of Jiangnan. In the sound of the divided waters flowing below there is the weeping of that day, from the height.
translations.songci-300-36: Red leaves, yellow flowers—autumn's feeling grown late; a thousand li away I think of the traveler. The flying clouds are all gone; the homing swan brings no word—where can I send a letter? Tears, flicked off unending, drip by the window; then, at the inkstone, I grind the ink as it falls. Gradually I write on to the parting—and where this feeling runs deepest, the red paper loses its color.
translations.songci-300-37: The spirit's dreams at the mountain passes stretch long; from the frontier geese, letters and news are few. My two pitiable temples, still green—in one night grow old with longing. Home beside the green gauze window, I will say to her, tell everyone: truly parting is hard—not like meeting, which is good.
translations.songci-300-38: Like a flower, yet also like no flower—no one pities it, let it fall. Cast from home beside the road, on reflection it is heartless, yet has feeling. Winding, it wounds the tender bowels; sleepy, it drowses with dainty eyes, about to open, closing again. The dream follows the wind a myriad li, seeking where the wanderer went—and then is called back by the oriole. I do not hate that this flower flies all away; I hate that in the west garden the fallen red is hard to re-string. Dawn's rain passed—where are its traces? One pond, duckweed crushed. Three parts of spring's color: two parts dust of the earth, one part flowing water. Look closely—it is not the willow-catkins, dot by dot—it is the tears of the parted one.
translations.songci-300-39: When did the bright moon first appear? Lifting my wine, I ask the blue sky. I do not know, in the palaces of heaven, what year it is tonight. I would ride the wind to go home—yet fear the jasper towers and jade halls, where the high places cannot bear the cold. I rise and dance, playing with the clear shadow—how is that like being in the human world? Turning the vermilion chambers, lowering the carved windows, it shines on the sleepless. It should hold no grudge—why then is it always fullest at times of parting? People have their sorrow and joy, their parting and reunion; the moon has its dimness and brightness, its waning and waxing—this matter has never been perfect since olden days. I only wish that we may live long, sharing the bright moon though a thousand li apart.
translations.songci-300-40: Drinking at East Slope by night, sobering and drunk again, I come home—it seems already the third watch. The houseboy's snores thunder. Knocking at the gate, no answer at all—I lean on my staff and listen to the river's sound. Long I have resented that this body is not my own; when shall I forget all that scurrying and striving? The night deepens; the wind stills, the rippled silk of the water smooth. From this night on, let the little boat drift away—lodging my remaining years to the rivers and seas.
translations.songci-300-41: Do not heed the sound of rain beating through the forest. Why not chant and whistle, walking slowly? Bamboo staff and straw sandals—lighter than a horse. Who's afraid? A palm-cape of misty rain, and let it be my life. The biting spring wind blows the wine awake—a slight chill. The slanting sun on the mountain-head greets me instead. Looking back on the bleak place I have come through—going home: there is neither rain nor shine.
translations.songci-300-42: The waning moon hangs on the sparse paulownia; the water-clock has run out, the man first grows still. From time to time I see the secluded one walking alone to and fro—dim, the lone swan's shadow. Startled, it rises and turns its head; it has a grief no one understands. Picking over every cold branch, it will not deign to roost—the maples fall, and the Wu river runs cold.
translations.songci-300-43: A nursing swallow flies into the splendid house. Quiet, no person; the paulownia shade turns past noon, the evening cool, freshly bathed. Her hands toy with the white silk round-fan—the fan and the hands for a moment both like jade. Gradually sleepy, she leans into a lone, deep sleep. Outside the curtain who comes pushing the embroidered door?—vainly making a person's dream break off in the Jasper Tower's winding halls. Again it is only the wind knocking on bamboo. The pomegranate half-opens, its red kerchief knotted. Waiting till the drifting blossoms and wanton stamens are all gone, it will keep you company in your solitude. Pick a single splendid bloom and look closely—its heart a thousand layers, as if bound. I fear again it will be startled by the autumn wind into pallor. If I must wait till you come to face it here—I could not bear to touch it, flower against wine. Together with the powdered tears, both falling in streams.
translations.songci-300-44: Ice flesh and jade bones, of themselves cool, without sweat. The wind comes to the waterside palace; the hidden fragrance fills. The embroidered curtain parts—a bit of bright moon peeps at the person; the person not yet asleep, pillow-pin across, hair in disarray. Rising, she takes her white hand; the courtyard hush; from time to time sparse stars cross the Silver River. I ask how the night goes—the night is already at third watch; the golden waves pale, the Jade Cord turning low. Only counting on my fingers—when will the west wind come?—and all unawares, the flowing years secretly steal the days away.
translations.songci-300-45: Ten years: life and death—both boundless and dim. Not thinking of it—yet never forgetting. A thousand li from her lone grave, nowhere to speak my desolation. Even if we met, you would not know me—my face full of dust, my temples like frost. Last night in a dim dream I suddenly came home. By the small window she was doing her makeup. We looked at each other, wordless—only a thousand lines of tears. I reckon that year after year, where my heart breaks: the bright-moon night, the hill of short pines.
translations.songci-300-46: The bright moon like frost, the fine wind like water—the clear scene is boundless. In the winding harbor, leaping fish; in the round lotus-leaves, spilled dew—lonely, no one sees. As if at the third drum—one leaf, ringing clear—the dim dream-cloud breaks in alarm. The night stretches vast; I seek it again and find no place—waking, I walk the whole small garden through. A weary traveler at the world's end; the road home to the mountains—I gaze till the heart of home breaks. The Swallow Tower stands empty—where is the fair one now? In vain it locks the tower's swallows within. Ancient and present, all a dream; when was the dream ever woke? Only old joys and new sorrows remain. In some other age, facing the night view of the Yellow Tower—someone will sigh long for me.
translations.songci-300-47: Three years on my pillow, the road to Wu. I send the yellow-eared dog to follow you. If you reach the Song River, hail the little ferry. Do not startle the gulls and egrets—every one of the Four Bridges is a place where your old man once walked. In the Wangchuan scroll I look on late spring; always I remember the lines of that lofty man, the Right Chancellor. To fix a date of return—Heaven already permits it. My spring gown still bears the stitches of Xiaoman—it was once wet by West Lake's rain.
translations.songci-300-48: The last cold has burned away; a sparse rain has passed—the time after Pure Brightness. The flower-path gathers its remaining red; the wind-pond winds its new wrinkles. Nursing swallows dart through courtyard and door; flying floss clings to lapel and sleeve. Just the fine season, still late in the day's light. The taste that clings to a person—truly thick as wine. Time and again I shift my girdle's holes—all in vain, just this languid thinness. Not seeing you, I long; seeing you, it is still the same. Let me ask: to meet so often—how is it like keeping each other long? Heaven does not grow old; we two are not paired. For now, hand this regret over to the willow before the court.
translations.songci-300-49: I live at the Yangtze's head; you live at the Yangtze's tail. Day after day I long for you and do not see you—yet we drink the Yangtze's water together. When will this water rest? When will this longing end? I only wish your heart were like my heart—then surely you would not betray the thought of longing.
translations.songci-300-50: The lotuses fallen away, the sky holds the water; at dusk the grey waves rise. The paired swallows fly back-to-back past the cloud's cold. Alone I lean by the railing at the tower's eastern side. The drifting life should simply grow old before the wine-cup. Snow fills the roads of Chang'an. My old friend, morning or evening, climbs the high terrace—send me the spring colors of Jiangnan, one spray of plum.
translations.songci-300-51: Again and again I hear the silver tally; once more I light the crimson candle—the years roll on, startling the heart. Sending off the old, welcoming the new—how many moments of time can they consume? In old age can one be used to drinking all night? Waiting sleepless, I fear the cold's invasion still—I veil the clear cup. My thanks to the plum blossom for keeping my soft chanting company. The neighbor girls have already tried their spring makeup; more bee-waists clustered kingfisher, swallow-pins of gold. Luring the east wind, they know the fragrant thought is hard to forbid. The rosy face has no guarantee of being fine year after year—flaunt the gorgeous outing and win the present. Give yourself to climbing and gazing: the snow-remaining tower terrace, the slow-sun gardens.
translations.songci-300-52: The spring wind stays only at the western edge of the garden. Shepherd's-purse blossoms riot, butterflies swarm. The ice-cold pond's clear green reflects the emptying sky; the fragrant path's fallen red, blown, is all gone. My feeling runs long—I turn and regret the gossamer's shortness. All day the longing slackens my girdle-band. The treasure mirror's bright moon does not deceive a person—come home tomorrow, and you shall see for yourself.
translations.songci-300-53: Countless lamps steal the clear splendor; festive drums press on toward the dawn's first light. The look of things is as of old; the savor differs—middle age parts from it. Lightly she paints her brows in the mirror; deeply she bows to the moon west of the tower. The crowd scatters, the market's voices die away—gradually entering the season of sorrow.
translations.songci-300-54: Leaf meets leaf, the orioles nest; level waves roll the floss; at the Broken Bridge, the slanting sun, the homecoming boat. How many more excursions can there be?—to see the blossoms will be next year again. East wind, stay a while with the roses—by the time the roses come, spring is already pitiable. More desolate still: at Xiling in the ten-thousand green, a single streak of wasteland smoke. The swallows of that year—where do they know to go now? Only moss deep at Wei Quarter, grass dark at Xie Riverbank. It is said the new sorrow now reaches even the gulls' side. My heart has no strength to go on the dream of pipes and song; I veil the doubled doors, lightly drunk, sleeping idly. Do not open the curtain—I fear to see the flying blossoms, fear to hear the weeping cuckoo.
translations.songci-300-55: In the deep courtyard the pomegranate blossoms open. The painted curtain parts; fans of white gauze ride the noon wind, clearing the heat. The boys and girls in turn boast their dress-up—the new-style hairpins with charms, the mugwort tigers. Already the sightseers crowd the shore for the race. I am old now, too listless to join the play on the field; let the young ones at the road's end contend with drum and banner. The stream's rain comes urgent; the wave-flowers dance. Qu Yuan's emblem was lofty as this. I remember his life—wearing the orchid girdle, and cherishing the peppered offering. Who would believe that a thousand years after the Sao poet's soul, fish at the wave's bottom drool over the horn-shaped dumplings?—and some say it is the flood-dragon, greedy and the flood-dragon, wroth. If one were to wake up now, as then—reckon that in those days, dying drunk was hardly worse than misery. Let us merely laugh once, mourning a thousand ages.
translations.songci-300-56: The vast sky, black. And then to bear it—the slanting wind, the fine rain, tangled sorrow like woven silk. My old eyes all their life have scanned the four seas—thank goodness for a tower a hundred feet high, to watch the boundless autumn hues of a thousand cliffs. A white-haired scholar's tears for the divine land—not one drop falls toward Ox Mountain in that desolation. Chasing the past affairs—they go without a trace. In youth I prided myself on a brush that pierced the clouds; by now the spring flowers have all fallen, my breast full of soughing chill. Ever I regret that the world's people have too little new thought—they love to talk of the madcap guests of the Southern Dynasties, fetching out the broken hat year after year. If facing the yellow flowers I should betray the wine—I fear the yellow flowers too would laugh at a man so still. The great swan flies north; the sun sinks west and is gone.
translations.songci-300-57: Year after year riding at full gallop in the markets of Chang'an. The guest-lodge like home; home like a lodging. Copper cash traded for wine, the days doing nothing; red candles, calling the dice, sleepless till dawn. Easy to pick out the weaver-wife's letters in the loom—hard to win the mind of the jade-hearted one. A man has the northwest—there is a divine land there. Do not shed tears by the bridge on the west of the water.
translations.songci-300-58: At the head of the old D ningbi Pool—the moment I heard the pipes and strings, piercing grief. How many Pear-Garden sounds remain within—all unbearable now that my hair is white. The apricot blossoms have no way to flee spring's grief; they too bloom beside the wilderness mist. Only the sound of the imperial moat stops—as if it knew a person's choking sobs.
translations.songci-300-59: The east wind, with intent, climbs first onto the little peach branch. Pink and soft, tipsy as if drunk, leaning on the vermilion door. I remember that year—her new makeup half-hidden, her face toward the water's edge. Spring nearing its half; clouds and sun warm; the slanting bridge turns; within the twin walls west of the pass, the grass soft, the sedge flat, we trod the horses; at the willow ferry the jade bridles vied in neighing. I knew those moth-brows' fixed smile, the thin cheeks brushed with rouge. I once peeped from her embroidered door—regret trailing on and on. Where we walked hand in hand, the fragrance like mist, the red following every step—I resent spring for coming late. Thinned and wasted—who asks now? Only the flowers know; tears fall in vain. The swallows of old before her hall, with the misty rain, are pairing to fly again. A person grows old; spring stays ever good; dreams of the tryst. The Liu Lang of before—those lands of such grace and charm—the flowers too must grieve for. Only the boundless evening haze; my eyes break against the Wuling stream; the past is hard to chase.
translations.songci-300-60: Twin watch-towers mid-heaven; the phoenix towers, twelvefold, in shallow spring chill. Last year on the fifteenth night I attended the imperial progress, once serving at the Jasper Pool banquet. The jade halls' pearl blinds all rolled up—a throng of immortals, Penglai and Langyuan. Deep in the five-colored clouds, amid ten thousand candle-lights, sky-blotting pipes and strings. The galloping-gap years flow by—as if in one blink the stars and frost have changed. Tonight who pities the weeping lone minister? Looking back, Chang'an is far. Can it be my worldly bond is not yet cut? Vainly despondent—the Hua Xu dream runs short. My breast full of hidden bitterness—several cold lamp-points, a few cries of homing geese.
translations.songci-300-61: The rivers and hills of a thousand ages—no hero is to be found at Sun Quan's old place. The singing stages and dancing towers, the grace and glory—all were carried off by wind and rain. In the slanting sun among grass and trees, in the ordinary lanes, people say Liu Yu once lived there. Thinking of those years—golden spears and iron horses, a spirit that swallowed ten thousand li like a tiger. In the Jiahe years, all too rashly, he sought the wolf-jushan triumph—and won himself a panicked backward glance. Forty-three years past—I still remember in my gazing, the beacon-fires along the Yangzhou road. How can one bear to look back: beneath the shrine of Bali, a field of sacred crows and festival drums. Let me ask: Lian Po is old now—can he still eat his fill?
translations.songci-300-62: The jade-green rounds keep themselves pure—toward the shallow isles and distant shoals, upright and cleanly peerless. Still there is the lost hairpin, its autumn heart unopened—how much of summer's heat can it furl away? The mandarin-ducks murmur close under one leaf-parasol—and do not tell it to the laundry-girl by the stream. I fear the grieving song will suddenly break off in the flower-wind, shattering a thousand folds of kingfisher cloud. Looking back on the Han dances of that year—I feared she would fly away, and idly pleated the stay-immortal folds of her skirt. Clinging, the blue gown still stained with withered fragrance—lamenting again that the temple-silk drifts like snow. The cup-heart's clear dew like molten lead—and again one night, the west wind snaps it. I rejoice to watch quietly: a bolt of autumn light upside down, pouring out half the lake's bright moon.
translations.songci-300-63: Evening clouds gather; the pale sky, one sheet of glass. The bright silver tray rises from the sea's floor—white radiance clear-shining for a thousand li. Lustrous, dust-free, the moon lady standing pale; still enough to count the crimson cassia's staggered spires. Jade dew first falls; the golden wind not yet cold—no time in the year matches this fine hour. Long I sit in the dew; from time to time sparse fireflies pass; the crows and magpies are flying south. The Jasper Terrace cold; the warmed railing I lean on; the jade disk sinks slow. Thinking of my fair one—since word from her ceased, facing this she must know longing. It touches me most—the clepsydra's sound runs on and on; secretly heartbreaking, the flower-shadows steal away. I reckon that tomorrow night the clear light will not have waned—but fair or foul weather, who can tell? Together we held our gaze—yet now, after parting, it is still a year apart before we meet again. May we be strong of body—clear cup and pale shadow—long may they follow each other.
translations.songci-300-64: The snow-clouds scatter; the morning clears over pool and courtyard. The willows give a person a glad eye. More charming still, in many ways: a single plum heart mirroring from afar—a light smile, faint. One spring's best time is not in the thick fragrance; small charm and sparse scent are the tenderest. When Pure Brightness comes, a hundred purples and a thousand reds—the flowers in their riot—half the spring breeze is already lost. Seize early your share of the lovely light, rove and chase together—never mind the spring chill; the drunken red warms of itself.
translations.songci-300-65: Fine rain drizzles; the wind blows gently. Ten thousand households' willows in the light mist. The rain-loving flowers cling to the trees and cannot fly up—grief beyond compare; together with spring it is given to the west-flowing water. Ninety days of light—how many can there be? All the gold turtle spent, no plan can hold it back. I send word to the eastern city's wine-market: strive for one full drunkenness—for today's joy is a future year's tears.
translations.songci-300-66: Hu horses neigh at the wind; Han banners flap the snow; the red clouds again breathe forth, one pole of sinking sun. Ancient trees join the sky; jumbled mountains beyond number—the traveler's road runs out in dusk-sand and fading grass. Stars and constellations lie across the lonely lodge; the night, sleepless, the lamp-flowers vainly age. Mist thick in the incense-duck, ice congealing on the tear-candles—in the frosty sky, dawn is hard to come. Long I remember: the morning makeup just done, one cup unfinished—how much of parting's feeling! Drunken autumn-waves, morning rain in dreams—all the troubles of the waking hour. Where there must be a place that holds the heart—I bear to think of it: the words once at my ear—'When will you ride your horse back—and know again the light smile that greets me at the gate?'
translations.songci-300-67: Plum blossoms sparse and pale; the ice-currents melt and loosen; the east wind changes the years unseen. Golden-Valley outings of old, the lanes of the Bronze Camel—newly cleared, we trod the level sand in light shoes. Long I remember mistakenly following a carriage—just then floss flew and butterflies danced, fragrant thoughts intermingling. Beneath the willows, along the peach paths, spring's colors scattered wildly into people's houses. At night in the West Garden we drank to the horn's sound—lamps of splendor blocking the moon, flying canopies impeding the flowers. The orchid garden is not yet empty; the traveler grows old; coming again, every matter is worth a sigh. Mist dark; the wine-flags slant. Only leaning on the tower, gazing to the limit—now and then a roosting crow is seen. Helpless, the heart that would go home—secretly it follows the flowing water to the sky's end.
translations.songci-300-68: Mountains daubed with faint cloud; sky joined to the withering grass; the painted horn's sound breaks off at the watchtower gate. Pausing the traveler's oars for a while, let us together raise the parting cup. So many old affairs of Penglai—in vain I turn my head: mist and haze in swarms. Beyond the slanting sun, ten thousand points of cold crows; the flowing water winds round the lone village. Soul-melted. At just this moment—the sachet secretly untied, the gauze belt lightly undone. Carelessly I have won it: a fickle name that lingers in the green houses. After this, when shall we meet again? Upon lapel and sleeve, in vain I gather tear-tracks. Where the heart is hurt—the high city gazed through to breaking—the lamps are already at dusk.
translations.songci-300-69: Into the little tower rises the vast thin chill. The dawn's gloom, tiresome, like late autumn. Pale mist, flowing water—the painted screen's seclusion. At ease the flying blossoms, light as dreams; boundless the silk rain, fine as sorrow. The precious curtain idly hangs on its little silver hook.
translations.songci-300-70: The Xiang-sky wind and rain break the first cold. Deep and dim, the courtyard stands empty. The painted tower's 'Little Chanyu' is blown to its end; the clear night wears on, far and long. The dream of home breaks off; the traveler's soul is lone; the jagged year ends again. At Hengyang there are still geese to carry letters—to Chenyang there are not even geese.
translations.songci-300-71: Dawn's light breaks the clouds open; spring follows the heart's wish—the driving rain has just passed and cleared again. On the old terrace, the fragrant pavilion, the flying swallows kick the red petals. The danced-out elm-coins fall of themselves; beyond the swing, the green waters lie level with the bridge. In the east wind, vermilion gates mirror the willows; low, low, the little Qin zheng is pressed. Full of feeling—the place of pleasure: jeweled pendants, kingfisher canopies, jade bridles, crimson tassels. Gradually the wine runs out of the golden cups, the flowers tire of Penglai and Yingzhou. The old regret at the cardamom bud-tip—ten years a dream, counting on my fingers, startling. Long I lean on the railing: sparse mist, pale sun, in solitude sinking below Wasteland City.
translations.songci-300-72: The fragrant grass's green spreads lush over every southern lane. Warm floss, jumbled red—they too know a person; spring's grief lies powerless. I remember the slim beauty, my companion of the kingfisher-gathering days; together we roamed and enjoyed the Cold-Food of Phoenix City. Till now—meeting spring at the sea's corner, a guest at the sky's end. Grief unknits—then weaves again. Tears, secretly wiped—then steal down again. Vainly I stand, leaning all along the perilous railing through the whole dusk—but it is only evening clouds congealing green. Strive: if I strive it now, I have striven it; forget: how could I ever forget? Again I ask of the fish-and-geese—try once more to seek her tidings.
translations.songci-300-73: I would thin my gauze gown, but the cold has not gone. Not rolling up the pearl curtain, the person deep within. On the red apricot's branch, how many blossoms remain? The tear-traces only resent the Pure Brightness rain. All day, the sunken incense, one thread of smoke. Overnight wine wakes late; spring's mood is vexed to breaking. The flying swallows again bungle the homeward word's coming. On the small screen, the West River road.
translations.songci-300-74: Do not believe that fragrant spring dislikes the old. How many times has the old man seen spring home? Cherish spring, make merry—do not refuse it often. Dainty smiles and gorgeous songs are all to my taste; vexing the flowers, mad for wine, I brave your reproach. The heart of things is only true in drunkenness.
translations.songci-300-75: Orchids and irises fill the fragrant isle; wandering thoughts cross the road. Dust rises on the steps of her gauze-socked feet—she turns to greet me. Arranging her chignon, knitting her brows, silently our two hearts' feeling finds no words. A fine wind blows the willow-floss. The person crosses to the south. I look back on our old rovings—the mountains, past counting. Deep in blossoms, her vermilion-gated house—where? The half-yellow plum-fruits; toward evening, one curtain of sparse rain. The broken soul I have handed over—spring is about to go.
translations.songci-300-76: Her beauty, truly full of moods. And ever so clearly, again and again her sidelong glances. Then I knew—the zither's heart had pledged to me; she wrote it for me on the lucky-boy double sash. I remember the painted hall, the slanting moon hazy and dim; her light frown, her faint smile—helpless in her loveliness. The kingfisher screen parted, the lotus-canopy veiled—and for me she secretly loosed the fragrant gauze. Since the Lantern Festival passed, I have seen nothing of her—not at the grave-mounding, not at the herb-picking. Several times I leaned on the paired swallows to carry my deep intent; coming and going, I only hated the doubled curtains for hindering them. When shall we meet again? Just now, spring thick, wine warm, people idle, the long day flat and boundless. Languidly waking from sleep—there is still the day's sun at the flower-tips.
translations.songci-300-77: Mist binds the stretching woods; the mountains sink the distant light; winding on, the dusk's bells and drums. Candles shine through the lattice; crickets hurry the loom; together we suffer the clear autumn's wind and dew. The sleepless longing wives—in chorus they answer to a few sounds of pestle and stone. It startles the world-wandering, weary official: the year's splendor is running to its evening. In those years I was a wild drunkard, self-assured—I told the Spring Lord I had already given her spring. Wandering, a journeying steed on the northern road, a guest at the southern shore. The hidden grief has no one to speak with. Thanks to the bright moon that once knew where I roamed—come well with the clouds, and carry the dream back too.
translations.songci-300-78: One year's spring business—altogether how much? Already more than two of its three parts are gone. The green darkening, the red charming—all of it the merest affair. In the green-willow courtyard, the warm wind's curtain, there is a person, haggard. Buying flowers, loading wine in the markets of Chang'an—how is it like seeing peach and plum in the home mountains? Not in vain the east wind blows the traveler's tears. Longing is hard to express; the dream-soul has no footing. Only returning home will do.
translations.songci-300-79: Tall bamboo, frozen in makeup; drooping willows halting the horse—leaning on the railing, a light painting becomes a picture. The mountain hues—who inscribed them?—before the tower, wild geese write slanting. The east wind hurries the slanting sun down below; stirring the old chill—the remnant of last night's wine waking. Melting away of myself—how much longer before flower-time can I stand, suddenly grown old like Xiangru. Wounding at spring is not on the high tower—it is before the lamp, the pillowed head tilted; beyond the rain, the incense stove. I fear to moor the painted boat—to face the stream, how can I bear my clear-thin frame? If the flying red sinks to West Lake's bottom, stirring the emerald ripples, even the grieving fish would all be stirred. Do not come again—when the fragrant floss is all blown away, tears will fill the level wilds.
translations.songci-300-80: Palace-powder traces carved; immortal-cloud shadows fallen—into a watery wilderness with no one, a deserted bend. Old rocks bury the fragrance; golden sands chain the bone, ring upon ring. At the southern tower I do not resent the horizontal flute's playing—I resent the dawn wind: a thousand li of mountain passes. Half drifting, half fallen—in the courtyard's dusk, the moon cold on the railing. At Shouyang she vainly arranges her grieving luan-mirror—I ask who blended the jade marrow to secretly mend the scent-scar. In fine rain the homing swan; at Lone Hill, boundless spring chill. The departed soul is hard to summon with the clear summons; in dream she unlooses her white-gowned girdle-gems by the stream. Most grieving of all—the weeping birds in the clear light, beneath the leaves the green rounds.
translations.songci-300-81: Lakes and hills—I have grown used to them drunk. My spring gown soaked with tear-tracks and wine-tracks, without end. Again a guest in Chang'an—I sigh at my torn collar and scattered sleeves: who would wash their dust? The purple-lane gates lie waste; along the ruined wells the wind sways the green creepers. Chattering, the eastern neighbors—it is still the pair of swallows that once nested in the Xie halls. Spring dreams among mortals must break. Only I marvel that the dream-fate of those years could run so short. The embroidered chamber's Qin zheng—beside the crabapple she loved it most; deep at night we opened the feast. The dance rested, the song sank; the blossoms not yet lessened—the rosy face changed first. Standing long by the river bridge, about to go—the slanting sun, tears full.
translations.songci-300-82: Dim and far, empty mist on four sides—what year was it that a long star fell from the blue sky? Phantom now: grey cliffs and cloud-trees, the golden house of the famous beauty, the palace-walls of a fallen hegemon. Along Arrow Lane the sour wind shoots at the eyes; the greasy waters dye the flowers rank. From time to time the slapping sound of her paired slippers—the corridor-leaves in autumn's voice. Within the palace, the King of Wu lay sunk in drunkenness; he begged the weary wanderer of the five lakes to fish alone, awake, awake. I ask the grey waves; they give no word—what can I do, white-haired, against the green mountains? The waters hold the sky; at the railing's height I see off the jumbled crows, the slanting sun sinking at the fishing strand. Calling again and again for wine—up to the Lute Terrace we go; autumn lies level with the clouds.
translations.songci-300-83: Willows dusk the river bridge; orioles clear the terrace gardens; my short cane again and again stirs the spring fragrance. In those days mooring at night, tenderness led me deep into a land of depth. The rhyme of words ran narrow, the wine-cup ran long; we trimmed the candle-flowers, the pot's arrow hurried us on. Together where we roamed and chased: her wave-treading step on the green lanes, boats linked on Crosswise Pond. Ten years—one dream, desolate. Like the swallows gone from West Lake, the nests ruined at the Wu lodge. Coming again, ten thousand feelings; as before I call for wine in the silver jar. The stream's rain runs urgent; the bank-flowers riot. Riding the last crows, we fly past the grey vastness. On the old friend's tower—who is there now to point out for me the fragrant grass in the slanting sun?
translations.songci-300-84: Jade skin veiled in gauze; her sandalwood-cherry lips resting on the fan; the embroidered hoop still carries the faint scent of rouge. The pomegranate's heart folds empty layers of dancing-skirt red; the mugwort sprays must press her grieving chignon awry. A midday dream crosses a thousand mountains; the window's shade, one arrow's span. The scent-scar newly fades from her red-corded wrist. The person across the river, in the sound of rain; the evening wind in the wild-rice leaves breeds autumn's grievance.
translations.songci-300-85: The man is gone; at the west tower the wild geese vanish. In the parting dream I tell it—'a single Yangzhou dream.' The clouds pale, the stars sparse; the Chu mountains at dawn. Listening to the weeping crows, standing at the river bridge—the words never finished. Beyond the rain the crickets sound early, finely weaving how many frost-threads of white hair. Tell it to the Xiao girl—she cannot know yet. Facing Chang'an, facing the autumn lamp—how many have grown old?
translations.songci-300-86: On the pond the red-clad lotus keeps me company leaning on the railing; the roosting crows always carry the sunset home with them. The ruddy clouds bring rain; sparse paulownias shed their leaves; the bright moon breeds coolness; the treasure fan lies idle. The dream of home is narrow; the water-and-sky is wide. At the small window the grieving brows faint as autumn mountains. O Wu swan, be good and carry a homeward word—by the gate of Changmen, a few rooms among the willows.
translations.songci-300-87: Where is sorrow made of? On the heart of the parted one, an autumn. Even if the plantain does not rain, it still soughs and soughs. All say the late-cool weather is fine—yet though there is a bright moon, I fear to climb the tower. The year's business ends in dreams; the flowers fall empty, the misty waters flow. The swallows take leave and return; the guest still lingers. The drooping willow never held her skirt-band fast—endlessly it ties only the traveler's boat.
translations.songci-300-88: Tall trees breed cloud-breath. I visit the traces of the restoration heroes, secretly chasing the former affairs. The war-fleet's east wind grudged its favor—the dream broke off, the homeland of the divine land. Then a small retreat on the Wu palace's idle ground. On the bright moonlit huabiao the night crane returns—I sigh: the flowers and bamboo of those years are like this now. The dew on the branches splashes clear tears. The excursion-leader's little spring-outing band: treading the green moss, seeking out the hidden cove, asking whether the plum has opened. Again we sang by the plum, drawing out the tune, urging the frozen buds on the cold tips. This heart and the Spring Lord are of one accord. After—never as good as before, not as of old: two people wordless, facing each other over the grey-blue waters. Holding this regret, I send it to the remnant drunkenness.
translations.songci-300-89: Before the Playhorse Terrace, beneath the flower-picking hedge—I ask the year's splendor: is it the Double Ninth again? Just returning—the southern hills' green colors as of old. Last night by the window-frame I heard wind and rain—nothing like the time of the climb-and-return. A whole stretch of Song Yu's mood; ten parts of Wei Jie's clear thinness. The red-dogwood pendant, facing the wine in vain. The pounding-staffs stir a faint chill, secretly bullying the gauze sleeves. Autumn has not much left—already the ruined lotus, the withered willows. Forcing my cap-brim awry, once toward the sky's end I scratched my head. Several times I recall the homeland's water-shield and perch—before the frost, behind the geese.
translations.songci-300-90: Seeing spring off—spring goes; in the human world there is no road. Beyond the swing the fragrant grass joins the sky—who sends the wind-blown sand to darken the southern shore? Tugging and lingering—what frame of mind? Vainly I remember the flying floss at the sea's gate. The jumbled crows pass; the Dipper turns; the city lies waste; the place where we once tried the lamps is seen no more. Spring goes—who suffers most? Only the arrow-swans sunk at the frontier, the ridge-swallows masterless; in the cuckoo's voice, the dusk of Everlasting Gate. I think of the jade trees fallen to earth, the tear-plates like dew. Seeing off the guest at Xianyang, again and again looking back—the slanting sun cannot pass. Spring goes—will it still come back? Just now Secretary Jiang's regret at parting, Yu Xin's grieving fu. On the Su causeway, all day, wind and rain. I sigh: the spirit roams the old country; the flowers remember the former visit. A life adrift in the world—look at the child, together with the night rain.
translations.songci-300-91: Red-dressed spring riders, treading the moonlight's shadow, pole-flags threading through the market; gazing without end at the towers' singing and dancing; fragrant dust, puff after puff, beneath lotus-thread steps. The flute's voice breaks off—an appointment with the colored luan to go home; not fearing the imperial guards' scolding the drunk. What a racket on the imperial way—hold on a moment: I hear Niannu begin to sing. The elders still remember the Xuanhe days, embracing the bronze immortal, clear tears like water. They turn and look again—Shahe so lovely, light rippling and joining the mansions, the curtain-frozen shadows scattering red light into brocade, the moon steeping ten li of grape-blossom hues. I watch the comings and goings of the immortal-talented—would any smash the mirror-flower? Heartbroken, the bamboo-horse children—vainly they speak of the three thousand music-making fingers. Waiting long, spring does not come back; when spring comes, one wants only to sleep. And again she speaks before the lamp, hugging her chignon, secretly letting the mermaid-pearls fall. Even if that day I had seen the Rainbow Skirts myself—heaven and human world, all within a dream.
translations.songci-300-92: The jade-moon just cleared; the black clouds faint and far—who is master of the spring business? The forbidden park's tender chill, the lake-dike's weary warmth—the former visit passed so swiftly. Fragrance-dust dimmed the lanes; flowery lamps lit the day as daylight—always I was too listless to take her hand and go. Who would have known: breaking smoke, night curfew—the whole city as if grieving in wind and rain. The Xuanhe days of old, the southward crossing to Lin'an—the fine scenes remain just as before. The pale-yellow booklets scattered in flight; the wind-disheveled hair, the fifteenth night—those who could write ci suffered most. In Jiangnan there is no road; at such a night in this prefecture—who else knows this bitterness? Vainly we face each other, sleepless by the dying lamp, while the village festival drums fill the whole village.
translations.songci-300-93: How to know where spring has gone? Meeting again, let us drain the cup first. The young man's curling regret of the sky's end long since knotted among West Lake's misty willows. Do not turn your head—only the fine rain at the Broken Bridge, the haggard ones after returning home. The east wind is as of old. I ask the peach-blossoms of the former visit: can the Liu-lang remember?—will the blossoms recognize the man? Stay a while, friend; roughly I keep you, cutting leeks; the night before was just such an hour. The deep cup would flow with the smooth song—and instead wets half the spring gown's sleeve. Vainly the brows knit: I see before the white-haired elders it is already as if everyone had them. Parting, hands clasped—I sigh: the smile, the talk of letters, the pure madness over music—when shall this gathering come again?
translations.songci-300-94: At the Chu river's edge—suddenly I seem to see the Xiang consort, wordless, spilling clear tears. Faint is the spring's mood. Vainly I lean alone on the east wind—her fragrant thought, to whom is it sent? The wave-treading road is cold; autumn without bound; fragrant clouds rise with every step. Carelessly I remember the Han palace's bronze palm, standing slim beneath the bright moon. The ice strings write regret, more full of feeling; the Sao poet's grievance—vainly he gave the fragrant orchid and the secluded iris. The spring thought runs far—who sighs over and savors the state-incense's flavor? Together we shall be companions of the year's cold: the small window clean, aloes-wood smoke fumigating the green sleeves. From the dim dream I wake—trickling clear dew, a single spray within the lamp's shadow.
translations.songci-300-95: Vermilion pendants, treasure clasps—the Flying Jade of the sky, compared with the spring of the human world, is different. South of the river, north of the river, never once seen—idly I likened them to pear-clouds and plum-snow. Late spring on the Huai hills—who knows her heart's purity and height? Several rounds of blossom-fall and blossom-opening—and the heroes of Jade Gate have aged. From the golden pot I cut and send a jasper branch; see the single rider in the red dust—the fragrance crosses the jasper palace. The splendid time is just right; she should be glad to newly know the bees and butterflies of Chang'an. Du Mu is old now—I think the old affairs, the flowers must be able to tell. I remember my youth: one dream of Yangzhou, the bright moon over the Twenty-Four Bridges.
translations.songci-300-96: Misty waters wide; the tall woods toy with the last sunlight; the evening cicadas cry so bitterly. The green pounding-stones carry their rhythm; the silver bed drifts its leaves. My clothes damp in the paulownia shade, the dew cold; gathering the cool-blooming flowers, from time to time I compose the autumn snow. I sigh at the light parting—one lapel of secluded matters, which the wall-crickets can tell. The guest's thought, chanting the shang-note, still shrinks. The grieving song long—the jasper pot secretly nicks. The green fan's favor grown sparse; the red-clad fragrance faded—turned to dissolution. Jade bones in the west wind—the most hated, most hated: idled is the fresh-cool season. The Chu flute grieves. Who leans on the west tower in the pale moon?
translations.songci-300-97: Beyond the Chu park's east wind, the warm threads and feeling floss, spring thoughts woven tight as cloth. The swallows' trysts, the orioles' appointments—annoyingly the fragrant feeling lodges just in the green's depths, the red's gaps. Vast, the fragrant dust divides us. Boiling for ten li, tangled strings and clustered flutes. I watch the painted boats all enter Xiling—idling half the lake's spring colors. The willow lanes: the new smoke congeals green, mirroring the palace brows beneath the curtains, the riders on the dike. The light dusk cages the chill; I fear the pear-clouds' dream is cold, the apricot scent's grieving veil. The pipes answer the Cold-Food feast—but the butterflies resent the fine night's stillness. Just now the whole lake: broken moon, shaking blossoms—how can one bear to go?
translations.songci-300-98: Banners shining on the wilds, coaches and horses facing the court; the level sands, ten thousand li, the sky hanging low. Precious sashes and golden seals; before the wine the fur caps tousled by the wind. The lands we passed—Qin passes and Bian waters—climbing and gazing there, all entrusted to new poems. Gallantly we roamed: piled drums and clear reeds, fine horses and famed beauties. Wine-flushed, we should face the Yan mountains' snow—just then the frozen moon over the ice-river, dawn clouds flying over the ridge. Cast into my remaining years, who in Jiangnan remembers Fang Hui? The east wind gradually greens West Lake's willows; the geese have returned, but the man has not come back south. It touches me most: I broke off every plum branch—hard to send the longing.
translations.songci-300-99: Facing the west wind, my temples sway, smoke-blue; the former affairs, uneven, flow away like water. The purple-silk sash with its mandarin-duck knot, the mirror-vows and hairpin oaths—clear as could be. I remember not at all; carelessly I wove the returning pattern—how many times my heart nearly broke. Setting flowers on their stems—yet rain overturns and clouds turn, feeling wide, the lot narrow; on the stone, the jade hairpin snaps. Beyond the vermilion tower, sorrow presses the empty clouds as if they would fall; the moon's mark still shines on the sleepless one. Fair or foul, it only follows heaven's will—vainly the jade wastes and the fragrance perishes. Drink, my lord. Have you not seen—at Everlasting Gate, the green grass, the spring-wind tears? A moment's wrong reckoning: I regret not taking the thorn hairpin early—to the evening sky's tall bamboos, white-haired, leaning on the cold green.
translations.songci-300-100: The river empty, no crossing. I grieve the sweet sedge and the pollia, fallen beyond counting. The long road, bleak and cold; the soft-turning years flow on and on; I gaze and gaze—the fair one, late in the day. Wind, mist, rain, snow, fair and foul at dusk—what need even of the spring wind's thousand trees? The whole lone city: falling leaves sough-sough, day and night the river's sound flows away. The sun late, the hills deep—I hear a flute: I fear that in some year, drifting and fallen, I shall write of it with you. Our matters wide, our hearts at odds; our friendship thin, the go-between's toil; the creepers' grass dew soaks the clothes. On the isle, dim and distant, she wakes from what dreams left behind, sunk and floating, at the Feng shore? There is a white gull, a pale moon, a microwave bearing a message—free and easy, unhurried.
translations.songci-300-101: As if the east wind had grown old—whence again the air of those times? Having feeling, it gathers none: the rivers and hills, the body is but a lodger. Vast, what world is this? I only remember drawing near the official road: it came for a moment, would not stay, and was out the gate a thousand li. My besotted heart hoped for the turning wind to let it fall—meeting beneath the fan, tiny pendants at the hairpin's tip. Her house had ten thousand strands, a thousand wisps, that know how to screen the pavilion and shade the post—but they do not bar the river's water. At Guazhou we once moored, waiting for the traveler year after year. Beneath the sun, the long autumn; the city crows rise at night. The tent-lodging still good for spring sleep: together we flew back to the lake's shore—but the grass greened and there was no place. Rain, rain—the spring heart rich as grease. I would wait to transform before the Fengle Tower—but the Green Gates are all ruined. Who pities that the drifting and fallen are few and far between? Dot by dot I knead them—snow floss, pine-soft—into tears for you.
translations.songci-300-102: Cheek-rose red prints the pillow. Since waking, her little cap is still not put straight. Cold the musk-ink between the screens. Only her brow-peaks press the kingfisher; tear-pearls flick off the powder. The hall is deep; the day's light long. Swallows cross in flight; the wind-blind, the dew-well. Bitter that no one is there to speak the longing of—recently my girdle's whole width has gone slack. I think it over again: the dying lamp, the vermilion curtain; the pale moon, the gauze window—that scene of those days. The Yangtai road lies far; the cloud-and-rain dream has no certainty. When you come home, first point out the blossom-tips for her to see—then take her heart's secret and ask it gently. Ask why, dawdling, she let the youth slip by—how could she ever feel secure?
translations.songci-300-103: At the tower's corner one thread of rosy light first melts away. The pale-yellow willows darkly house the roosting crows. My jade-like love, with the moon, plucks plum blossoms. Laughing, she fingers the powdered fragrance home to the grotto-chamber; further she lets fall the curtain to guard the window-screen. The east wind's chill is a touch sharper than last night.
translations.songci-300-104: Niuzhu, the Heavenly Gate's peril—confining north and south, seized by seven warlords in their pride. The clear mist gathers: with idle men we climb and gaze. Waiting for the moon to rise, the tide to level, the waves to gleam—the frontier pipes softly sound the new 'A Lan.' The wind fills the balustrade; distinct, distinct, I count the watches sounding west of the city.
translations.songci-300-105: Thin rain, first chill; the slanting light plays at clearing—the spring mood, wide and empty. The long pavilion's willow-hues twine with yellow; the far traveler breaks off one spray first. Mist lies across the waters, mirroring a few dots of homing crows; the east wind melts away all the Dragon-Sands snow. I still remember my first crossing of the pass—it was just this season. About to set out: the painted tower, the fragrant wine, the red tears and clear song—in a twinge it became a clean parting. Already a full year; dim and far, word and dust mostly cut off. I would know, within the square inch, how much clear sorrow there is—the plantain does not unroll; the lilac stays knotted. In vain I gaze to the breaking of the sky's end; both of us, weary, the wind and moon.
translations.songci-300-106: Weary of the oriole's voice reaching my pillow, the flower-scent stirring the blind—my drunk soul and sad dreams half and half. The quilt pities the leftover incense; the sash startles at the loosened holes. So much of wounding at spring, spring late. The tear-bamboo's traces fresh, the worn-orchid's scent old—the Xiang sky thick and warm. I remember the little river, the fine wind and moon of the time, the repeated trysts with my companion beyond the mist. Trust me: the phoenix strings break easily. Yet the Yun-he lute is plucked again—when the tune ends, the person is far. I know her gauze-socked track no more; at the old place she toys with the waves, clear and shallow. The blue-bannered boat moors by the white-duckweed isle; all the way to the woods, the riverside watchtower flies. It would not carry a single word of my longing—thank goodness there is the returned pair of swallows.
translations.songci-300-107: So much of wounding at spring—spring grows late again. The willows' clear shade just hinders the gossamer's crossing. The tiny hills at the sky's edge, the Taoye steps; the white-duckweed blossoms fill the place where her skirt was rinsed. All day softly I hum long and short lines; the curtain's shadow, the lamp's dusk—my heart entrusts its words to the Hu lute. A few dots of rain, the wind holds back; dim, the pale moon comes and goes among clouds.
translations.songci-300-108: The sky wide, the clouds high; the stream athwart, the waters far; the evening sun breeds a faint chill-halo. The idle steps are still; the poplar-floss grows few; the vermilion gate closes; the oriole's voice stays tender. I regret, in my haste, letting Pure Brightness slip past—then seized my share of the remaining fragrance, already turned to hidden sorrow. All those days dark and sunken, whole nights languid and drowsy; rising, I find the splendid season all gone. The grievance enters her paired brows, idly knotted and thinned. Just tasting this feeling, I see her regard is wholly near; the deep, deep airs—nothing but self-assurance; the listless, listless mood—in the end shamed before others. How could one know—in dream, Penglai—waiting till the leftover scent is forgot, from time to time send word and tidings? Even if the orioles and flowers are kept, the east wind will not stay—there will still be only present vexation.
translations.songci-300-109: Free and easy, the riverside plum; toward the sparse places at the bamboo's tips, it thrusts out two or three branches. The Spring Lord, after all, cherishes it not; snow presses and frost bullies it. The heartless swallows fear the spring chill and lightly miss the blossoming time—only there are, year after year, the frontier geese, returning, that have seen its opening. The clear shallow stream like white silk—I ask, how does the jade hall compare with the thatched hut and sparse fence? Heartbroken: after my old friend left, the new poems grown cold. Faint clouds, pale moon—facing the river sky, to whom can I entrust them? Vainly I remember: the clear fragrance undiminished—the grace and charm lie not in being known by men.
translations.songci-300-110: The seal-script smoke burns out in the incense tripod. Kingfisher-dark, the courtyard shade turns past noon; the painted hall, the man silent. Where does the prince of the fragrant grass now dwell? Only willow-floss sprinkles the path. Just on the jade pillow I drowse, first waking. Beyond the door the ruined red—spring already gone; always listless, sick of wine, sick at heart. The cloud-coiffure, not yet arranged. The old affairs of Jiangnan—let them not be recalled in detail. Only at the sky's end, seeking word and tidings—the broken swan is hard to entrust. The moon fills the west tower; long I lean on the railing; still the homeward date is not fixed. Then I only fear: the vase sunk in the golden well. The neighing rider does not come; the silver candle darkens—in vain she stands till the paulownia shadow is spent. Who is with me, facing the luan mirror?
translations.songci-300-111: Lush, lush the fragrant grass—'I remember the prince.' Beyond the willows the tower high—in the empty sky the soul breaks. The cuckoo's voice, cry after cry—I cannot bear to hear it. Nightfall approaches; rain beats the pear blossoms; deep inside she closes the gate.
translations.songci-300-112: The seal-script thread burns out in the golden tripod. Drunk-dark, the courtyard shade turns past noon; the painted hall, the man silent. Where does the prince of the fragrant grass now dwell? Only willow-floss sprinkles the path. Gradually on the jade pillow the spring sleep stirs awake. Beyond the curtain the ruined red—spring already gone right through; always listless, sick of wine, sick at heart. The cloud-coiffure, disheveled, unarranged. The old affairs of Jiangnan—let them not be recalled in detail. All through the sky's end, seeking word and tidings—the broken swan is hard to entrust. The moon fills the west tower; long I lean on the railing; still the homeward date is not fixed. Again I only fear: the vase sunk in the golden well. The neighing rider does not come; the silver candle darkens—in vain she stands till the paulownia shadow is spent. Who is with me, facing the luan mirror?
translations.songci-300-113: Chanting the Chu lyrics high to repay the Noon Day festival; at the sky's edge the seasons hurry by. The pomegranate flowers are not as red as her dancing skirt. No one knows this heart of mine; when the song ends, the wind fills the whole curtain. The ten thousand affairs—one body, wounded by age. The hollyhocks gather their smiles east of the wall. The wine-cups' depth and shallowness—as last year's. Let me try pouring a libation into the water beneath the bridge—tonight it will reach the Xiang.
translations.songci-300-114: I remember drinking on the bridge at Wucao of old; among those seated were mostly men of heroic mettle. The long canal carried the moon away without a sound; in the sparse shadows of the apricot blossoms we played the flute till dawn.
