More than twenty years are like one dream; though this body still lives, it is cause for wonder. Idly I climb the little lodge to watch the clearing sky. Ancient and present, how many affairs—the fisherman's song rises at the third watch.
translations.songci-300-115: Rolling up the vermilion blinds: the morning rain's light gloom just lifts. Beyond the railing the misty willows toy with the clearing light; the fragrant grass invades the steps, mirroring the red peonies. The east wind, jealous of the blossoms' loveliness, blows down the tender calyxes on the tips. The screen-mountain veils; the aloes-wood's weary fume; the wine-heavy heart fears cup and ladle. I think back on olden-day Jingluo: just then, young and wildly gay, lost in song and laughter. The mud-guards and painted carriage hurried on her coiffure; once we rode the same road in the imperial park, hand in hand; after the lamp-night we had just made our vows. Who would have believed the drifting and wandering? Lonely. I think of the merrymaking—the powder light on the lapel, the strings' sounds cut off. The jasper branches and jade-moon spring were like yesterday. Grieving, after parting—the huabiao of that parting, that time's pair of cranes. My longing can only, in drunkenness, for a while be forgot.
translations.songci-300-116: The cold water keeps to its marks; the spring mood gradually returns; the sands' edge, mist widening. The stream-plums in clear sunlight breathe their scent; their cold hearts, several sprays, vie to open. Old grief at the sky's end—try and see how much soul-melting there is: beyond the long pavilion's gate, the mountains fold upon fold. Unending, the green in the eyes—the season when sorrow comes. Deep is the feeling. The painted chamber shut fast; I imagine the east wind secretly melting her skin like snow. I have betrayed the cloud-and-rain before the pillow, the blossoms and moon before the wine. Where the heart's hopes run deepest—how much more desolation there is—earnestly I save it to tell you on the homeward day. But when we do come to meet again—it will have been exactly a year of parting.
translations.songci-300-117: In the green houses, late spring. The day is hushed; too listless to dress her hair properly. Suddenly I hear the crows cry and orioles trill, stirring new sorrow without end. I remember that year I stole the casting of my spring heart; beyond the blossoms, through the mist, we gazed at each other from afar. Then on the horn-pillow I wrote poems; the precious hairpin pawned for wine; together we got drunk in the deep mossy courtyard. How could I forget—beneath the winding corridor, where we walked hand in hand, blossoms bright, moon full. Now there is only the evening rain; the bees' grief, the butterflies' regret; at the small window, idly facing the banana-leaves unfurled. But who is there to constrain? All wordless, idly she fingers the Qin zheng; tears fill the uneven bridges. Her waist, ever slimmer—her heart, with the willow-floss, gone far away.
translations.songci-300-118: My hair bristles against the cap as I rage—where I lean on the railing, the pouring rain has just ceased. Lifting my eyes, I howl long into the sky; my great heart burns fierce. Thirty years of fame—dust and dirt; eight thousand li of road—clouds and moon. Do not idle away—let the young head whiten in vain, grieving in vain. The shame of Jingkang is not yet washed clean. When shall a subject's hatred be extinguished? I would drive the long war-chariots through the gap of Mount Helan. My high ambition: hungry, to feast on Hu-flesh; laughing and talking, thirsty, to drink Xiongnu blood. Wait, from the start, to set the old rivers and mountains in order—and pay court at the heavenly palace!
translations.songci-300-119: Deep within the riotous blossoms, storied towers; the painted curtain half-rolled, the east wind soft. Spring returns to the green lanes; the level sedge is velvet-tender; the drooping willows gold-pale. The lingering sun hastens the blossoms; pale clouds hold back the rain; light chill, light warmth. I grieve: this fragrant world, which the rovers have not yet savored, is all given over to orioles and swallows. Lonely, leaning on the height, longing for the far one: from the southern tower, one cry of the homing goose. Gold hairpins in the grass-game, green silk reins on tethered horses—the grace and glamour scattered like wind and clouds. The silk sash shared its scent; the green gauze sealed away the tears—so much hidden grievance. Just now, soul-melted—again it is the sparse mist, pale moon, and the cuckoo's cry breaking off.
translations.songci-300-120: From the dim dream I first turn back; the heavy gloom has not yet opened; the dawn's light blows into a sparse rain. The bamboo-rail's breath chill; the orchid-bed's sounds sway; the new green secretly joins the southern shore. No person has yet passed; only half-open, the winding gallery's vermilion door. Without will. In vain I gaze to the limit of the rainbow banners; the brocade letter is hard to trust. Along the mossy path I recall our rovings of old—who was her companion at the swing's ropes and fragrant posts? The rhinoceros-rouge box, moth-brows unrolled; the phoenix pillow, cloud-hair alone—she too must have stood several times in fixed gaze. How could I get her to come—flower-mist winding round the deep of the little hall? Keep her here. Till the end of age, never letting her go home.
translations.songci-300-121: Reed-leaves fill the sandbars; frontier sands carry the shallow current. Twenty years—again I pass the southern tower. Beneath the willows I moor my boat, not yet steady—how many more days, and it is Mid-Autumn again. At Yellow Crane's broken crag-head—my old friend is here no more. The old rivers and hills—all of them new sorrow. I would buy cassia flowers, and wine to go with them—but it can never be like the wandering of our youth.
translations.songci-300-122: The Yan geese have no heart; by the western edge of Lake Tai they follow the clouds away. Several peaks, clear and bitter, deliberate the dusk rain. By the Fourth Bridge I mean to lodge, together with Tian Sui. Where is he now? Leaning on the railing, remembering the olden days—the remnant willows dance, ragged and uneven.
translations.songci-300-123: The Fei waters flow east without end. I ought not, that first time, to have planted longing. In dreams I have not seen her so well as in the painted likeness; in the dark, startled suddenly by the mountain-bird's cry. Spring not yet green; the temples already silk-white. In the human world, long parted, sorrow no longer forms. Who makes it so that year after year, on the red-lotus nights, the two of us brood in our separate places, each knowing it?
translations.songci-300-124: Green threads low-brush the Mandarin-Duck ford. I think of Taoye, who called the ferry in those days. Again I give my grieving eyes to the spring wind; about to go, I lean on the orchid oars—stay a little longer. The Jinling road: orioles chant, swallows dance. Reckon it—the tide alone knows how bitter a man can be. The fragrant grass fills every sandbar; no going home. The sun sets; further, my boat moves—toward what place?
translations.songci-300-125: Yanyan, light and lithe; Yingying, tender and soft—clearly I have seen them again in my Huaxu dream. The long night—how could the cold-hearted one know? Early spring is already dyed through with longing. The letters since parting, the needlework at parting; the soul of parting secretly follows the traveler's going, far away. The Huainan's bright moon chills a thousand mountains; dimly she returns, with no one to mind her.
translations.songci-300-126: From the riverside flats I gaze to the limit: the river-lotus falls in tangles—I cannot get home. Sickly, without any strength. And the silk fan grows thinner, the gauze gown first tightens. The flowing light passes the crack. I sigh at the pair of swallows on the apricot beams—guests like me. Where is the person? One curtain of pale moon, dimly shining on her features. Secluded, still. Jumbled crickets chant on the walls, stirring Yu Xin's clear sorrow, woven tight as cloth. I ponder deeply my youth's wild wandering: in the flute, the mountain passes; beneath the willows, the pleasure lanes. The fallen red brings no word. Vainly the dark waters, trickling, run green. Drifting long—now, what is my intent? Lying drunk by the wine-shop's side.
translations.songci-300-127: Twin oars in the water-shield waves; a palm-cape in the pine-rain; evening sorrow gradually fills the vast emptiness. Calling my gull-ally—fluttering, about to alight, it turns past the treetops behind my back. That time returning home, we drifted through cloud-snow; the lone boat set out at night. Heartbroken to see again, dim and faithful, the eyebrow-mountains, the dark trace pressing low. In the Fragrance-Gathering Lane, spring chill; the old man sways and staggers—who answers his own singing? West of the Rainbow Bridge, drifting free, drawn away—this mood all my life is hard to restrain. The wine wakes; the waves are far—just then, brooding, I imagine her pale silk socks. Where is she now? Only the railing, keeping a person company for a moment.
translations.songci-300-128: Young Lord Yu himself first chants the Grief Fu; mournful, mournful—I further hear the whispered words. Dew soaks the bronze door-ring; moss invades the stone well: all places where I once listened to them. The mournful note seems to plead: just then the longing wife, sleepless, rises to find her loom. Hill upon hill, the screen-fold mountains—what mood is this, alone in the night's cool? At the west window the dark rain blows again: for whom, breaking off, resuming, do they answer the pounding-stones and pestles? The lodge meets autumn; the palace mourns the moon—there are, besides, countless hidden griefs. The Bin poems come idly to mind. I laugh at the children of the world calling for lamps by the hedge—writing it into the lute-strings, note after note, ever more bitter.
translations.songci-300-129: In the old city's shade there are, at the official plum trees, several whose red calyxes are not yet fit to pin. The pool's face is ice-glued; the wall's waist is snow-aged; the cloud-intent turns heavy again. Green vines together idly thread the path's bamboos; gradually the laughter and talk startle the shore-birds asleep on the sand. The old men of woods and springs, the retired king's terraces—we call each other to climb and gaze. South-going, north-coming, what affairs? Tossed on the Xiang clouds and Chu waters, my eyes reach their limit in sorrow. Vermilion doors with pasted chickens, golden platters clustered with artemisia—vainly I sigh at the seasons' pressing on. I remember once together at the western tower's elegant gathering—I imagine the drooping willows still sway ten thousand threads of gold. By the time my saddle of return arrives, I fear only that spring will be deep.
translations.songci-300-130: A boat amid the riot of red; I remember when I came, I once took the mandarin-ducks for companions. Of the thirty-six ponds, no one had reached them; water-girdles and wind-robes beyond counting. The green leaves blow their coolness; the jade face melts the wine; more is spilled as caltrop-and-reed rain. Smiling, swaying—the cold fragrance flies up into the poem-lines. The sun sets: the green canopies stand tall; the loved one I do not see—how can I bear to tread the waves and go? I only fear the dancing-dress, chilled, falls easily—sorrow enters the west wind at South Pond. The tall willows hang their shade; the old fish puff the waves, keeping me to lodge among the flowers. Leaf upon leaf—how many times on the sandy shore, the road home?
translations.songci-300-131: When the twin oars came over, there was a person like the Taogen and Taoye of the old song; the song-fan lightly fanned the flying blossoms; her moth-brows were matchless. Spring grows far; the isle greens of itself—and are added a few cries of the cuckoo. Ten li of Yangzhou, the third-life Du Mu—leave the former affairs unspoken. Again it is the time of 'palace candles dividing the smoke'—but in my sorrow the seasons are changed in haste. I gave all the fragrant thought of my lapel to the elm-coins on the empty steps. A thousand, ten thousand strands—the crow-hiding willows, fine and slim—dance for the jade cup, whirling back like snow. I imagine the westward exit through Yangguan, the old friend first parting.
translations.songci-300-132: Fragrant lotus sheds its powder; sparse paulownia blows its green; in the courtyard the dark rain has just ceased. Groundlessly, at the place where I hold my shadow, soul-melted—I again see the dim fireflies by the thin wall, the urgent crickets on the mossy steps. Seeing the guest off, I trace again the westward road: I ask the water's surface—who plucks the pipa? Most pitiful of all: this one stretch of river and hills is wholly given over to the weeping cuckoo. My long regret: we were never together long enough; and now for what reason, again, do I part from you before the west wind? The isle chill, the mist pale; the oar moves, the person far—dim, the traveling boat like a leaf. I imagine Wenjun gazing long, leaning on bamboo, sorrow bred, her steps in gauze socks. After coming home—the green cups drunk in twain, the pearl curtain let down—idly we watch the bright, bright moon.
translations.songci-300-133: The famed city on the left of the Huai, the fine site by the bamboo's west—I unsaddle my horse and rest a while on the first leg of the journey. Passing the ten li of spring breeze, all I find is green shepherd's-purse and wheat. Since the Hu horses peered at the river and went, the ruined ponds and aged trees still shrink from speaking of war. Gradually the dusk: the clear horn blows its chill through the empty city. Du Mu, that fine appreciator—reckon that if he came again today he would be startled. Even with his skill at the cardamom verse, his fine dreams of the green houses, hard would he find it to give deep feeling. The Twenty-Four Bridges are still there; in the wave's heart the cold moon rocks without a sound. I think of the red peonies by the bridge—for whom do they bloom, year after year?
translations.songci-300-134: Gradually blown away, the fragrant floss on the branch-tips. Everywhere the homesteads, the green deep at their gates. The far shore winds round; the evening sails scatter—toward what place? I have seen many people—who is like the long-pavilion tree? If the tree had feeling, it would never stay so green, green as this. The sun sets: the high city I cannot see—only jumbled mountains beyond counting. Wei Lang is gone; how could he forget the jade ring's charge? The first of it: come home early—I fear the red calyxes, with no one to be their master. Reckon it: all I have is the paired blade—and it can hardly cut a thousand threads of parting grief.
translations.songci-300-135: The empty city, the dawn moon, blowing into the lane of drooping willows. On horseback, a single gown—the chill stings. I have seen all the goose-yellow and tender green—all old acquaintances of Jiangnan. Just now, so still. Tomorrow again is Cold-Food. Forcing myself to carry wine to the little bridge's house—I fear the pear blossoms all fallen, turned to autumn hues. Yanyan flies here, asking where spring has gone; only the pond keeps its own green.
translations.songci-300-136: The moonlight of olden days—I count how many times it shone on me, playing the flute by the plum. It called up my jade-like love; careless of the clear chill, she climbed and plucked. He Xun grows old now by degrees; all forgotten, the brush of the spring breeze's words. Only I marvel: the sparse blossoms beyond the bamboo—their cold fragrance stealing into the jasper mat. River-land: just this stillness. I sigh: the road of sending is long; night's snow first gathers. The green cup easily weeps; the red calyx, wordless, keeps its steadfast memory. Long I remember where once we walked hand in hand—a thousand trees pressing down West Lake's cold green. Again, flake by flake, it has all blown away—when shall I see it once more?
translations.songci-300-137: Moss-branch studded with jade; a tiny kingfisher bird roosting with me on the branch. Meeting by chance as travelers, at the hedge's corner in the dusk, wordless, she leans alone on the tall bamboo. Zhaojun never grew used to the far Hu sands—only she secretly remembered Jiangnan, north and south of the river. I imagine her girdle-rings coming home on a moonlit night, turned into this flower's secluded loneliness. I still remember the old affairs of the deep palace: that person, just as she slept, flew near the moth-green brows. Do not be like the spring wind, caring nothing for her graceful lightness—arrange her a golden house early. Yet again you let one petal drift away with the waves—then in turn grieve the jade dragon's mournful tune. Wait till that time when you seek again the hidden fragrance—it has already entered the small window's hanging scroll.
translations.songci-300-138: The moon cold over the dragon sands; the dust light on the tiger-moat—this year the new-favored one at the Han feast. Newly composed music of the Hu bands: hear, from the felt tents, the commander's pipes and song. The storied tower stands high. I see the railings winding red, the eave-teeth flying green; the people, lovely; the powder-scent blown down; the night wind, fine. This place should have its lyric immortal, clasping the white clouds and yellow crane, sporting with you. Long I gaze from the jade stair—alas, the fragrant grass, lush for a thousand li. The savor of the sky's edge: relying on wine to clear sorrow, on flowers to spend heroic spirit. Beyond the western hills, evening comes, rolling up again one curtain of autumn clearing.
translations.songci-300-139: On the city walls the scene is all oriole-chatter; below the walls the misty waves beat the spring shore. The green willows and fragrant grass—when will they rest? My tear-eyes and grieving bowels have long since broken. The feeling in my breast gradually turns to late-life decline. In the luan mirror the rosy face, startled, changes unseen. In other years, sickly, I hated the fragrant cup; today I fear only the fragrant cup runs shallow.
translations.songci-300-140: The blue sky with its clouds; the yellow-leaved earth. Autumn's hues join the waves; on the waves the cold mist greens. Mountains reflect the slanting sun; the sky meets the water. Heartless is the fragrant grass—farther still, beyond the slanting sun. My dimmed country soul; my chasing travel-thoughts. Night after night, unless a fine dream keeps me sleeping—do not lean alone on the high tower in the bright moon. Wine entering the grieving bowels turns to tears of longing.
translations.songci-300-141: Leaves fall thick and fast, scenting the mosaic pavement. The night is hushed; the cold sounds go brittle. The pearl curtain rolled up—the jade tower empty; the sky pale, the Silver River hangs to the ground. Year after year, tonight, the moonlight white as silk—the man is ever a thousand li away. The grieving bowels already broke—there is no way to get drunk; before the wine arrives, tears form first. The lamp wanes and flares; the pillow tilts. I have tasted to the full the flavor of sleeping alone. All told, in this matter, between the brows and on the heart, there is no plan by which to escape it.
translations.songci-300-142: Clouds fly over the ridge-top; the river bank at day's end; misty waves fill the eyes—long I lean on the railing. Standing, I gaze on the passes and rivers, bleak and bare: a thousand li of clear autumn—and I cannot bear to hold my gaze. Dim and far, the divine capital; light and graceful, the immortal maiden—since parting, her brocade letters have never once matched. The broken swan brings no proof; slowly it flies down to the sandbar. My thought stretches long, long. Secretly I recall the first times: how many were the hidden joys and fine meetings—who knew gathering and scattering cannot be foretold, turned instead to rain's regret and cloud's sorrow? They block the roaming and chasing. Every climbing of a hill, every facing of waters stirs up a lifetime's heart-affairs; one bout of gloom, and all day wordless—I descend the tower again.
translations.songci-300-143: The cold cicada cries so bitterly. Facing the long pavilion at dusk, the driving rain has just ceased. At the capital gate, no mood for the parting feast; where I linger, still—the orchid boat hurries departure. Hand in hand we look at each other's tear-wet eyes—until, wordless and choked, we can only sob. I think: from here, a thousand li of misty waves; the dusk haze deep, deep; the Chu sky wide. The tender-hearted since olden days have always grieved at parting—how much less can I bear the Cold-Food season, bleak and forsaken? Tonight, where shall I wake from wine?—willow banks, the dawn wind, the waning moon. From here a year will pass; surely the fine hours and fine scenes will stand empty. Even if I should have a thousand manners of feeling—with whom could I speak them?
translations.songci-300-144: The moonlight withdraws; the clouds thin; the frosty sky dawns. The westward-traveling guest—at this moment the feeling is bitter. Her kingfisher brows, hand in hand, see him off at the forked road; creak, creak, she opens the vermilion door. A thousand graces in her face—she stands there, light and full; wordless, with tears; heartbroken, how can I bear to look back? One orchid boat—and just like that, with urgent oars it cleaves the waves away. Greedy for the road's look, how could she know the parting's feeling? The square inch of heart in ten thousand ways—only swallowing regret, silently, to whom can she speak it? Turning back once more—the walled city is seen no more; beyond the cold river, at the sky's edge, faintly, two or three trees in the mist.
translations.songci-300-145: Long I stand leaning on the high tower, the wind fine and thin. Gazing to the limit, the spring grief rises dimly from the sky's edge. In the grass's hue and the mist's light and the last sunshine—who understands, wordless, the meaning of my leaning? I would take my wild abandon and plot one drunkenness—facing wine and song, forcing the joy, it still turns tasteless. The girdle grows ever wider; in the end I do not regret it—for her sake I have let this person waste away.
translations.songci-300-146: Waking from dream, one thread of wind steals through the window and blows out the cold lamp. How can I bear, sobering from wine, to hear again the empty steps, the night rain dripping on and on? Alas, through my own slackness I have long been a traveler at the sky's end. I betrayed my fair one—how many were the vows; yet I could bear to let all our former joy turn in an instant into grief and gloom. Grief at its extreme: again and again I chase the memory—the depths of the bridal chamber, how many times the wine scattered and the song ended, the fragrant warmth of the mandarin-duck quilt—was that merely a moment's loosening that cost her heart's strength? Cloud-delights and rain-charms had ten thousand sorts, a thousand kinds of mutual pity, mutual cherishing. Just now, as it is—heaven long, the clepsydra endless—groundlessly I have parted myself from her. When will I again hold the Qin-cloud grace? Would that with lowered curtain, close-pillowed, I might gently, softly tell her all of it—nights on end by the river's land, counting the cold watches in memory.
translations.songci-300-147: Since spring came—green gone sad, red gone grieving—my tender heart has been so-so about everything. The sun climbs the blossom-tips; orioles thread the willow-bands—still I lie pressing the fragrant quilt. The warm softness melts; the oiled cloud-hair falls; all day listless, too weary to dress. Helpless. I hate the heartless one's going—no letter, no word at all. Had I known it would be like this, I would have regretted not locking the carved saddle in the first place; facing the study-window I would have given him only paper and brush, binding him to his verses. Always together, never dodging away; idly plying the needlework, sitting by my side with me. Ah, with me—then the young years, the light and time, would not have passed in vain.
translations.songci-300-148: On Chang'an's ancient road the horse plods slow. The tall willows riot with roosting cicadas. Beyond the sunset isle, on the autumn-wind plain, my eyes break at the four quarters of the sky dropping down. The homing clouds, once gone, leave no tracks; where is the tryst of former days? My roaming pleasures grow strange and stiff; my drinking companions are few and bleak; it is not like the year before last.
translations.songci-300-149: A late-autumn day. In one blink a thin rain sprinkles the courtyard pavilion. The threshold-chrysanthemums grow sparse; the well-side parasols fall in tangles, stirring the lingering smoke. Desolate. Gazing toward the river passes: the flying clouds darken among the setting suns. In those days Song Yu grieved here, facing this water and climbing this mountain. The long road winds on; the traveler is wretched; weary of hearing the Long waters babble. Just now the cicadas chant in the ruined leaves; the crickets sound in the fading grass, answering one another in noise. The lone lodge passes days like years. Wind and dew slowly change; quietly it reaches the night's deep. The long sky clean, the Crimson River clear and shallow, the bright moon graceful. My thought stretches on, on. The night eternal, facing the scene—how can I bear to count on my fingers, secretly recalling the former days: no name, no salary; the flowery lanes and red towers—time and again whole years drifted by. The imperial city had fine sights: in those youthful days, feasts at dusk, joys till dawn—moreover there were wild friends and strange companions; meeting song, facing wine, we vied in lingering. Since parting, the swift scene has flown like a shuttle; the old rovings seem a dream; misty waters—how far the journey. I think of fame and gain: haggard, long entangled. Chasing the past affairs—in vain the grieving face. The arrow-clock moves; a slight chill is felt. Gradually, whining, the painted horn sounds a few times, faint. Facing the idle window's edge, the lamp stopped, toward dawn—I hold my shadow, sleepless.
translations.songci-300-150: The frozen clouds darken the sky; a single leaf of a boat—I ride my whim away from the river isle. Crossing ten thousand ravines and a thousand cliffs, into the Yue-stream depths. The angry waves gradually rest; the woodcutter's wind rises sudden; more I hear the merchants calling one another. One sail hoisted high; drifting the painted prow, light and easy, past the southern shore. In my gazing: the wine-flags flash and flash; one cluster of misty village, several rows of frosted trees. Beneath the last sun the fishermen drum their clappers home. The ruined lotus scatters; the withered willows screen and mirror; by the bank, twos and threes, the sand-washing outing girls—shying from the passing traveler, laughing and talking with covered smiles. Coming here, I recall: lightly I threw over the embroidered chamber; the wave-tossed duckweed could not stay. I sigh at the later tryst, so earnestly promised—on what does it rest now? Miserable, this parting heart; in vain I grieve that the year's late homeward date is blocked. With fixed tear-eyes: the road to the dim divine capital. The lone swan's cry fades; the long sky at dusk.
translations.songci-300-151: Where I gaze the rain has gathered in and the clouds broken off; quietly I lean on the railing, eyes escorting the autumn light. The evening scene sparse and bleak—enough to stir Song Yu's desolate sadness. The water-wind light; the duckweed blossoms aging; the moon-dew cold; the parasol leaves drifting yellow. It sends the heart wounded. The old friend—where? Misty waters, vast and dim. Hard to forget. The letter-meetings and wine-gatherings; how often I have betrayed the wind and moon; how many times the stars and frost have changed. The sea wide, the mountains far—I know not where lies Xiao-Xiang. I think of the pair of swallows: hard to entrust with a far letter; I point at the evening sky: in vain I recognize the returning sail. Dimly we gaze at each other. In the broken swan's cry I stand through all the slanting sun.
translations.songci-300-152: Facing the pouring, pouring evening rain spilled over river and sky, one round of cleansing of clear autumn. Gradually the frosty wind turns grim; the passes and rivers lie cold and bare; the last sunlight rests on the tower. Everywhere the red fades and the green wanes, slowly the splendor of things comes to its rest. Only the long river's water, wordless, flows east. I cannot bear to climb high and gaze far: my homeland dim and distant, the homeward thought hard to gather in. I sigh at the tracks of recent years: for what affair have I bitterly lingered on? I imagine my fair one at her dressing-tower, gazing-yan—how many times she mistook a returning boat at the sky's edge for mine. How could she know that here, where I lean on the railing, I am just like this, fixed in sorrow?
translations.songci-300-153: Climbing the lone rampart, desolate; the perilous pavilion, gazing wide, still overlooks the misty isle. Facing the paired rainbow hung with rain, the fierce wind brushing the rails, the sticky heat slightly drawn in. Gradually I feel one leaf startle the autumn; the remnant cicadas drone the evening; the white-autumn season's order. Surveying the scene I think of the former joy—I point toward the divine capital, deep, deep within the not-mist, not-smoke. Here I turn it into chasing sorrow: the new grief easily heaps up; the old friend is hard to gather. Leaning on the height, all day I stand fixed—winning only soul-melted wordlessness. Gazing to the limit: clearing haze, fine and faint; the dusk crows scattered; the bleak river city at dusk. From the southern tower the painted horn again escorts the last sun away.
translations.songci-300-154: A single leaf, a light sail rolled. Moored for now on the Jiangnan shore of Chu. The lone city's evening horn leads the Hu-reed's grievance. The waters stretch boundless; the level sands' geese startle and scatter at a turn. The mist gathers in cold forest-clusters—a painted screen unrolled. The tiny hills at the sky's edge—moth-brows, faint. The old delights lightly cast away: here I became a wandering official. I feel the traveler's road weary, the year's light late. The foreign land's scenery—how can I bear the bleakness filling my grieving eyes? The imperial city far; the Qin tower blocked; the traveler's soul in disarray. The fragrant grass joins the empty vastness; the last sunlight fills all. My fair one—no word at all; the broken clouds far.
translations.songci-300-155: Twin butterflies embroider her gauze skirt. At the eastern pool's banquet—we first met. Vermilion powder, not deeply blended: an idle blossom in faint spring. Looking closely, every part is fine—everyone says so: a willow's waistline. Yesterday among the jumbled hills' dusk—when she came, clouds were on her clothes.
translations.songci-300-156: When shall the hurt of heights and thoughts of the far one ever end? No thing is like feeling, so thick. The parting's grief draws a thousand strands tangled; worse, on the eastern lanes, the flying floss. The neighing rider grows ever farther; the traveler's dust unceasing—where shall I trace his track? The paired mandarin-ducks' pool, the waters melt and melt; north and south the little oars pass through. Beyond the dusk, the ladder lies across the painted chamber—and again it is the slanting moon at the curtain-rail. Sunk in hatred, I think it over finely: I am not as good as the peach and apricot—they at least know to marry the east wind.
translations.songci-300-157: Several strains of the Water-Melody, cup in hand I hear. Waking at noon from drunk sleep, the sorrow has not waked. Seeing spring off—when will spring, gone, return? Facing the evening mirror I grieve at the flowing scene; the past affairs and later trysts I vainly recall. On the sand the paired birds; on the pond the darkening. The clouds break, the moon comes—the blossoms toy with their shadows. Curtain upon curtain closely shields the lamp; the wind unsteady; the man just still. Tomorrow the fallen red should cover the whole path.
translations.songci-300-158: A few cries of the cuckoo: again they report the fragrant season's end. Cherishing spring, still I break off the remaining red. The rain light, the wind's mood fierce—the season of green plums. The Yongfeng willows—no one all day: flying flower-snow. Do not pluck the thinnest string: at grief's extreme the strings can tell it. Heaven does not age; the feeling cannot sever. The heart like the double-silk net, within it a thousand, thousand knots. The night passes; east of the window the waning moon congeals, not yet white.
translations.songci-300-159: Suddenly warm, then turning light-cold; the wind and rain only settled at evening. The courtyard pavilion lonely, near Pure Brightness—mid the ruined blossoms, wine-sick again with last year's ailment. At the tower's head the painted horn, the wind wakes me sober. Into the night the doubled gates are still. How can I bear further the bright moon sending across the wall the swing's shadow?
translations.songci-300-160: One new song to one cup of wine; the weather of last year, the old terrace-pavilion. The setting sun sinks west—when will it return? What can be done—the blossoms fall, gone; the swallows return, like old acquaintances. In the little garden's fragrant path I wander alone.
translations.songci-300-161: The year's light is but a single span, the body limited. Ordinary partings easily melt the soul. At wine-feasts and song-gatherings do not refuse the frequent cup. Filling the eyes, rivers and mountains—in vain I long for the far one; amid falling blossoms and wind and rain I grieve the more for spring. Better to cherish the person before my eyes.
translations.songci-300-162: The golden wind, fine and thin; leaf by leaf the parasols fall. The green wine, first tasted—a person easily drunk. One pillow by the small window, deep in sleep. The purple hibiscus flowers ruined; the slanting sun instead shines on the railing. In the season when the pair of swallows is about to go home, last night the silver screen held a slight chill.
translations.songci-300-163: Red paper, small characters—writing out a lifetime's feeling. The wild geese are in the clouds, the fish in the water; desolate, this feeling is hard to send. The slanting sun, leaning alone on the west tower; the far mountains squarely facing the curtain-hook. Her face—I know not where it is now; the green waves flow east as of old.
translations.songci-300-164: The swallows and swans have passed, the orioles gone home. Counting carefully, the drifting life has a myriad threads. Longer than a spring dream—how many hours? Scattered like autumn clouds—no place to find it. She who understood the lute and loosed the pendant—a companion of the immortals. I tug the gauze gown till it breaks and cannot keep her. I urge you: do not be the lone sober one; to lie dead drunk amid the flowers there must be a limit.
translations.songci-300-165: The pond waters green, the wind mild-warm. I remember first meeting Yuzhen. The doubled stanzas' song-rhymes rang clear-jingling; entering the break, the dancing waist whirled red and wild. Beneath the jade-hook railings, by the fragrant steps' edge—drunk, I never knew the slanting sun had grown late. Those who then viewed the blossoms with me—counting them now, not half remain.
translations.songci-300-166: The farewell songs at the ancestral feast, the parting banquet at the long pavilion. The fragrant dust already parts us, yet still I turn my face. The stayer's horse neighs mirrored in the woods; the traveler's boat turns, following the waves. The painted chamber's soul melts; from the high tower the gaze breaks. The slanting sun only escorts the level waves afar. Endless, without limit, is parting's grief—I ponder it through the world's end and the earth's corner.
translations.songci-300-167: On the small path the red grows sparse; the fragrant outskirts are green through and through. The tower's terrace, tree-shades, dimly seen. The spring wind will not forbid the willow-floss—it flaps wildly into the traveler's face. Green leaves hide the orioles; vermilion curtains bar the swallows. The stove-incense idly follows the gossamer's turning. Waking from one bout of grieving dream—the slanting sun instead shines on the deep, deep courtyard.
translations.songci-300-168: The willow-green, fragrant-grass road of the long pavilion. In youth, to cast a person off was easy to do. At the tower's head the remnant dream, the fifth-watch bell; beneath the blossoms the parting feeling, the third-month rain. The heartless do not know the suffering of the tender-hearted. One inch becomes a thousand, ten thousand strands. The sky's edge and the earth's corner have their limits; only longing has no ending place.
translations.songci-300-169: In the eastern city I gradually feel the scene turning fine. The wrinkled wave-patterns greet the visitors' oars. Beyond the green-willow mist the dawn chill is light; on the red-apricot branches the spring mood riots. The drifting life—ever I regret that joys are few. How could one spare a thousand gold and slight one smile? For you I hold wine and toast the slanting sun—stay a while, at least, shedding evening light among the flowers.
translations.songci-300-170: After the crowd of blossoms has passed, West Lake is lovely—all in disarray, the ruined red; the flying floss drizzling; by the railings the drooping willows wind-blown all day. The pipes and songs scattered, the rovers gone—only then I feel the spring emptied. I let down the curtain-frames; a pair of swallows returns through the fine rain.
translations.songci-300-171: Early morning, the curtain rolled up on light frost; breathing on my hands, I try the plum makeup. All because I carry parting's grief within, I paint my brows long, like distant mountains. Thinking of the past, cherishing the flowing fragrance—easily turned to hurt. About to sing I first gather my voice; about to smile I knit my brows instead—most of all it breaks a person's heart.
translations.songci-300-172: At the waiting lodge the plum is half-gone; by the stream bridge the willows are slender. The grass's scent, the wind's warmth sway the traveler's reins. The parting's grief grows ever farther, ever endless—stretching on, unbroken, like the spring waters. Inch by inch the tender bowels; brimming, brimming the powdered tears. High tower—do not lean near the perilous railing. Where the level wilds end stand the spring mountains; the traveler lies beyond the spring mountains.
translations.songci-300-173: Alone I lean on the high tower, the wind fine and thin. Gazing to the limit, the parting's grief rises dimly from the sky's edge. In the grass's hue and the mountains' light and the last sunshine—no one understands the meaning of my leaning. I too would take up wild abandon and plot one drunkenness; facing wine and song, forcing the drink, it still turns tasteless. The girdle grows ever wider and I never regret it—much less could she bear to waste this person to haggardness.
translations.songci-300-174: The pond waters green, spring mild-warm. I remember first meeting Yuzhen. From the head the song-rhymes rang clear-jangling; entering the break, the dancing waist whirled red and wild. Beneath the jade-hook blinds, by the fragrant steps' edge—drunk, I never knew the red sun had grown late. Those who then viewed the blossoms with me—counting them now, not half remain.
translations.songci-300-175: The swallows and swans have passed, spring gone home. Counting carefully, the drifting life has a myriad threads. Coming like a spring dream—how many hours? Going like morning clouds—no place to find it. Hearing the lute, loosing the pendant—a companion of the immortals. I tug the gauze gown till it breaks and cannot keep her. I urge you: do not be the lone sober one; to lie dead drunk amid the flowers there must be a limit.
translations.songci-300-176: Since parting I know not whether you are near or far; everything I see is desolate—so much gloom. You go ever farther, ever on, letters ever fewer; the waters wide, the fish sunk—where could I ask? Deep in the night the wind-bamboo knocks its autumn rhythm; ten thousand leaves, a thousand sounds—all of it is grievance. So I tilt my lone pillow, seeking you in dreams; the dream will not form—and the lamp gutters out.
translations.songci-300-177: Raising my wine, I toast the east wind: stay a while, stay unhurried with us. The purple lanes and drooping willows east of Luo city—always the place where we once walked hand in hand, roving through all the flowery clusters. Gathering and scattering—bitter in their haste; this regret has no end. This year the blossoms are redder than last year's. A pity—next year the blossoms will be better still; I know not with whom I would share them.
translations.songci-300-178: A whole spring I have long spent flower-money; day after day drunk among the blossoms. My white-maned steed knows well the roads of West Lake—neighing proudly past the wine-shops' front. Amid red-apricot fragrance, pipes and drums; within green-willow shadows, the swing. The warm wind for ten li, the season of lovely ones—blossoms weighing her cloud-coiffure awry. The painted boat carries spring off home with it; the leftover feeling I entrust to the lake's waters, the lake's mist. Tomorrow, again propping my remnant drunkenness, I come to seek on the lanes the fallen hairpins.
translations.songci-300-179: Making the cold to bully the blossoms, taking the mist to trap the willows—stealthily it hurries the spring's dusk along a thousand li. All day dim and blurred; in my sorrow it would fly yet stays. Startled that the powder grows heavy, the butterflies lodge in the western garden; gladdened that the mud runs soft, the swallows return to the southern shore. Most it hinders those fine trysts and gallant meetings—the jeweled carriage cannot come to the road of Duling. Deep, deep on the river I gaze to the limit—and the spring tide, late and urgent, hides the public ferry. Faint and far the distant peaks, and her tearful brows' charm that thanks Niang. By the broken bank, when the new green is born—that is where the fallen red, bearing grief, drifts past. I remember that day: the gate shut against pear-blossoms; we trimmed the lamp and spoke deep into the night.
translations.songci-300-180: The Spring Festival just past, they slip between curtain and screen—the dust of last year lies cold. Uneven, they would settle; trying to enter the old nest side by side. They inspect the carved beams and the coffered ceiling; then, soft-tongued, they consult without deciding. Lightly they skim past the blossom-tips, kingfisher tails parting the red reflections. The fragrant path: celery-mud, rain-softened. They love to hug the ground, vying in flight, each boasting its lightness and grace. Home late to the red tower, they have seen their fill of willows dimming, blossoms darkening. Surely they now roost deep and steady in the fragrance—and have quite forgotten the fragrant letter from the sky's end. It wears away her kingfisher-dark moth-brows—day after day she leans alone on the painted railing.
translations.songci-300-181: Cleverly soaking the orchid's heart, secretly gluing the grass's scales—the east wind would fend off the new warmth. Vainly it congeals on the green tiles, loath to stay; truly we know the evening chill runs light and shallow. Walking the sky, entering the mirror, it makes a show of turning out something light, loose, and soft. I imagine the homeland: the doubled curtains not rolled up, betraying the swallows newly arrived. The green not yet ended—the willow turns a white eye. The red about to break—the apricot opens its plain face. I remember the old roaming to Shanyin; the thick pledge then hindered the upper garden. The cold stove rekindled warm—then let slow down the spring-gown's needlework. I fear that in her phoenix boots, back from the herb-picking, we might by chance meet at Ba Bridge.
translations.songci-300-182: The moon-waves seem about to drip. Gazing—the jade flask sky close by, no speck of dust between. The kingfisher-ringed eyes circled with blossoms, the ice threads woven like white silk, the yellow-path treasure-light striking true. I pity myself, worn thin by poems and wine; hard to keep up with so much spring splendor. Most shameless of all: it follows the incense, seeks the candle—once it kept company with my mad self. The tracks: I remember them in vain. Du Mu grown old—how can I bear to hear the east-wind flute? In the willow courtyard the lamps sparse; in the plum hall the snow remains—with whom to pour slowly the spring-green wine? The old feeling not yet bound and settled; still I imitate the roaming of those years. I fear only that by some chance I may betray her—through the night's cold, at the gap of the curtain.
translations.songci-300-183: Mist-light sways the pale-blue tiles. The sunny eaves so windy, the willow-floss like scattering. The brocade lute lies across the bed; I imagine the tear-tracks and dust-shadows, its phoenix strings often slack. Weary of going out beyond the rhinoceros curtain; again and again I dream of the proud horse of the prince. I will not speak my longing; secretly I smooth the silk skirt—and startle at how loose the waist-slits have grown. Despondent, the southern tower on a far night. I remember the kingfisher blinds hung with lamps, the song done, her head on my shoulder. Then I entered the bronze-camel quarter, all through the old house-lanes, asking first after her price and fame. A pity the east wind—it carried the hatred off, to wither together with the idle blossoms. I will keep Dame Cui Hui's likeness in mind; come home, I will paint it secretly.
translations.songci-300-184: The willows lock the oriole's soul; the blossoms scatter the butterfly's dream; I know my own grief dyes me a Pan Yue. My light gown not yet gathered, I still hide the tear-dots away. Thinking of former matters, I flinch at the flowing light. Early spring peeps in—the buttering rain on the pond. In the melting, fixed gaze: the plum opens its half-face; her feeling fills the slowly-made makeup. The wind's threads are one inch of tender bowels. They once stirred hatred beside the song, wound fragrance beneath the candle. The fine loom's auspicious brocade—why has it never woven mandarin-ducks? The man propped drunk; the moon leans on the wall. In that first time—who dared be wild and bold? All those idle words, the long night in the flower-chamber—each of us pondering alone.
translations.songci-300-185: The autumn river girdled with rain; the cold sands winding with waters; a person looks down from the painted tower, grieving alone. The rush-cloak's scattered clatter startles the poem-thought; still, the jumbled gulls fly off—the fine line cannot be continued. The cold eye sees all return into the picture: I recognize, across the shore, the faint cloud-roofed houses. I imagine half of them belong to fishing markets and woodcutter hamlets, bamboo blazing as the dusk comes on. Trust me, the grace and spirit are not yet old; holding to the wine, I soothe these chill eyes and heart. One whip along the southern lane; several punts at the public ferry—thank goodness for the singing brows that unfold the green. Only, gazing afar in haste, I early feel the idle sorrow hanging on the tall trees. It must be hard to bear: the old friend at the sky's edge, gazing through the Huai mountains—no swan-feet for my longing.
translations.songci-300-186: The evening rain has not yet wrecked the palace trees; pitiable, the idle leaves still hold the cooling cicada. The short scene returns to autumn; the chanting thought again touches grief's edge. The clepsydra first runs long; the dream-soul can hardly be restrained; the person slowly ages; wind and moon both turn cold. I think of our hidden joy: earthen-flower courtyard moss, insect-nets on the railing. Groundless. The weeping mole-cricket churns the night; the grievance follows the round fan; the bitterness nears the autumn lotus. One flute from the tower—Xie Niang, suspended tears, stands before the wind. The old garden late—I force myself to keep poems and wine; the new geese far—they do not bring a word of greeting. Beyond the grey mist, the Chu-fragrant gauze sleeves—who is her companion in beauty?
translations.songci-300-187: The river waters stretch grey-blue; gazing at the weary willows, the grieving lotus—we together feel the autumn's hue. The ruined pavilion turns chill first; the old blind empties into dusk; the wild geese's journey most hates the wind's force. News of the homeland: I love its southern mountains' green that meets the eye. I think of the imperial land: who is the traveler who has not gone home for the sliced-broc perch? Again the year runs late; my thin bones face the wind; at night I hear autumn's sounds blow through the stillness. Dew-cricket grieving; clear lamp, cold chamber; turning the pages, sorrow climbs white into my temple hair. The gallant rovings of youth are wholly cut off. Only the pitiable place: helpless, my very soul startled time and again—the plucking of fragrance at South Pond, the pruning of plum at the misty post.
translations.songci-300-188: The spring tidings fleet down the jasper pipe. The wind and sun run thin; past the wall the birds' cries tangle. River city by river city: pipes and songs merge kingfisher; gauzes and silks warm with fragrance. Melt-melt, the ravine's green ice breaks. In drunk dreams the years turn over unseen. I imagine her moth-brows locked again over the Sui dike; her tender heart stirred still by Liang Garden. Newly come, the geese wide of cloud-word; the luan-parted cage-shadow—no plan to meet again. Weeping-spring fine rain; cage-grief pale moon—that kind of courtyard. The parting bowels break before words. Reckon it: there is still the climbing, gazing eye. Worse still: the fragrant grass joining the sky; the flying plum toying with evening.
translations.songci-300-189: The painted tower's blinds and curtains roll up on the new clearing; she veils the silver screen—the dawn chill is light. Falling powder, drifting fragrance, day after day call the grief to birth. Secretly I count the years on the lakeside roads—how many more times will she be there, so graceful? The year's splendor I vainly feel in my drifting; hugging the spring drunkenness—for whom to wake? The sky wide, the clouds idle—nowhere to find the sound of pipes. Carrying wine, buying flowers—the affairs of youth: nothing at all like the heart of old.
translations.songci-300-190: The dark willows, the bright blossoms—spring's business runs deep. By the little railing the red peony has already thrust forth its hairpin-buds. After rain the wind turns soft; the calling birds shatter their songs. The slow, slow sun still keeps a portion of shade. Do not brood on the past. The body at leisure, the season's order fine—climb and gaze for now. The old rovings: no place not worth the seeking. The place with no seeking: only the heart of youth.
translations.songci-300-191: The moon washes the tall parasols; dew chills the secluded grass—outside Treasure-Hairpin Tower the autumn runs deep. Earthen flowers trail the green; fireflies fall in the wall's shade. Listening still to the cold sounds, breaking off, turning with a slight cadence—sobbing, grieving, sinking. They strive to find a mate; earnestly they urge the weaving; they press the dawn loom's heart. In childhood I remember: calling for the lamp to flood the burrow, reining my steps to follow the sound; letting the flower-shadows cover me all over, still I pursued. Carrying them to the flower-hall for playful fights, the small terraces and pavilions cunningly gilded in their cages. Say no more of it now—from my bed, on the cool night, they keep my lone chanting company.
translations.songci-300-192: Little and graceful; clear lead-white on her plain cheeks; the bee-yellow darkly blushing. Her kingfisher tail-pin tips at her temples. Last night, in the cold courtyard, I knew her by moonlight. The sleep deep, and cruel the bitter wind's tightness; I startled awake, the heart not yet steady. Seeing the dawn's color—a pot of verdant green—then I knew the blossom-dream was true. The Xiang consort changed into this hidden fragrance; on the wave-treading road the old bank's cloud-sand keeps its regret. Facing the stair-shadows, the cold fragrance jumbled—the frozen plum hides its rhyme. By the incense-stove's edge, turning, shifting, nearing the pillow—there again I see the jade one's drooping dark-green tresses. I imagine her summoned to admire it at the Clear-And-Graceful pool-hall—the terrace cups must be filled and drained.
translations.songci-300-193: The gate parts me from the flowers' depth; I dream the old roaming. The wordless sunset; the swallows return in grief. Jade fingers stir the small curtain-hook with fragrance. The falling floss makes no sound; spring sheds tears; the wandering clouds cast shadows; the moon holds her shyness. The east wind, arriving at night, is colder than autumn.
translations.songci-300-194: On the wave-face, the bronze-blossom cold ungathered. The jade one fishes, working her slender hook. Moon-bright, the pool-pavilion turns autumn overnight. The river swallows' homeward talk becomes a dawn parting; the water-blossoms' red fades as if spring had ended. The west wind in the parasol-well—the leaves grieve first.
translations.songci-300-195: The grieving clouds all rolled away; the moon lady, at night, newly washed and combed. The dim dust does not rise; the buttering dampens the wave-treading ground. The imperial road I cross again—dimly, the affairs of the lamplight. My feeling is like water. In the small tower the incense warms the quilt—within the dream of pipes and song.
translations.songci-300-196: Gathering the hidden fragrance, patrolling the ancient garden—the bamboo cold on the kingfisher-faint path. The grass-fight at the stream's root; the sand prints of her tiny lotus steps. I pity my two frost-touched temples; the year's Cold-Food come round again—and my body deep within cloud-mountains. The day idles past. Why is Heaven too so stingy of spring—light gloom turns at once to rain? The green darkens along the long pavilion; the homeward dream rides the wind-blown floss. The feeling blossoms cast their shadows on the railing; the oriole's voice at the gate-path—they know how to keep me standing in fixed gaze, if only for a moment.
translations.songci-300-197: Cutting red feeling, trimming green mood—the flower-tidings rise to the hairpin's prong. The sinking sun, the east wind, will not let the year's splendor go. There is one who adds candle-light by the west window, unsleeping till dawn, her laughter turning to the new year's oriole-chatter. The old goblets and platters; her jade fingers once split the yellow tangerine; the soft fragrance ties the hidden white. The dream of return by the lake's shore—still I lose the road within the mirror. Pitiable, the thousand flecks of Wu frost; the cold melts, not quite gone—and again we face each other as falling plum rains down.
translations.songci-300-198: Coiled silk binds the wrist; cunning seal-script hangs from the hairpin; the jade hidden in dark gauze sleeps. The silver bottle at the dew-well; the colored clouds at the window—old affairs of youth, dim and faithful. For her sake back then I once wrote on the pomegranate skirt; heartbroken, the red silk fades its calyx. Millet-dream years slowly age; islet mist, reed-thatch. Do not sing the old tunes of Jiangnan—their grievance too choked to summon the Chu river's drowned soul. The warm wind, the swallows nursing; the dark rain, the plums yellowing; the noon mirror, the orchid-bath behind curtains. I think of the Qin tower—she too must expect the man's return, and pluck sweet-flag to pour alone. Only, gazing in despondence: one thread of new moon, following the man to the sky's corner.
translations.songci-300-199: Cut from ice-silk, folded in several layers; the cold pale rouge, evenly poured. The new-style lovely makeup, its beauty overflowing, fragrance melting—enough to shame the Ruizhu palace maids. Easily it comes to withering—how much more the heartless wind and rain. Grieving, bitter. The idle courtyard, desolate—several springs have turned to dusk. I would entrust the layered layers of parting grief to this pair of swallows—but when have they ever understood human speech? Heaven far, earth distant, ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains—who knows where the old palace lies? How can I not long? Only in dreams, sometimes, can I go. Without proof. And even dreams, sometimes, will not come.
translations.songci-300-200: The spring sky, mist upon mist; the painted towers, forest-tall, rise to the cloud-bank. Climbing and gazing at the crape-myrtle moves the heart most—marvelous to praise, she who could compose. Desolate, the longing in the late day. I remember that day: by the vermilion railing we spoke together. The frontier swan is hard to ask after; the shore willows, endless; the parting's grief a tangle of floss. The year's light is hurried on; the old flowing water—I know not where it has gone. Heartbreak—why need there even be a sinking sun? Straining my eyes I grieve at the level Chu wilds. The evening clearing: the wave-sound carries rain. Quiet, no person—a boat lies across the wild ferry. Several peaks on the river; fragrant grass to the sky's end; the ragged, uneven trees in the mist.
translations.songci-300-201: Cold the incense in the golden lion; the quilt turns red wave upon wave; rising, her hair still uncombed. Let the precious toilet-box lie shut; the sun climbs the curtain-hook. Dreading above all that idle grief and secret bitterness—how many affairs, about to speak, she swallows back. This year I have grown thin—no fault of wine-sickness, no fault of grieving at autumn. Tomorrow, this time I go—ten thousand repetitions of the 'Yangguan' could not keep me. I think of Wuling's late spring, the clouds locking the layered tower. Remember the green waters before the tower—surely it too will think of me, gazing all day fixed. The place of fixed gazing—from now on, count a few more stretches of new grief.
translations.songci-300-202: Thin mist, thick clouds—the sorrow of the long day; the aloes-brain melts in the golden beast. The fine festival, Double Ninth again; the jade pillow, the gauze curtain—at midnight the chill first seeps through. By the eastern hedge I hold wine after dusk; a hidden fragrance fills my sleeves. Do not say it does not melt the soul: the curtain rolled up by the west wind—the person is thinner than the yellow flowers.
translations.songci-300-203: Desolate courtyard; slanting wind and fine rain; the doubled gates must stay shut. The pampered willows and tender blossoms—Cold-Food draws near; every sort of weather vexes a person. The perilous-rhyme poem made; the head-propping wine sobered; it is a different kind of idle savor. The traveling geese all flown past; the ten thousand thoughts of my heart are hard to send. For days on the tower the spring chill; the curtains hang on four sides; the jade railing I am too listless to lean on. The quilt cold, the fragrance gone, waking from a fresh dream—I cannot be allowed, grieving one, not to rise. Clear dew streams in the morning; the new parasols first draw up—how much spring-roving feeling. The sun climbs high; the mist gathers in; let me see whether today will clear.
translations.songci-300-204: The sinking sun molten gold; the evening clouds joined like jade—where is the person now? The dyeing-willow mist thick; the plum-blaming flute grieving—how much spring mood is there to know? The fine festival of lanterns, the mild and gentle weather—in their turn, could there be no wind and rain? Those who come inviting me with fragrant carriages and jewel-horses—my thanks to those wine-companions and poem-friends. In the Central Plain's splendid days the women's quarters had much leisure; I remember we favored most the fifteenth night. Kingfisher-feather caps, pinching the gold willow-sprays, clustered on our sashes, vying in chic. Now worn and haggard, wind-tousled hair and frost-touched temples—I dread to go out at night. Better to lie beneath the curtain, listening to others' laughing talk.
translations.songci-300-205: Seeking, searching; chill and still; drear and bleak, desolate and sore. In the time of turning warm then cold again, hardest of all is to settle the breath. Two or three cups of thin wine—how can they withstand the evening's wind so urgent? The geese pass, too—just when the heart is sore, they are old acquaintances of former days. Yellow flowers pile the ground. Worn and ruined—who plucks them now? Keeping by the window, alone, how can I get through to dark? The parasol and the fine rain besides, till dusk—drip by drop, drop by drop. In this pass, how can a single word, 'grief,' ever suffice?
translations.songci-300-206: The geese alight on the level sands; the mist veils the cold waters; the ancient ramparts' horn-sounds break off. Green mountains faint and far; the ruined leaves sough-sough; at the sky's edge the dusk crows scatter. On the tower at dusk—a lone sail, a thousand-li homeward journey; the year's splendor runs late. Gazing: the blue clouds, the empty dusk—my fair one, where? Both dream and soul have gone far. I remember the old rovings: the deep lodge, vermilion doors; the little garden's fragrant path—I still think of the peach-blossom face. Letters filling the brocade scrolls; regret filling the gold zither-stops—hard to write the inch of heart's hidden grievance. The parting grief of two places, one gracious cup of wine—the chill perils of the leaning-railing leaned through all. In the end I linger on, relying on the west wind to blow dry these tear-wet eyes.
translations.songci-300-207: A few cries of the cuckoo: pitiable—once again the season when spring goes home. The whole courtyard in east wind; the crabapples spread their embroidery; the pear-blossoms drift like snow. The lilac's dew weeps on the broken sprays—still it cannot match the inch-knotted grieving bowels. This is me, Xiuwen: full of feeling, full of feeling—nothing to do with wind and moon.
translations.songci-300-208: How much more can it bear—a few rounds of wind and rain? In haste spring goes home again. Cherishing spring, I have always grieved that blossoms open early—much less now, with fallen red beyond counting. Spring, stay a while! They say at the sky's end the fragrant grass blurs the homeward road. I resent spring's silence. Reckon it: only the diligent bead-net under the painted eaves catches the flying floss all day long. The Everlasting-Gate affair—the fine tryst was fixed, and missed again. The moth-brows once had their enviers. Even with a thousand gold to buy Lord Xiangru's fu—this silent feeling, to whom can it be told? Dance no more, my lords. Have you not seen—Yuhuan and Feiyan are both dust? Idle grief is the bitterest. Do not go lean on the high tower: the sinking sun rests just there, at the heartbreaking place in the misty willows.
translations.songci-300-209: The Chu sky, a thousand li of clear autumn; the waters run with the sky away, autumn without bound. The distant peaks, my gazing eyes—offering grief, serving regret—jade hairpins, spiral chignons. At the tower's head the setting sun; in the broken swan's cry—the wanderer of Jiangnan. I look long upon my Wu-hook blade; I smite the railing through and through; no one understands the meaning of my climb. Speak not of the perch worth slicing—though the west wind blows all the way, has Jiying gone home yet? To seek fields and houses for myself—I would be ashamed, I fear, before Liu Lang's talent. A pity, the flowing years, the sorrowing wind and rain—even the trees are like this. I beg you, someone: call for me the light-limbed green sleeves, to wipe the hero's tears.
translations.songci-300-210: The wild crabapple blossoms fall—and in haste the Pure Brightness season has passed. The east wind from nowhere bullies the traveler's dream; all night the cloud-screen cold with dread. By the winding shore we held the cup; beneath the drooping willow I hitched my horse—in this place we once parted lightly. The tower stands empty, the person gone; of our old roaming only the flying swallows can speak. I hear that at the eastern end of the flowery lanes the passersby often see, beneath the curtain, the slender moon. The old grief, the spring river flows on, unended; the new grief, the cloud-mountains fold a thousand deep. I reckon that tomorrow morning, meeting again before the wine-cup, the flower in the mirror will be hard to pluck. She too should ask in wonder: how much frost has come into my hair of late?
translations.songci-300-211: The pillow and mat in the streamside hall turn chill, autumn-near. The broken clouds lean on the waters, gathering in at evening. Red lotuses lean on each other, all as if drunk; the white bird, wordless, must be grieving of itself. I write my tut-tut on paper—enough, enough. One hillock, one ravine have their own grace. I know not how much my sinews' strength has waned; I only feel that lately I am too listless to climb the tower.
translations.songci-300-212: Beneath the Solitary-Sorrow Terrace the clear Jiang waters flow—within them, how many travelers' tears? Northwest lies Chang'an—pity it: mountains beyond counting. The green mountains cannot hold it back; in the end the river runs on. The river at dusk, grieving me just then; deep in the mountains the partridge is heard.
translations.songci-300-213: In old age the savor of feeling has lessened; facing the parting's wine, I dread the flowing years. And counting on my fingers—the Mid-Autumn, that perfect bright moon—shines not on any reunited circle. The heartless waters none of them care; with the west wind they only wait to see the homeward boat off. Late autumn, water-shield and perch on the river; deep in the night, children by the lamp. The traveler's gown—high time you go to court audience; the jade hall is just longing for the worthy. I imagine the midnight summons at the Chengming, kept to review the drafts, then dispatched to plan the borders. If the old friends of Chang'an ask after me, tell them: as always, I am merely sodden with wine as of old. My eyes break at the autumn sky's falling geese; drunk as I come, the empty bowstring sounds.
translations.songci-300-214: The precious hairpin split—the Taoye ford; the misty willows darken the southern shore. I dread to climb the storied tower: nine days in ten, wind and rain. Heartbroken, the flying red in flakes—no one minds it at all; I beg you, who will call the oriole's song to stop? I peek beside my temple—try reading the flower to foretell the heart's tryst; just pinned, I count it over again. The gauze tent, the lamp dim; in dreams the sobbing words. It was spring that brought the grief here—but where has spring gone? It does not understand taking the grief home again.
translations.songci-300-215: The east wind at night sets a thousand trees of blossoms ablaze, and blows them down, further—star-rain. Fragrant-road filling: jewel-horses and carved carriages. The phoenix-flutes sound; the jade bottle's light wheels; all night the fish-and-dragon lanterns dance. Gold-threaded moth-knots and willow-snow hairpins—laughing talk, light and full, a hidden fragrance goes. Among the crowd I seek her a thousand, a hundred times—suddenly turning my head: that person is there, where the lantern-light wanes.
translations.songci-300-216: The phoenix-tail plectrum, dragon-fragrance strings. Since the Kaiyuan reign, when the Rainbow Skirt tune ended—how many rounds of wind and moon? Bitterest is the traveler at the Xunyang river's head; the painted barge stands tall, about to sail. I remember the frontier exit—the yellow clouds piled with snow. The parting's grief on horseback, thirty thousand li; gazing toward Zhaoyang Palace—the lone swan gone. The strings can speak—yet the grievance is hard to tell. The Liaoyang courier: word and dust cut off. Cold at the latticed window; softly she gathers, slowly she plucks—the teardrops brim her lashes. Pushing the hand away with feeling, then drawing it back again—one sweep of 'Liangzhou,' grieving through and through. A thousand ages' affairs—cloud-flying, smoke-dying. Old He who stilled the field: no news. I think of the north of the Aloes Pavilion—the splendor done. Played to this point—it sets me sobbing.
translations.songci-300-217: Green trees—I hear the cuckoo; worse to bear: the partridge pauses, the azalea cries on. They cry till spring's going has no place to be found; bitter grievance that the fragrance is all spent. Reckon it: not equal to human parting. On horseback the pipa, the passes and ramparts black; longer still—at Everlasting Gate, the kingfisher carriage leaving the golden palace; watch the swallows, seeing off the returning concubine. The general of a hundred battles: his name and body torn apart. At the river-bridge, turning his head—ten thousand li behind, his old friend cut off forever. The Yi waters sough-sough, the west wind cold; the whole company, caps and gowns like snow—just then the strong man's grieving song not yet done. The weeping birds still know such grievance as this—I wager they do not shed clear tears but weep blood all along. Who is with me, drunk beneath the bright moon?
translations.songci-300-218: Spring has come home—look at the ladies' heads, the spring-banners swaying light. Groundless wind and rain, still unwilling to gather in the last of the cold. The swallows of those years—I imagine that tonight they dream of the western garden. Not yet prepared: the yellow-tangerine wine offered, much less the green-chives heaps on platters passed along. I only laugh: from now on the east wind will have no leisure—busy fumigating the plums and dyeing the willows. And in its leisure it will visit the mirror again, changing my rosy face. The clear grief unbroken—I ask: who can undo the linked rings? I dread above all to see the blossoms open, the blossoms fall—and the morning geese from the frontier return home first.
translations.songci-300-219: Wind and rain came hurrying in the night; in the old garden the blossoms must be few by now. Grieving, grieving to the utmost—carelessly I have betrayed a whole year's fragrant intent. The willows weary, the flowers listless; the apricots green, the plums small—it treats a person lightly. Reckon it: fine spring stays forever, fine blossoms are seen forever—only it is the person who grows haggard. I turn my head to the old affairs south of the pond. I hate the starry flecks—not to be borne recalling. Now there is only: blossom-viewing eyes grown old; tears that grieve at the times. I do not fear meeting blossoms in their thinning—I fear only the savor of age come on. Wait till the place where red riots in profusion—holding back the clouds, borrowing the moon—still I must force myself drunk.
translations.songci-300-220: At the jade one's house—the painted tower with pearl blinds facing the ford. Trusting to the light wind, the colored flute pours its grievance; on horseback, once, I heard it to heartbreak. The swallow hall opens; among the gorgeously dressed—she tunes her lute-thought, I know her song-frown. Musk-wax smoke thick; the jade-lotus clepsydra short; changing gowns before waiting for the wine's first flush. The embroidered screen veiled; the mandarin-duck pillows meeting; the fragrance slowly grows warm. The winding corridor's shadows, the sparse bell, the pale moon—how much soul-melting there was. The kingfisher hairpin split; the silver paper seals the tears; the dancing-shoes from this day gather dust. I lodge in the orchid boat, carrying the parting's grief away—turning at South Pond, my back to the western sun. Remember next year: after the roses fall, the fine tryst should not fail the wandering clouds. Phoenix City far; the Chu plum's scent tender—first send a spray of spring. Outside the Blue Gate—relying only on the fragrant grass, I will seek my lord.
translations.songci-300-221: I ask spring: why so hurried? Bringing wind and company rain like a gallop's rush. The secluded blooms and slender calyxes—the low railings of the small garden—not yet banked and trained. Blow all the riotous red away: to hold spring long, better the drooping willow. Reckon it: spring is forever unwithered; people grieve that spring grows old—grief, after all, exists only in the human world. Spring's regret: nine times in ten. How can one bear lightly to betray the fragrant brew passing one's lips? Who knew it is nature's way—that the peach blossoms set their fruit, not growing thin because of spring. Worldly fame and gain; the savor of age; the season spring goes home. Even if before the wine-cup I drink deep and sing wildly as of old—the heart's feeling cannot be as of old.
translations.songci-300-222: Endless the official willows; heartless the painted barges; rootless the traveling guest. The southern mountains still see me off—only the high city walls part us. The dyed-picture gardens and streams, blue-green. Reckon it: coming again, all will have turned to old traces. Liu Lang's temples are like this—much less the peach-blossoms' color.
translations.songci-300-223: Where the grey smoke thickens, over the blue sea flies the golden mirror. All night long on the idle steps lies the cassia's shadow. When the dew turns chill, how many cold moths flutter down—the divine capital far; only the road to Blue Bridge runs near. The crystal blind not let down, the mica screen parted—the cold soaks the fair one's light rouge. Wait till I gather all this brightness and give it to the golden cup, pouring at dawn together with the rosy clouds, drained to the dregs. Further I would carry the folding-stool up the southern tower—to see the jade-made human world, the white swing-frames tipping over.
translations.songci-300-224: Zhang Terrace Road. I still see the faded-powder plum-tips, the peach-trees trying their blossoms. The lane-and-street houses, the nest-fixing swallows returning to the old places. Dimly I stand fixed. For I think of that person—little and lovesick, first peeping from her doorway. In early morning, the light palace-yellow makeup, her wind-screening sleeves, her laughter light and full. The Liu-lang of before has come again; I visit the neighbors, search the lanes, the singing and dancing of those same days. Only the old house's Qiuniang—her price and fame as of old. My chanting paper and composing brush still remember the Yantai lines. Who knows whom she now accompanies—drinking dew in famed gardens, strolling idly east of the wall? Those affairs have gone with the lone swan. All my spring-seeking is only the feeling of hurting at parting. The official willows hang low their gold threads. My homeward ride late; fine, fine, the pool-side flies the rain. Heartbreaking courtyard—a whole curtain of wind-blown floss.
translations.songci-300-225: Dark willows; weeping crows; a single gown standing long; the small blind, the vermilion door. The parasol-blossom half an acre still, quietly locking a whole courtyard of grieving rain. Spilling on the empty steps, deep in the night not yet ceased—my old friend and I would trim the candle by the west window to talk. Like mooring overnight on the Chu river: the wind-lamp scattered and wild—the wanderings of youth. Late in life. The places of play: just now the inns without cooking-smoke, the forbidden city on the hundred-and-fifth day. Calling for wine at the flag-pavilion—leave it to the companions of Gaoyang. I think of the eastern garden: peach and plum blooming of themselves in spring—do her little lips and charming dimples still live? By the time I return there are bound to be remnant blossoms—waiting for me to bring the wine-cups and stands.
translations.songci-300-226: In the small pond the new green. The wind-blind stirs; the broken shadows dance in the slanting sun. I envy the swallows, coming and going to the golden house, the nests of old; the earthen flowers winding round, the berry-wall of former visits. How deep runs the embroidered chamber, its phoenix curtain?—I once heard her tune the silk strings. About to speak, she stopped; fretting that the fragrant word would fail me; not yet singing, she choked first—grieving that the clear cup drew near. I know from afar: her new makeup done, opening the vermilion door, she must wait by herself for the moon in the western wing. Bitterest of all: tonight my dream-soul cannot reach her side. I ask when it may be told her—the good word, the secret word—to send her the Qin mirror, to steal and trade the Han incense. Heaven, if you would only let us meet, if only for an instant—what harm?
translations.songci-300-227: The branch-wind spreads warmth; the feathery mist toys with clearing; the pond brims over with spring's color. Just then the night hall without moon; the Cold-Food dark and deep. The swallows between the beams—guests of the former nest-festival—they seem to laugh at me, closed-door, grieving in stillness. The jumbled blossoms pass; the rue-scent from the next courtyard; a floor in wreck and ruin. Long I remember that time: meeting by chance, the painted carriage halting in the outskirts. Again I see the Han palace passing out candles; flying smoke in the five lords' houses. The green, green grass—blurring the road-lanes. Forcing myself to carry wine, I carefully trace the former tracks. The market bridge far; beneath the willows the household—still knows me.
translations.songci-300-228: My grievance has nothing to rest on. Alas—the beloved is cut off; word and tidings stretch far and dim. Trust the clever hands that can undo the linked rings—it is like wind scattering, rain gathering, mist thinning, cloud gone pale. The swallows' tower stands empty; the dark dust locks a whole bed of strings. I imagine the transplanting of roots, the changing of leaves—all of them of old planted by her hand, the red peonies. On the isle the pollia slowly grows. I imagine the boat moored where the shore bends—the person at the sky's very horn. Carelessly I remember the letters of that day—all those idle words and idle phrases—I would burn them all up. The waterside post turns back to spring—look, send me the plum-buds of Jiangnan. Staking this whole life: facing the flowers, facing the wine, for her I shed tears.
translations.songci-300-229: Still, the outskirts girdle the city wall. The road runs long; the guest's gone; the carriage-dust, dim and dim. The slanting sun mirrors the mountains' sinking. Gathering the last red, it still yearns for the lone city's railing-corner. Her wave-treading step is weak—passing the short pavilion, what need of a prior tryst? A roaming oriole urges me: once more unloose the embroidered saddle, slowly draw on the spring wine. I do not remember whether I came home early or late—when I mounted, who held me? waking, I slept in the vermilion pavilion. The sudden gale stirs the curtains; propping my remnant drunkenness, I wander round the red peonies. I sigh at the western garden: already the blossoms deep, no ground left—why is the east wind so cruel again? Let the flowing light pass by. Still I rejoice: a cave-heaven, a joy of my own.
