translations.songci-300-230: The daylight gloom heavy; the frost withers the bank-grass; the mist hides the city-walls. At the southern lane the lacquered carriage about to start; at the eastern gate the farewell feast just ended. Just then the drooping willows brushing the face could be knotted and haltered. Hiding the red tears, her jade hands break the spray herself. I think: at Han Ford the parting swan went—which place? A whole season now, word and tidings cut off. Deep runs the feeling. In my gazing, the land far, the sky wide. Toward the dew-cold, wind-clear, place without people—bitterly the chill clepsydra sobs. Alas, the ten thousand affairs none forgotten—only this: the light parting. The green cup not yet drained—let the broken clouds keep for me the west tower's waning moon. The silk sash's light worn away; the patterned quilt folded; the linked rings undone; the old fragrance suddenly ceased. The grieving song unending—I knock the jasper pot till it dents. I hate that spring went without keeping tryst with a person—tricking the night-hues, leaving only the whole ground pear-blossom snow.
translations.songci-300-231: The wind ages the oriole-chicks; the rain fattens the plums; at noon the fine trees' shade turns clear and round. The ground low, the mountains near—the clothes damp, wasting the stove's smoke. The people still; the crows and kites at peace; beyond the little bridge the new green splashes. Long I lean on the railing: the yellow reeds and bitter bamboo—I mean to float the boat of the Nine Rivers. Year after year, like the altar-swallows: drifting over the vast desert-sea, come to lodge beneath the long rafters. For now do not think of what lies beyond the body; stay always near the wine-cup's front. The haggard, weary traveler of Jiangnan—he cannot bear to hear the urgent pipes and the dense strings. By the feast's edge, first lay out the mat and pillow: suffer me to sleep when I am drunk.
translations.songci-300-232: The waters bathe the clear toad; the leaves clamor in the cool gust; the lane-and-street horse-sounds first break off. Idly by the dew-well, laughing at the swatted fireflies, I broke the painted gauze fan. The people still; the night long; I lean on the railing—grieving, not returning to sleep, standing till the arrow-clock dies. I sigh: the year's splendor in one blink; the person now a thousand li away; the dream sunken, the letter far. In vain I hear it said: her temples flinch at the jasper comb; her face wastes in the golden mirror; gradually too listless to keep up the timely makeup. The plum-wind season, the ground steaming; the rainbow-rains, moss breeding—a whole trellis of dancing red all changed. Who would believe that for her sake—for her alone—my talent has thinned like Jiang Yan's, my heart wounded like Xun Qian's? Only beneath the bright river's shadow, I still watch the few sparse stars.
translations.songci-300-233: Beneath the leaves the slanting sun shines on the water; light ripples roll—deep, deep—a thousand li. On the bridge the sour wind shoots at the eyes. Long I stand, watching the dusk, the lamps-and-torches market. In the old house beneath the cold window. I hear several parasol-leaves from the well fly and fall. Not loving the lone quilt, again and again I rise. Who knows—for Xiaoniang, a single sheet of paper.
translations.songci-300-234: The wind melts the flame-candle; the dew warms the brazier; the flower-market lights shoot one into another. The cassia splendor streams over the tiles; the fine clouds scatter; the bright moon lady is about to come down. The clothes, faintly elegant—look at the Chu girls' waists, a single span. Pipes and drums in uproar; the people's shadows ragged and uneven; the whole road floats with fragrant musk. For I remember the capital's night of released lanterns: a thousand gates bright as day, laughing and sporting in the roamings. The jeweled carriages, the gauze kerchiefs—where we met, of itself there was the dim dust following the horse. The year's light is the same. Only I see: the old feeling withered and falling. The clear clepsydra shifts; the flying canopy returns home—after the dancing rests and the singing ends.
translations.songci-300-235: Toward the night's gathered mist rolling in; the spring birds still; the flying rain from time to time drums on the high roof. At the wall's head the green-jade banners—their washed-lead frost all gone—the tender tips touch one another. The damp presses the lute-strings; the chill invades the pillow-screens; the insect-nets, blown, cling to the blind-bamboo. At the post-house where no one is, I listen to the eave-drippings unceasing—drowsy sleep first grows deep. But grief at the extreme startles me sudden; the dream light is hard to remember; I pity my own secluded solitude. The traveler's homeward thought is swift: first I think how the streaming puddles will hinder the wheel-hubs. Helplessly: like Lan Cheng, haggard; like Wei Jie, thin—at any idle moment, easy to wound the eye and heart. No wonder the guest of Pingyang—twin tears falling at the grieving tune in the flute. And the bleakness: the green-weed country. Red crumbs pave the ground; beyond the gate the hedge-peaches are like beans. At night, roaming—with whom to hold the candle?
translations.songci-300-236: The whitewashed wall low; the plum-blossoms dazzle the eyes—the flavor of old, as of old. The dew-traces lightly speckled—as if washed clean of all lead-white, matchlessly lovely. Last year at the finest viewing I leaned alone; with the ice-plate we shared the feast's joy. More's the pity—the high tree in the snow, the fragrant brazier fumigating the plain quilt. This year I am most hurried before the blossoms; meeting them as if they held a grudge—clinging, grieving, haggard. Chanting, gazing long—upon the green moss I turn to watch them fly and fall. Presently we shall see them—the crisp globes offered with wine—and the person just then amid the empty river's mist-waves. Only I dream of: one spray, free and easy, in the dusk's slanting light shining on the water.
translations.songci-300-237: Just as, in a single gown, I taste the new wine—I grieve that in a traveler's lodging the light and time are idly cast. Would that spring stayed a while; spring goes home like a passing wing—one gone, no trace. I ask: where are the blossoms?—last night's wind and rain buried the Chu palace's beauty. Where the hairpin-diadems fell, their fragrant balm remains; jumbled they speck the peach-paths; lightly they turn in the willow-lanes. For whom does this tender feeling chase and mourn? Only the bee-go-betweens and butterfly-envoys, from time to time, knock at my window-frame. The eastern garden still and silent. Gradually the dusky green thickens and dims. Quietly I circle beneath the precious clusters, heaving sighs. The long sprays deliberately tease the traveler—as if tugging the gown, waiting to speak—the parting's feeling without bound. A tiny remnant bloom—I force it into my cap. In the end it is not like a single blossom trembling on the hairpin, tipping toward a person. Drifting place—do not ride the tide. I fear the broken red still bears the words of longing—how could one ever see them?
translations.songci-300-238: The willow-shade straight; within the mist the silk-thread tips toy with green. On the Sui dike I have seen several times—brushing the waters, drifting the floss—the seeing-off's look. Climbing high, gazing toward the old country: who knows—the weary traveler of the capital? The long-pavilion road: years going, years coming—I must have broken willow-sprigs past a thousand feet. Idly I seek the old tracks: again wine keeping time with the mournful strings, the lamp lighting the parting mat. Pear-blossoms and elm-fire hurry the Cold-Food on. Grievous—that one gust of arrow-wind swift, half a punt-pole of warm wave—and turning my head, far, far, already several relay-stations gone. The person I gaze at—at the sky's northern edge. Mournful. The regrets pile up. Gradually the parting shore winds round; the ford-watches still. The slanting sun slowly sinks—spring without bound. I think of the moonlit pavilion, hands clasped; the dewy bridge, hearing the flute. Sunk in thought over the former matters—like a dream—the tears fall unseen.
translations.songci-300-239: A land of beauty—who remembers now the splendid affairs of the Southern Dynasties? The mountains girdle the old country, winding round the clear river; the chignon-coils rise facing each other. The angry waves beat lonely at the lone city; the wind-masts cross far at the sky's edge. At the cliff's edge the trees still lean inverted; Mochou's boat once moored here. Nothing but old traces remains, lush and grey-green; the mist sinks over half the ramparts. Deep in the night the moon crosses the battlements and comes; from Appreciation Tower eastward I gaze toward the Huai waters. The wine-flags and show-drums—what market is that now? I imagine, dim and dim, the neighborhood of Wang and Xie. The swallows know not what age this is; they enter the ordinary lane-and-street households, facing each other as if telling of rise and fall—in the slanting sun.
translations.songci-300-240: Mounting the horse, others prop my remnant drunkenness; the dawn wind has not yet blown me sober. Mirrored where the waters bend—the kingfisher tiles, the vermilion eaves—amid the drooping willows I suddenly see the ford-pavilion. Back then I once inscribed on a ruined wall—spider-webs veil it; the pale ink, the moss-halo, green. I think: coming and going, the years flow like a stream; long I pace, sighing, my grieving thoughts brimming. On and on, weary of seeking the road. The old affairs of Jiangling—when did I ever ask after Yang Qiong again? The old tune, chill and clear. Gathering her grieving brows—for whom to hear? If before the wine my old friend were as if here, missing me—most it touches the heart. Why need there be the 'Wei City' song? Before the song is done—the tears already fall.
translations.songci-300-241: The night-hues press the watch onward; the clear dust gathers the dew; the little lane's hidden quarter, the moon gone dim. Bamboo-rail, lamp-window—I know it: Qiuniang's courtyard. Laughing we met; it seemed like jasper branches and jade trees leaning on each other, the warm sun and bright clouds shining glorious. The waterside glance, the orchid feeling—rarely seen in all my life. In a painting I knew of old her spring-wind face; who would have known I would come myself to the Jasper Terrace's edge? Clinging to her rain-moist, cloud-warm tenderness—cruelly the wind startled us apart. I think of the bleak cold where I lodge, a house with no one; the doubled gates shut; the ruined wall, the autumn insects' sigh. Helpless against it: this single thread of longing, parted by stream and mountain, unbroken.
translations.songci-300-242: The Sui dike road. Gradually the day wanes; thick haze rises in the deep trees. Dim, dim, the pale moon cages the sands—I lodge again deep by the river bridge. The heartless painted barge cares nothing that misty waves part the southern shore; it waits for the traveler, drunk, hugging the doubled quilt, to carry the parting's grief home with him. For I think of the old guest in the capital: long we nestled close, at the sparse grove's little railing, in happy gatherings. The yielding leaves and singing branches all knew me; still I was used to the pearl songs and kingfisher dances. Now I head toward fishing villages and water-posts; the night lasts like a year; burning incense, I speak alone. Is there anyone who thinks of me, sleepless? My dream-soul fixed in longing on my mandarin-duck mate.
translations.songci-300-243: The moon bright; the startled crows roost unstill. The water-clock runs out; the windlass creaks at the golden well. He wakes her—both eyes clear and shining; tear-blossoms fall on the pillow's red cotton, cold. Hand in hand, the frost-wind blows the temple-shadows. The going's intent wavers; the parting words, grieving, are hard to hear. Above the tower the railing spans the Dipper's handle. The dew chill; the person far; the cocks answer one another.
translations.songci-300-244: At the river bridge, the place of seeing her off—the cool night, how late it runs! The slanting moon drops its last radiance far away. The bronze dish's candle-tears have all run out; the thick, thick cool dew soaks my clothes. Together we leave the parting gathering; we listen for the ford-drum in the wind, for the Shen-banner at the treetop. The piebald steed understands; even if I whip it on, it too goes slow of itself. The road winds far through the clear wilds; human voices fade, unheard; in vain I carry my grief home. How to bear it—the ground full of fallen red again, her lost diadem-plumes unseen, the slanting paths all lost? The mallows and oats, toward the last sun, grow level with a man. Only pacing among the rank-and-file grass, weeping, pouring the wine, gazing to the limit at the sky's west.
translations.songci-300-245: The autumn gloom, now clearing, turns gradually toward dusk—changing the whole courtyard to chill desolation. Standing, I listen to the cold sounds; the clouds deep, no wild-geese shadows. Deeper in the night the people go; stillness only—my lone lamp answers its shine on the wall. The wine has all worn off—how shall I get through this endless night?
translations.songci-300-246: The wind grieves in the painted horn; I hear the 'Chanyu' tune, three strains falling at the watchtower gate. Putting up for the night, the traveler's horse—flying snow fills the lone village. The wine-market slowly empties of lamps and fire; just then the jumbled leaves dance and flutter, beating at the window. They escort a few cries of the startled geese—down through the parting mist-and-waters, their clear cries crossing the cold clouds. Good, that half-veiled stream-moon: till now, no place that does not melt the soul. The old country's plum-blossoms, the dream of return—grieving away her green-gauze skirt. Let me ask the hidden-scent, idle allure: does it too give its ten thousand dots of longing over to tear-tracks? I reckon her kingfisher screen: surely she, the leftover hatred of two brows, leans at the dusk.
translations.songci-300-247: I remember drinking of old by the western pool—year after year, how much joy. Since parting, not a single line sent. Even meeting ordinarily again, one would still say it is not like the first. Safely, in my brocade-screen dream tonight, the moon bright, kindly carry me across the rivers and lakes. Do not ask how the longing surely fares. I know full well: after spring has gone, who minds the fallen blossoms?
translations.songci-300-248: Tears soak the railings; the blossoms wear their dew. Grief gathers at her brow-peaks' blue. This regret we take half each. More, no words at all—vainly we gaze at each other. Brief rain, remnant clouds—no heart for it all. Lonely, morning after morning, evening after evening. Tonight in the deep of the mountains—the broken soul I hand over: tide, carry it back.
translations.songci-300-249: The lone peak coils in smoke; the layered waves slough the moon; in the Li palace at night they gather the leaden waters. The raft-wind questions afar; the dream deep in rose-dew—it turns into the broken soul's heart-pattern. The red porcelain waits the fire; all at once I know it—the ice-ring, the jade fingers. One thread of kingfisher shadow curtains the air—dim and faithful, the sea-and-sky cloud-breath. How many times, dainty and half-drunk, she trimmed the spring lamp, the night chill, blossoms shattering. Better still: the old creek flying snow, the small window shut deep. Lord Xun is suddenly old now; wholly he has forgotten the old savor before the wine-cup. Carelessly I cherish the leftover incense—the empty brazier, the plain quilt.
translations.songci-300-250: Gradually the new mark hangs on the willow; the pale colors pierce the blossoms; dimly it breaks the first dark. Just so it bears the wish of reunion: bowing deep, deep—who, on the fragrant path, does one meet? The painted brows not yet steady—I reckon the moon lady still carries parting's grudge. Most lovable of all: one stretch of silver hook, so small; the precious curtain hangs in autumn's chill. For a thousand ages, waxing and waning—ask no more. I sigh: slowly grinding the jade axe, it hardly mends the golden mirror. The Great-Fluid Pool is still there—in its desolate corner, who would again compose the clear scene? The old mountains, night long. Wait for it to look squarely through the door. Watch the cloud-beyond rivers and hills: they have all aged away, even the cassia's shadow.
translations.songci-300-251: One lapel of leftover regret—the palace soul breaks; year after year in the kingfisher shade of the courtyard trees. Suddenly it chokes on the cold branch; then it shifts to the dark leaves—again, deeply, it tells its parting grief. Past the west window the rain has gone. Strange: jade pendants stream through the air; the jade zheng tunes its bridges. The mirror dark, the makeup ruined—for whom are her charming temples still thus? The bronze immortal's leaden tears seem washed; I sigh: carrying the dish, he went far—hard to store the fallen dew. Sick wings startled by autumn; the withered shape reading the world—how many rounds of slanting sun can it bear? The lingering tone grows bitterer. Why must it alone hold this pure height, turned in a breath to chill desolation? Vainly I dream of the fumigating south wind, the willow-silk a thousand, ten thousand strands.
translations.songci-300-252: Remnant snow in the courtyard's shade; light chill in the curtain's shadow; thick and feathery the jade-pipe's spring reed. The small gold-mud notice—whose house does spring grace now? All night long, by the window, a dream of longing—only that person, parted by water, screened by sky. Only chill and bare: the whole tree's hidden fragrance; the whole ground's slanting boughs. Jiangnan of itself knows the bitterness of parting—much less the roaming steed on the old road, the homing geese on the level sands. How could I get a silver paper to tell the year's splendor earnestly? Now everywhere the fragrant grass springs—even leaning on the height, the sky's end is not seen. Worse, to bear: how many more rounds of east wind, how many more rounds of flying blossoms?
translations.songci-300-253: Layered green, towering high; slender jade, gleaming white—they over-press the wave-traces, clear and shallow. The passing year's splendor; the stirring secluded thought—meeting several times as springs turn. I remember the place where we called for wine and sought the fragrant: light and full, late in the undone makeup. Already faded and dim. And the chill desolation—lately the parting thoughts—one should have forgotten the imperial carriage's return by the bright moon's depth of night. Slowly it goes, this one spray of spring—I hate the east wind: the person is as far as the sky. Even if there are remnant blossoms spilling onto the traveler's coat—the leaden tears all brimming—only earnestly break one off, to send away one lapel of hidden grievance.
translations.songci-300-254: Drifting a lone boat, I have crossed every reach of Eastbank. I still remember that day: the green shade closing at the gate. The clog-teeth on the mossy steps—the wine-traces on the gauze sleeves—affairs without end. I would seek the former traces: in vain the despondence—it has turned into an autumn garden. The blossom-viewing companion I promised myself—since parting, all gone, scattered like wind and clouds. The waters stretch far. Who would know: beyond the flowing waters, the jumbled mountains run farther still. The dream at the sky's end runs short. I imagine she has forgotten the carved rails and openwork balustrades. Gazing without end at the slowly sinking sun, I stroke the tall tree—the year's splendor runs late. Only a few dots of red blossom still know the West Garden's desolate song.
translations.songci-300-255: Near the Double Ninth—wind and rain run over-much; I dearly cherish this day's warmth and brightness. I ask whether the autumn fragrance is full yet—waiting to lead my companions out the western wall. Just so my traveler's breast holds many feelings; I dread the wilderness tower's height—I could not bear the feeling. Before the wine-cup I remember again the one who sprinkled wine and tucked flowers; only at the seats—there are no old comrades left. Desolate. Light-drunk, then awake again; the grief will not level with my poems. I remember galloping along the tall catalpas, the carved bow shooting at the willows—the former affairs, leave them unjudged. The purple dogwood, one spray bestowed—in dream, who reaches the Han house's tombs? Let the black gauze cap go with the wind if it will; I would have Heaven know: my flowered hair stands now so starry. The song done, the tears fall.
translations.songci-300-256: Cold the dream in the golden house. I sigh at the Qin zheng—in the slanting wild-goose ranks, the plain strings dust-blown. She changed into a tender oriole and flew home; she still knows the old green of the gauze window. Just passing the rain—the hedge-peaches are like beans. This grievance is hard to level—do you know, my lord?—like the chessboard surging up at the Jasper Terrace. Her thinning shadow—she begrudges the bright candle. The mandarin-duck tower's east-and-west jade smashed and spilled. I ask her fragrant heart: when will it unfold again? The kingfisher hairpin is hard to cast. I would take the palace-brow, horizontal like the clouds, and paint it upon a length of plain silk—I fear it is not her new-style makeup. The colored fan and red ivory clapper are both still here—hateful that no one understands to hear the Kaiyuan tune. In vain she hides her sleeves, leaning on the cold bamboo.
translations.songci-300-257: The orchid's fragrance wafts. Snow cleared, the pool-side halls are like a painting. The spring wind flies to Treasure-Hairpin Tower; a whole stretch of pipes and reeds; the glassy light shoots forth. Today the lanterns hang at random—not the dark dust and bright moon of that year's festival night. Worse, year by year the heart turns lazy and timid, shamed to vie with the little moth-knots for favor. River city, the people hushed; the first watch sounds. Let me ask: who understands all that splendor—could one borrow it again from the Lord of Heaven? Picking at the dying red wick. Only in dreams, faint and dim, the jeweled carriage, the gauze kerchief. On the Wu paper, silver-powdered—wait till I write the old homeland's scene into idle talk. I laugh: the green-tressed neighbor girl leans at her window still singing, 'The slanting sun sinks west.'
translations.songci-300-258: The dark smoke hides the wild geese's tracks. Gradually the broken drums and scattered bells fade; the street's uproar first dies down. The wind-lamp backs against the cold wall; it lets the ice-toad fly in, thread by thread through the window-gaps. The jasper gems weep unseen. I think of the homeland—the frosted weeds woven thick. Carelessly I turn my body into a crane returning home, forgetting wholly the truth of my old rovings. Joy at its height. In Penglai's lotus-steeped pools, the pear-melt of the flower courts, drunk through the spring evenings. The Que-axe game stopped; the cherries remain—the dream, hard to find. I beg the clear light: rather keep the dark window company; do not shine on the red tower's night flute. I fear among mortals the tune has changed to the Yi-Liang style—the moon lady has not learned it yet.
translations.songci-300-259: I remember the Jade Pass—treading snow in pure excursion; the chill air brittle in my sable coat. By the withered woods of the old road, watering the horses at the long river—this thought drifts on and on. A short dream, still on the river's surface; my old tears spill at Xizhou. Not a single word could I inscribe where I passed—the falling leaves all grieving. Carrying the white clouds home with me, I ask: who keeps the Chu pendant, toying with its shadow mid-isle? I break a reed-blossom to send afar—fallen, all autumn in my person. Toward the ordinary wild bridge and flowing water, wait till I call them over—they are not the old sandbar gulls. Vainly I hold this feeling: at the place of the slanting sun, I fear instead to climb the tower.
translations.songci-300-260: The mountains empty, the sky sinks into the sea; leaning on the tower I gaze to the limit—the wind urgent, the evening tide first rising. One blind beyond the dove's call, the rain; a few patches of idle fields—across the waters stir the spring hoes. The new smoke, the forbidden willows: I imagine by now they green all the way to West Lake. I still remember: the deep seclusion of those years, the gate shut against two or three trees. I am full of gloom. The waste isle, the old channel; broken stem, scattered duckweed—further drifting, to what place? In vain I feel it myself: the girdle ashamed, its width shrunk; the shadow timid, the lamp lone. Often I suspect I shall soon see her peach-blossom face—but lately, perversely, she laughs: not a single letter. Letters even if far—how could there be none at all?
translations.songci-300-261: The Chu river, empty, at nightfall. Desolate—parted from the flock ten thousand li, in a daze startled and scattered. Watching its own shadow, about to drop to the cold pool—just then the sands are clean, the grass withered, the waters level, the sky far. It cannot write its message into formation—it sends only a single dot of longing. I reckon its dawdling has betrayed it: the remnant felt hugging snow, an old friend's heart and eye. Who pities the traveler's gloom as it drags on? Vainly, at Everlasting Gate in the night's stillness, the brocade zheng plucks its grievance. I imagine its companions still lodging among the reed-flowers—they too must think that before spring the homeward leg should turn. Calling to each other in the evening rain—I fear that suddenly at Jade Pass we meet again. It would not be shamed before the pair of swallows' return, the painted blind half-rolled.
translations.songci-300-262: Ten thousand li of lone cloud; the pure excursion grows ever farther—where is my old friend? In the cold window, within my dream, I still remember the old roads I once traveled. The willows of Lianchang are, roughly, not many left; the first and worst is the night rain, hard to hear. Vainly startled back into chill stillness, we look at each other by the candle-shadow—hugging the quilt, who is there to speak with? Zhang Xu—why so late in coming home? Half scattered and fallen—the Broken Bridge's gulls and egrets linger still. The weary traveler at the sky's end: at this moment the heart's affairs are truly bitter. I only dread to spill Xizhou tears again; let me ask: the Du-Quarter households—do they still live? I fear that in her kingfisher sleeves, just now in the sky's cold, she leans still on that plum tree.
translations.songci-300-263: The new moon, lovely and clear; the night chill, the river still, the mountains hold the Dipper. Rising, I scratch my head—the plum-shadow lies lean across the window. Fine is this frosty sky—but idle now are the cup-passing hands. Do you know? After the jumbled crows' crying, the wish to go home runs thicker than wine.
translations.songci-300-264: Waking, the orioles are chattering. Veiling the green moss, the lattices turn toward evening; ruined red beyond counting. The last blossoms blown away, no one sees; only the drooping willows dance on their own. Gradually the warm haze first turns back on light summer. The precious fan seeks again the bright moon's shadow; the dark dust invades—still there is the maiden who rides the luan. Startled—the old grief, sudden as this. The Jiangnan dream breaks off at the river-crossing isle. The waves stick to the sky, the grape-vines swelling green; half the sky is mist and rain. The boundless meaning of the grey waves before the tower—who plucks the duckweed-blossoms to send? Only gazing in despondence: the orchid boat drifts slow, slow. When will the cloud-sail of ten thousand li arrive? Seeing off the lone swan, my eyes break at a thousand mountains' barring. Who will sing for me the 'Gold-Threaded' song?
translations.songci-300-265: The fallen blossoms already dance in the wind ahead of it—and then they see off the dusk rain too. At dawn the courtyard is half ruined red; only the drifting gossamer, a thousand fathoms, hangs in the clear sky. Earnest, beneath the blossoms we once held hands—draining still the wine within the cup. My fair one need not knit her moth-brows: I too am full of feeling, helpless at the wine's running out.
translations.songci-300-266: The dawn light hurries the horn. I listen: the night-roosting birds not yet startled, the neighbor's cocks wake first. Winding on, the misty village; the horses neigh, the men rise; the waning moon still threads the thin woods. The tear-traces, frost-touched, slightly congeal; the wine's strength against the chill still weak. I sigh, the weary traveler: quietly I cannot bear to be stained again with the wind and dust of the capital. I recall: since the parting of the one I love, the heart's affairs ten thousand layers—hard to find a lone swan to entrust. The kingfisher blind's dainty depth; the curved screen's fragrant warmth—who thinks of the drifting in the year's cold? The moon-grievance, flower-hatred vexation—not that I have not known them. This savor: I had hoped it would lessen by a tenth; newly come, it has grown worse.
translations.songci-300-267: The new moon, lovely and clear; the night chill, the river still, the mountains hold the Dipper. Rising, I scratch my head—the plum-shadow lies lean across the window. Fine is this frosty sky—but idle now are the cup-passing hands. Do you know? After the jumbled crows' crying, the wish to go home runs thicker than wine.
translations.songci-300-268: Washed of its makeup, its true face—wearing no lead-white powder. One branch slanting beyond the bamboo—I imagine my fair one at dusk in the sky's cold. In the small courtyard at dusk, nowhere for its clear scent to settle: the wind fine, fine; the snow hanging, hanging—much less the road by the river's head. The sparse shadow at the moon's edge—the place my dream melts away. When its fruit sets, turning yellow, again it must face the fine, lingering rain. Its lone fragrance all its life supplies the longing-grief of the tender-hearted: worn thinner even than Dongyang—let me ask the blossom, does it know?
translations.songci-300-269: I see the pear-blossoms just wearing the night moon; the crabapples half holding the morning rain. The inner garden's spring—one cannot help its passing the Green Gate; the imperial moat rises, secretly joining the southern shore. The east wind still; the slender willows hang their gold threads. Gazing toward the phoenix watch-towers—not mist, not haze. A fine age: court and country full of joy; through all the nine avenues, pipes and drums of peace. Suddenly the orioles' hundred turns, breaking off and resuming; the swallows fly back and forth. By the green waters the terraces mirror the swings; the grass-game gathers, the paired outing girls. The malt-sugar's scent, the cold wine along the greening road. One learns unawares the crimson-gated house of the lovely peach. Toward evening, suddenly—the jewel-horses and carved saddles; the drunken lapels catch the flying floss of jumbled blossoms. Just the light chill, the light warmth, the long clepsydra; half overcast, half clear, the clouds at dusk. On the fire-forbidden day, already they try the new makeup; the year's splendor reaches its third part of best. At Pure Brightness watch: the Han palace passes out its candles; the kingfisher smoke scatters, flying into the Locust mansions. The guards stand down; the Changhe gates open; halting the relayed decrees—again the offices rest.
translations.songci-300-270: The jade terrace hangs the autumn moon. The lead-white light, faint; the plum-blossoms daub their fragrant snow. The ice-pure grace; the gold lotus-feet shod in the tiny wave-treading gauze socks. The rain first ceases. Beyond the tower the lone swan's voice fades far; beyond the far mountains the traveler's word and tidings are cut. This regret: even facing it with words is hard—how much more, to tell it in a sent letter? It makes a person's red waste and green dwindle; I feel my gown's gold threads grow wide—all for that light parting. Too deep runs the feeling. The soul-melting place: the painted horn's dusk-hour. The sound sobs and chokes. The courtyard's blossoms all fall—spring has gone; the silver toad remote, heartless, rounds and wanes again. I hate her: she is not like the leftover scent, teasing the mandarin-duck knot.
translations.songci-300-271: End of the red-railed bridge, the fragrant street runs straight. Caging the street, the slender willows, delicate and strengthless. Gold and kingfisher scale the blue sky; the blossoms clear, the curtain-shadows red. The yellow-coated rider flies his white horse; day after day below the green towers. Wine-drunk eyes meet no one; the noon incense blows the dim dust.
translations.songci-300-272: Green creepers wall round the mossy courtyard. In the central court the sun's light is pale; the banana-leaves roll. Butterflies fly up the steps; the warmed curtain hangs at ease. The jade hooks—pair of swallows, chattering; the precious well-curb turns with the poplar-floss. Here and there the coin-tossing sounds; by the green window the spring sleep lies light.
translations.songci-300-273: A single dot of remnant red, about to burn out. Suddenly the cool autumn air fills screen and curtain. On the parasol leaves, the third-watch rain—leaf after leaf, sound after sound, all of it is parting. I tune the precious se; I stir the golden lion. In those days we sang together the partridge song. Now, on the west tower in wind and rain—the clear song I do not hear, and still the tears fall.
translations.songci-300-274: Feeling like drifting gossamer; a person like flying floss. The tear-pearls, held fast in the eye, gaze in vain. One stream of misty willows, ten thousand threads hang—no way to tie fast the orchid boat. The geese cross the slanting sun; the grass hides the misty isle. Already the griefs are beyond counting. Tomorrow I shall try not to think at all—but how shall I get through tonight?
translations.songci-300-275: Year after year on the altar day the needlework rests. How can one bear to see the paired flying swallows? Today in River City spring is already half gone. My whole person still lies deep in the jumbled mountains, beside the lone bridge on the silent stream. My spring gown worn to rags—whose needlework now? Dot by dot, line by line, the tear-tracks fill it. The sinking sun: I loose my saddle by the fragrant-grass bank. Blossoms—no one to wear them; wine—no one to press me; drunk as I am, no one minds.
translations.songci-300-276: The tower's shade, notched. The railing's shadow lies in the east-wing moon. East-wing moon: one whole sky of wind and dew; the apricot blossoms like snow. Through the mist the clepsydra urges the golden-dragon's sob. The gauze curtains dark; the lamp-flower knots. Lamp-flower knots: a moment's spring dream—the Jiangnan sky, wide.
translations.songci-300-277: The evening clears, the wind rests. One night's spring folds its might. Tenderly, the sparse blossoms in the pale sky; the clouds come and go—a few sprays of snow. Beauty supreme; grief supreme. This feeling—with whom can I share it? Only the two low lines of geese know: a person leans in the moon at the painted tower.
translations.songci-300-278: The sun's feet swim in a floating of purple mist; the lovely warmth breaks through the light fur. The sky's hue drowsies a person; the blossoms' breath intoxicates; the noon dream lifts my head. The spring languor is just like the spring-pond's water—a single stretch of rippled-silk grief. Melt-melt, drifting-drifting; the east wind strengthless—about to wrinkle, then resting.
translations.songci-300-279: Long I cherish, gazing to the breaking: the passes and ramparts run wild and flat. The campaign-dust dark; the frost-wind keen; the frontier sounds hushed. Dim, my melting gaze. I chase the affairs of those years: surely Heaven's decree, not human power—the banks of Zhu and Si, the lands of lute-and-song, were rank with barbarian stench too. Across the waters the felt-country; beneath the sinking sun the cattle and sheep come down; the border-pickets crisscross. I watch the famed prince's night hunt—the riders' fires light a whole river bright; the reeds and drums mourn and cry. They startle a man. I think of the arrows at my waist, the sword in its case: in vain the dust and moths—what have they ever achieved? The time slips easily away; the heart is strong in vain; the year's end approaches. The divine capital dim. With shield-and-feathers they just now court the far ones; the beacon-fires rest quiet for now—the arms at rest. The envoys in caps and canopies gallop off in swarms—how can that sit with feeling? I hear the old folks left in the Central Plain ever gaze south, toward the feather-canopied, rainbow-bannered host. Let any traveler come to this place: loyal wrath fills his breast; the tears pour like rain.
translations.songci-300-280: Dongting's green grass: near the Mid-Autumn, again not a breath of wind in the scene. A jade mirror, a jasper field, thirty thousand qing—bearing my single leaf of a boat. The plain moon divides its radiance; the bright river shares its image; within and without, all clear and bright. Calmly the heart comprehends—the wonder of it is hard to tell you. You should remember: year upon year at the ridge and sea, the lone light shining on itself, my liver and lungs all ice and snow. The short hair, sparse and windswept; lapel and sleeves cold—steadily I drift the grey waves' vast emptiness. I drink the West River dry; I ladle with the Northern Dipper fine; the ten thousand images are my guests. I beat the boat's side, laughing alone—I know not what evening this evening is.
translations.tangshi-300-321: Sunlight on Incense Burner Peak raises violet mist; from afar, the waterfall hangs before the river. Its flying torrent drops three thousand feet—perhaps the Milky Way has fallen from the ninth heaven.
translations.songci-300-281: Seen head-on, Mount Lu is a range; from the side, a peak. Near or far, high or low, it is never the same. I cannot know its true face only because I am within the mountain itself.
translations.songci-300-282: On a clear day, West Lake's waters glitter beautifully; in rain, the mountains are misty and marvellous too. If West Lake were compared to Xi Shi, light or rich adornment would suit her equally well.
translations.songci-300-283: I often remember that dusk at the creek pavilion, so drunk I forgot the way home. Returning by boat after the pleasure had run its course, I drifted by mistake into deep lotus blooms. Row, row—startling a whole sandbank of gulls and egrets into flight.
